chunk_findings.detail: The change documents the escape hatch for a large diff as `--delta` in both user-facing places — the config docstring ("`--delta` asks for one delta whatever the default (for a very large diff)") and the driver template ("`--delta` sends only the commits since the reviewed head") — while the stated intent for this change says delta-only "remains available, with `--delta-only`". Both cannot be true: either the CLI flag is `--delta-only` and every operator who follows these two documents types `--delta` and gets an "unknown option" error exactly when the diff is too large for a full re-review (the one case the flag exists for), or the flag is `--delta` and the change description is wrong. Since the new docs are the only guidance for the newly-introduced `--delta` path, the flag name must be made to match the implemented parser before this ships.

chunk_findings.detail: The help text and driver doc advertise the delta-only escape hatch as `--delta` ("`--delta` reviews only the commits since the head that review covered"), while the change's own stated design names that flag `--delta-only` ("Delta-only remains available, with `--delta-only`, for very large diffs"). A user who follows the new help text and runs `ddflow review <ID> --gate G --delta` on a diff too large to send twice will hit an unknown/unsupported option (or select nothing) instead of the delta-only round the design says exists. The `mcp_instructions.md` edit compounds this by exposing the same mode as `delta=true` without the tool side ever being described as `--delta`; whichever of the two names is authoritative, one of the three edited documents is now wrong about the user-facing interface.

chunk_findings.detail: `prior` is the value produced by `_announce_rerun(rerun, revs, item, gate, say)` on the line above, and it is the same variable the delta path uses to "merge into the record" the findings of the earlier review — i.e. it is truthy exactly when a previous review of this gate exists. The guard at the top of `_with_previous_findings` is `if kind != "full" or rerun or it is None: return context`, so passing `prior` there short-circuits precisely in the situation the function was written for: a full re-review of an item that already has gate findings. Concretely, re-run `ddflow review` on an item whose gate already recorded findings (`kind == "full"`, `_last_review(...)["chunk_findings"]` non-empty, triage present, `it` not None); the `or rerun` branch fires because `prior` is truthy/non-empty, `_with_previous_findings` returns the original `context`, and the reviewer is never shown the previous findings or their triage. That defeats the stated intent (D-gate-economy 3: a re-review must send the whole diff plus the previous findings), so the new code is effectively dead for every re-review. Note the actual rerun flag (`rerun`, the enclosing argument already in scope) is not what is being passed here; the guard should be fed that flag, or `_with_previous_findings` should not treat "a previous review exists" as "this is a chunk re-run".
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/review.py:1154 — `_with_previous_findings(..., rerun=prior)`

chunk_findings.detail: The change describes the escape hatch as `--delta-only` ("Delta-only remains available, with --delta-only, for very large diffs"), but both doc surfaces added here call it `--delta`: the config doc says "`--delta` asks for one delta whatever the default (for a very large diff)" and the template says "`--delta` sends only the commits since the reviewed head ... for a diff too large to send twice". These parentheticals ("for a very large diff" / "for a diff too large") identify the same flag the intent names `--delta-only`, so one of the two names is wrong. If the CLI option is `--delta-only` (as the intent states), then a user following the documented plain re-review workflow on a large diff runs `ddflow review <ID> --gate G --delta`, which the argument parser rejects as an unknown option, and no delta is produced; if instead the option really is `--delta`, the intent's naming is wrong and the operator/agent instructions shipped in the template point at a flag that does not exist. Either way the reviewed text and the stated feature disagree on the user-visible CLI surface, so at least one of these two documented invocations is unusable.

chunk_findings.detail: The rewritten help text tells the operator that a delta re-review is requested with `ddflow review <id> --gate G --delta` ("`--delta` reviews only the commits since the head that review covered"), and the driver doc repeats it ("`--delta` sends only the commits since the reviewed head"). This change's own specification names that flag `--delta-only`: "Delta-only remains available, with `--delta-only`, for very large diffs." If the CLI registers `--delta-only` (as specified) and not `--delta`, then the exact scenario this text exists for — a diff too large to send twice — is the one where following the help text fails: `ddflow review <id> --gate G --delta` exits with an unrecognized-argument error, and the operator has no delta escape hatch from the newly-full default round. Either both docs must say `--delta-only`, or the spec's flag name is wrong; as written the shipped help text documents a flag the change was not specified to add.

data.body:
For a diff under [review].combined_under_lines (default 150), ddflow review --gate rubber_duck,critic sends ONE request whose prompt covers both lenses and records the outcome for both gates, with the shared review id in evidence. Larger diffs keep both reviews, run in parallel. The round limit (max_rounds 2) also bounds delta rounds. After it, the gate is passed-on-refutation (flagged, D-unify 5) when every finding has a probe, or escalated to the operator.

Split into: B-gate-econ-review-combined, B-gate-econ-review-budget, B-gate-econ-review-refutation.

The one-gate review is unchanged and reused for both paths; diff measurement reuses diff_for/commit_diff.

chunk_findings.detail: `_any_out_of_rounds` is called only with `asked[1:]`, so the first gate's budget is never consulted when choosing the combined path. Input: `gate="rubber_duck,critic"`, a diff with `0 < lines < under`, rubber_duck already at its round limit and critic still in budget. `_any_out_of_rounds(..., ["critic"], ...)` returns False, so `_review_combined` runs and calls `_review_gate(gate="rubber_duck")`; that call is refused on budget, so `st.items[item].gates["rubber_duck"].evidence["review_id"] != rid` and the `for g in asked[1:]` loop is skipped entirely. The requested `critic` review is then neither run nor recorded (the returned outcome is just rubber_duck's refusal), even though critic had budget. The docstring's own contract — that out-of-rounds gates are refused "on its own" while the others still run — only holds when the gate lacking budget is not the first one; excluding `asked[0]` from the check silently drops every later gate whenever the first gate is exhausted.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/review.py `_review_gates` / `_any_out_of_rounds` (`asked[1:]`)

chunk_findings.detail: The filter distinguishes file-header lines from content lines purely by prefix, but a content line can itself begin with `+`/`-`. Input: a diff that adds the C/JS line `++counter;` — the emitted diff line is `+` + `++counter;` = `+++counter;`, which is discarded as if it were a `+++ b/file` header; likewise removing a line `-- counter` or a SQL/Ada/Haskell comment `-- note` yields `---note`, discarded as a `--- a/file` header. Each such line is subtracted twice from `lines`, so the count is wrong; e.g. with `combined_under_lines = 5` and exactly 5 changed lines one of which is `-- note`, `lines` computes 4 and the code takes `_review_combined` (one shared review) where the true count would have selected `_review_parallel` (one review per gate), which is the behaviour the threshold exists to control.

chunk_findings.detail: The docstring promises "one reviewer request whose intent names every gate's lens", but the appended instruction hardcodes the two lens names: "(rubber_duck)" for refutation and "(critic)" for criticism, regardless of `asked`. The function is reached for any comma-separated gate list from the CLI (gate names come from `GD.load_gates`), so for input `gate="rubber_duck,arbiter"` the single request tells the reviewer to apply rubber_duck's and critic's lenses and never describes `arbiter`'s, and the same (possibly wrong) text is recorded as the evidence/intent for both gates' records in the `for g in asked[1:]` loop. The combined review is recorded for every requested gate while only ever instructing the two hardcoded lenses.

chunk_findings.detail: The out-of-rounds probe deliberately skips the first gate, so the first gate's exhausted budget does not trigger the per-gate fallback — yet the combined review *is* recorded under that first gate, so the first gate's refusal poisons the whole call. Concretely: `combined_under_lines = 200`, a diff of 5 changed lines, an item where `rubber_duck` has already used its last round and `critic` has full budget, and `--gate rubber_duck,critic`. `lines = 5` satisfies `0 < 5 < 200`, and `_any_out_of_rounds(log, cfg, item, ["critic"], args)` is `False` because only `asked[1:]` is inspected, so `_review_combined` is taken. Inside, `_review_gate(gate="rubber_duck", ...)` refuses (out of rounds) and therefore records nothing, so `rec = st.items[item].gates.get("rubber_duck")` is the *previous* record and `rec.evidence.get("review_id") == rid` is false; the `if` body is skipped and `critic` is never invoked at all — the caller gets only rubber_duck's refusal. The docstring of `_review_gates` promises the opposite for exhausted gates ("then each gate runs, and is refused, on its own"), and the dispatcher docstring promises "one review per gate" whenever the combined path is not taken. If instead `_review_gate` records refusals, the second branch of the bug appears: because the refusal record carries the shared `review_id`, `asked[1:]` are then recorded with the *refusal* outcome, marking `critic` as exhausted/refused even though it had budget. Either way `critic` is not reviewed as promised. The condition needs to consider every gate in `asked` (i.e. `asked`, not `asked[1:]`), so that an exhausted first gate falls through to `_review_parallel` and the remaining gates still run.

chunk_findings.detail:
The new paragraph states the fallback for a big diff: "A larger change runs one review per gate, one after the other." That directly contradicts the stated intent of the change, which is that "larger diffs run both reviews in parallel." Concretely, for `ddflow review T1 --gate rubber_duck,critic` on a diff of, say, 200 changed lines (≥ `review.combined_under_lines`, so the combined path is not taken), the reviewed behavior is two reviewer requests issued concurrently, while the README just added tells the user the two reviews happen sequentially ("one after the other"). A user reasoning about the documented contract — e.g. assuming only one reviewer agent is ever live at a time, or reasoning about ordering of the two gates' outputs — is misled by the text shipped in this diff. Either the README should say the two reviews run in parallel, or the intent/implementation is wrong and the diff's fallback is actually sequential; as given, the doc and the described behavior cannot both be true.

(Note for the earlier HIGH finding on `_review_gates` / `_any_out_of_rounds`: the same paragraph now documents that "a pair where either gate is out of rounds" runs per gate rather than combined, which is the behavior that finding asked for, so it is not re-raised here.)

chunk_findings.detail:
The diff changes the call site to `_any_out_of_rounds(log, cfg, item, asked, args)` and the probe function now iterates `for g in gates`, so the first gate is no longer skipped. That part of the prior finding is addressed, but the guard still does not fire, and the author's own probe records the exact bad outcome ("rubber_duck at max_rounds, critic in budget: the combined path ran and critic was never reviewed").

The remaining defect is the round count handed to `_budget`. `_any_out_of_rounds` passes `_full_rounds(log, item, g)` — the number of full rounds *already completed*. But the review it is trying to authorize is the *next* full round; the same diff computes that prospective round as `done + 1` in `_rounds_for` (`"round": done + 1`). So when `rubber_duck` has consumed exactly its `max_rounds` (i.e. `_full_rounds == max_rounds`), `_budget(cfg, item, "rubber_duck", max_rounds, ...)` does not flag it (the actual refusal is for the `max_rounds + 1`-th round), `_any_out_of_rounds` returns `False`, and `_review_combined` is entered.

Concrete failure: `[review].combined_under_lines = 200`, a diff with 5 changed lines, `--gate rubber_duck,critic`, an item where `rubber_duck` is at its last round and `critic` is in budget. `lines = 5` satisfies `0 < 5 < 200`; `_any_out_of_rounds` checks `rubber_duck` with `_full_rounds = max_rounds`, sees no refusal, and returns `False`, so the combined path runs. Inside it, `_review_gate(gate="rubber_duck", full=True)` performs the real (prospective) budget check, refuses, and returns `unavailable`; the `elif item and out.data.get("outcome") == "unavailable"` branch then records `critic = unavailable` via `GD.record` without ever reviewing it. The fix (replacing `asked[1:]` with `asked`) is necessary but not sufficient: the argument passed to `_budget` must be the round being authorized (`_full_rounds(...) + 1`), otherwise the gate sitting at the limit is still judged in budget and poisons the whole combined call.

chunk_findings.detail: The earlier finding still holds, by the author's own triage. The triage line reads `confirmed -- probe: rubber_duck at max_rounds, critic in budget: the combined path ran and critic was never reviewed`. A probe that answers a *fixed* finding would have to show the opposite result — that with one gate exhausted the combined path is suppressed and the still-in-budget gate is reviewed on its own. Instead the probe records exactly the failure the finding describes: `--gate rubber_duck,critic` on a diff smaller than `combined_under_lines`, with `rubber_duck` at `max_rounds` and `critic` in budget, runs the combined request and `critic` is never reviewed. That is what happens when the out-of-rounds check still skips the first gate (`asked[1:]`): the combined review is recorded under the first gate, the first gate's refusal poisons the shared call, and the second gate loses its round without ever being reviewed. The fix (consulting all requested gates, including the first, before taking the combined path) is not present in this part, and the probe does not demonstrate it, so the defect remains.

chunk_findings.detail: The new umbrella fast-path returns `_complete_umbrella(...)` directly, before the function reaches `extra.update(_commit_events(log, cfg, f"complete {item}"))` (line ~173 in the new file). `_complete_umbrella` only does `log.append("item.completed", ...)` and `L.release(log, ...)`, and the auto path (`_complete_umbrellas_above`, called just above the commit) relies on that same outer `_commit_events` call to flush the appended events — that is why it re-folds via `fold(log.read_all())` rather than a commit. So the manual route is the only completion path that appends events and never commits them. Concretely: run `ddflow complete B-uni-fsio-writers` on an already-settled umbrella (its three sub-tasks merged and DONE, umbrella still open). `_require` passes, `_settled_umbrella` is true, `_complete_umbrella` appends the `item.completed` record and the lease release to the in-memory event log, returns `O.ok(...)`, and the handler returns without committing. The command reports success, but the appended events are never written, so a fresh `fold(log.read_all())` in the next process still sees the umbrella as open — the exact symptom the change is supposed to remove (`next` keeps offering it, `complete` can be re-run indefinitely) — and the released lease is likewise not durably recorded. The same omission also skips waking/refreshing and, because `_complete_umbrella` never re-enters `_complete_umbrellas_above` for the umbrella it just closed, a settled parent umbrella above it is left open even though the state that just made it settled was already applied. The auto path hides this because its events are committed by the caller; the fallback path the intent explicitly promises ("complete accepts an umbrella whose descendants are all settled") is the one that silently loses its own writes.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/lifecycle/complete.py:65 (`complete()` early return for `_settled_umbrella`)

chunk_findings.detail: The intent states two expected outcomes: the umbrella becomes completable, **and** `next never offers a settled umbrella`. The regression suite only verifies the first. `test_a_settled_umbrella_completes_without_a_pipeline_of_its_own` deliberately constructs the exact pre-existing state (both children done, umbrella untouched) and then asserts `_state(repo, "P.T") == "open"` before calling `complete P.T`. That assertion is direct evidence that an all-children-done umbrella keeps its own state at `open`; since `next` surfaces open items, this is precisely the item the bug report says was offered as `Next: ..., B-uni-fsio-writers`. Nothing in the change exercises `next` in this state, so the "next never offers a settled umbrella" half of the promise is unverified, and for an already-degraded repo (the B-uni-fsio-writers case the bug was filed against) an upgraded binary would still offer the umbrella as ready work until someone explicitly runs `complete P.T`. Either `next` gained filtering logic that no test covers, or the second half of the stated fix is absent; the tests cannot distinguish the two.

chunk_findings.detail: The stated intent has two outcomes: an all-children-done umbrella becomes completable **and** `next` never offers a settled umbrella. This diff only implements the first. The umbrella is left with its own state untouched until something explicitly calls `complete` on it (the fast path here, or the auto chain in `_complete_umbrellas_above` on the last child's completion), which means for any legacy/observed state like B-uni-fsio-writers (children `.1/.2/.3` merged before this change), `next` still presents the settled umbrella as ready work. The regression suite (`tests/test_umbrella_completes.py::test_a_settled_umbrella_completes_without_a_pipeline_of_its_own`) deliberately rebuilds exactly that pre-existing state, asserts `_state(repo, "P.T") == "open"`, and then calls `complete P.T` — i.e. it asserts the umbrella is *still* offered as open and only verifies the completability half. The triage note ("filed B797aff72d8") is a deferral, not a fix or a probe, so the second promised outcome still does not hold in this change: given children all done and no umbrella pipeline run, `next` still lists the umbrella.

chunk_findings.detail: The fast path returns `_complete_umbrella(...)` before the code that processes `regression_test`, so any bugs listed there are silently not closed. Input: `complete U --regression-test tests/test_x.py` where `U` is an umbrella whose descendants are all settled. The function matches `_settled_umbrella` and returns `O.ok("item.completed", …, bugs_closed=[])` with a success outcome, never computing `closing`/running the close logic. The caller sees success (and `forced=False` even if `--force` was passed, which the fast path also discards) while the requested regression test never closes the bug — a silent no-op that reports as done.

chunk_findings.detail: The stated intent has two halves: an all-children-done umbrella must become completable, **and** `next` must never offer a settled umbrella. This change only delivers the first half, and this test file is direct evidence of the gap rather than a check against it. chunk_findings.detail: `_is_settled_umbrella` decides "settled" from `any(state.items[i].state == DONE for i in below)` — i.e. "at least one sub-task is done", not "the sub-tasks are all done". Its only safety net is that `plan_blocker` reaches it after the `_is_umbrella` branch (the `kids`/`Work those; this closes when they do` return just above) has already returned for items with *open* descendants, so the code silently assumes that "has no open descendant" is equivalent to "every descendant is DONE". That equivalence is never established anywhere, and it is false as soon as a descendant is terminal-but-not-DONE (dropped/abandoned) — precisely the states the docstring's "at least one done" clause presupposes exist alongside DONE. Concretely: take umbrella `P.T` with sub-tasks `P.T.a` DONE and `P.T.b` dropped. `_is_umbrella(P.T)` is `False` (`P.T.b` is settled, not open), so control falls through to the new branch; `_is_settled_umbrella` returns `True` because `P.T.a` is DONE, and `next` reports `P.T` blocked with detail `its sub-tasks are all done: ddflow complete P.T completes it with them` — a false statement that instructs the user to close an umbrella that still has an un-done sub-task. Symmetrically, an umbrella whose sub-tasks are *all* dropped matches neither branch (no open descendants, no DONE descendant), so `plan_blocker` falls through and `next` still offers it as ready work, i.e. the exact B797aff72d8 shape survives for that input. The added regression test only completes both children (`P.T.a` and `P.T.b`), so it cannot distinguish this case and does not pin down the predicate's contract.

Fixes bug B5035a55092: The event-log reader splits lines with str.splitlines(), which also breaks on U+2028, U+2029, U+0085, \x1c-\x1e, \x0b, \x0c and \r. canonical() writes JSON with ensure_ascii=False, so an event whose text contains one of them (a pasted prompt with a Unicode line separator) is cut in two on read: both halves are unparseable, the event is silently lost from every fold, and doctor reports a 'torn append'. Probe: EventLog.append('session.note','s',{'text':'line sep'}) then read_all() -> the note is missing, skipped_lines == 2. infra/log.py _parse_lines. Data damage: logs already holding such lines are mended by the fixed reader alone (FOLD_ONLY entry in services/repairs). Found on B-upgrade.5-repairs.

chunk_findings.detail: The handler's whole purpose is to record, per repair, the identity of the findings that were settled so that `detect` does not offer them again ("so the same findings are never offered again", "second run finds nothing"). The key list is filtered to `str` and only accepted when `keys` is a `list`; any other key type is silently dropped and an empty list is recorded. The presence of the `isinstance(k, str)` guard shows the author anticipated non-string keys, yet dropping them is exactly the wrong action for a dedup key set: the finding's key never lands in `repairs_applied[rid]["findings"]`, so `services.repairs` judges it unsettled on the next run, re-offers it, and `repair` appends a *second* corrective event for damage it already annotated/quarantined. Concretely, take the seed "torn / mismatched-id lines" repair, where a torn line is most naturally keyed by its byte offset / line number (an int, or a tuple `(offset, id)`): detecting the crafted old-version fixture, applying the repair, then re-running gives findings again instead of nothing, and the byte-identical original lines get an extra quarantine note each run. The same holds if the writer ever emits `findings` as a tuple or set rather than a list. Either drop the type filter (record keys verbatim / `str(k)`) or make the writer and the handler agree on a single canonical key type, otherwise the recorded state cannot reliably suppress re-application.

chunk_findings.detail: `integrity` is documented to return `(problems, notes)` and to downgrade already-quarantined damage to a note rather than a hard failure. It carefully wraps the torn-line detector in `try/except Unavailable` and converts that into a problem entry a few lines later, but the preceding `_split(ctx, MISMATCHED)` call is left unguarded. `Unavailable` exists in `base` precisely for detectors that cannot run, and this module's own `_detect` catches it for *every* registry repair, including `MISMATCHED`. So if the mismatch detector cannot check the log (raises `Unavailable`, e.g. the same kind of I/O failure the torn detector is explicitly protected against), the exception propagates straight out of `integrity` and crashes `ddflow doctor`, instead of yielding the documented problem/note result — while the identical failure in its sibling detector is handled. Demonstrated input: any doctor run in which `MISMATCHED.detect(ctx)` raises `Unavailable` → `integrity` raises rather than returning `(problems, notes)`.

chunk_findings.detail: `plan_adoptions` is presented as the pure, reusable preview entry point ("pure, so `services.repairs` can show them before writing") and its `cfg` parameter is made optional with `cfg: Config | None = None`. However, in the one branch where `cfg` is actually consumed — the `else` branch taken when there are no `session.started` events — it calls `new_session_id(cfg, events)`. Before this refactor the only call site was `new_session_id(_cfg_of(log), events)`, i.e. `new_session_id` was only ever handed a real `Config`; nothing in the diff shows `new_session_id` gaining tolerance for `None`. So a caller exercising the newly advertised one-argument form, e.g. a `detect(state, log)` hook doing `plan_adoptions(log.read_all())` on a log that has orphans but no sessions, passes `cfg=None` into `new_session_id` and raises (`AttributeError`/`TypeError`) exactly in the orphan-with-no-session case this repair is meant to fix, instead of returning the planned implicit `session.started` plus the adoption copy. `adopt_orphans` happens to dodge this because it passes `_cfg_of(log)`, which is why the defect is invisible in the one in-file caller, but the default value makes the public pure API unsafe for the use the docstring advertises. Either require `cfg` (no default) or have `new_session_id` explicitly handle `None`.

chunk_findings.detail: The damage set fed to this test includes the line-repair fixtures (`_torn` writes two damaged lines, `_mismatched` writes one). The unnamed `R.apply(...)` on line ~190 applies the agent-consent repairs, so `unreadable-lines` and `mismatched-ids` both run. By design those repairs do **not** delete anything — they record a quarantine and leave the damaged lines in place (that is exactly what the sibling test `test_doctor_turns_quarantined_damage_into_a_note` asserts: after the same two repairs are applied to the same `old` fixture it expects the repairs-subsystem note `"3 damaged log line(s) quarantined by a data repair, left in place"`). After all repairs have run in this test the two torn lines plus the mismatched line are still physically in `old-agent.jsonl`, so the doctor must still surface that quarantine note; `R.doctor_notes(_ctx(old))` cannot be the empty list. Either this assertion (which would fail on any implementation where quarantine notes are reported through the repair module, as `test_a_detector_that_cannot_run_is_unavailable_not_clean` shows for the other repair-status note) or the expectation in `test_doctor_turns_quarantined_damage_into_a_note` is wrong; they cannot both hold.

chunk_findings.detail: The parametrization includes `\x0b`, `\x0c`, `\x1c`, `\x1d`, `\x1e` and `\r`, and the module docstring asserts that with `ensure_ascii=False` these "land in a shard raw", so that a `str.splitlines()`-based reader would cut the event in two. That is false for every C0 control: Python's JSON encoder escapes all characters in U+0000–U+001F regardless of `ensure_ascii` (`json.dumps({"t": "\x1c"}, ensure_ascii=False)` yields `{"t": "\u001c"}`; `\r` is emitted as the two characters backslash-r). Consequently, for `sep in {"\x0b","\x0c","\x1c","\x1d","\x1e","\r"}` the shard written on line 20 contains no character that `str.splitlines()` breaks on, and those six parametrizations pass identically with the old `splitlines()` reader and with the new `split("\n")` reader — they are not failing-first and cannot regress-protect the fix the file claims to cover. Only U+2028, U+2029 and U+0085 (ord ≥ 0x20, genuinely written raw) actually reproduce the torn-line bug; the docstring’s specific example "`\x1c` … land[s] in a shard raw" is simply wrong, so six of the nine cases do not exercise the intended input.

chunk_findings.detail: The baseline is lowered from `609` to `608`, but this change removes no deferred-import site. The only code change in the diff (the `adopt_orphans` → `plan_adoptions` refactor in `ddflow/services/sessions.py`) contains no function-level `import` statement at all in either the added or the removed lines, and the other edits are pure data additions (a dict entry in `history_verbs.py`, a fixture entry in `event_kinds.json`, a dict entry in `test_coherence_coverage.py`) that touch no imports. Per the file's own rule ("Lower the baseline in the same change that removes sites"), the deferred-import count is therefore still 609, so the guard compares 609 against 608 and fails. Demonstrated by running the deferred-imports guard on this tree: it reports the actual value 609 while the baseline asserts 608. If the intended removal lives in another part of the series, this baseline edit is misplaced and must travel with that removal rather than with this refactor.

chunk_findings.detail: The test is built on the premise stated in its docstring — that characters such as `\x1c`, `\x1d`, `\x1e`, `\x0b`, `\x0c` and `\r` land in the shard *raw* when the writer serialises with `ensure_ascii=False`. That is not how JSON writers behave: control characters below U+0020 are always escaped regardless of `ensure_ascii` — `json.dumps("\x1c")` yields `"\\u001c"`, `json.dumps("\x0b")` yields `"\\u000b"`, `json.dumps("\r")` yields `"\\r"`, and so on. So for `sep` in `{"\x1c","\x1d","\x1e","\x0b","\x0c","\r"}` the shard line contains the two-character escape sequence `\` + `u`, `\` + `r`, etc., which is *not* a `str.splitlines()` boundary. The buggy pre-fix reader therefore reads those six lines whole and the assertion `texts == [...]` would already pass before the fix — the "failing-first" property (the whole reason the fixture exists) holds only for the three genuinely raw separators U+2028, U+2029 and U+0085. The converse branch of the same premise is worse: if the writer really did emit a bare U+001C/U+000B inside a JSON string, that string is illegal JSON, `json.loads` raises "Invalid control character", and the test would fail for those six parameters even with a correct reader. Either way the parametrization's control-character cases are either vacuous or impossible to satisfy, so they contribute no regression coverage and mask that the set only exercises U+2028/U+2029/U+0085.

chunk_findings.detail: The module docstring states that for every repair "detect finds it, repair appends corrective events", and each of these repairs advertises in its `action` a note that must be written to the log: `FORCED` says "annotate it in the log (the repair record names the item and what was overridden)", `TORN` says "quarantine note: record each line's shard, number and digest", `MISMATCHED` says "quarantine note: record each event id". But `_forced_detect`, `_torn_detect` and `_mismatched_detect` put exactly that data into the `Finding` key/message, and the corresponding `repair` functions throw the findings away and return `[]`, so no corrective event is ever produced. Concretely, given a fixture line with `item.completed` carrying `data["forced"]` and `data["overridden"]`, `_forced_detect` yields a `Finding`, `FORCED.repair` appends nothing, and the log gains only the framework's `repair.applied forced-completions` — the item id and the overridden conditions are nowhere in the log, contradicting the `action`. Same for the `unreadable-lines` shard:line:digest note and the `mismatched-ids` event-id note. Because the underlying damage is also left untouched, the only thing that can make "a second run finds nothing" true is the id-level `repair.applied` suppression described in the intent, which then also permanently hides *later* instances of the same recurring damage class (e.g. a forced completion done next week is never reported once `forced-completions` has been applied once). Either `repair` must emit the note events (as `_orphans_repair` does with `plan_adoptions`), or the promised annotations do not exist. Note `_exports_repair` returns `[]` too, but it does mutate the document (regeneration), so it is not the same case.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/repairs/seeds.py: `FORCED`, `TORN` and `MISMATCHED` (the `repair=lambda _ctx, _found: []` entries)

chunk_findings.detail: The second half of this test cannot fail for the behavior its name claims ("a hand edit is left alone"). The sequence is: (1) `_old_render(old)` makes `ROADMAP.md` stale, (2) `R.apply(..., ["old-export-renders"])` applies the repair, which records a `repair.applied` event, (3) the doc is then hand-modified (`... + "hand edit\n"` and version reset to `0.1.3`), and (4) the test asserts `R.pending(_ctx(old), ["old-export-renders"]) == []`. But step (2) already guarantees pending is empty for the rest of the process: the design's own invariant, asserted immediately after apply in `test_detect_repair_then_nothing_and_old_lines_untouched` ("a second run applies nothing") and in `test_failing_first_old_log_with_every_damage`, is that an applied repair is not re-offered. So the final assertion passes whether or not the detector treats the hand-edited document as stale, meaning a regression that clobbers hand-edited exports on a legitimate re-detection would not be caught. To actually exercise "left alone" the hand edit must be introduced before the first `detect`/`apply` (and the test must check that applying the repair does not overwrite the edited body, or that detection does not fire), which this test never does.

chunk_findings.detail: Six of the nine parametrized separators — `"\x1c"`, `"\x1d"`, `"\x1e"`, `"\x0b"`, `"\x0c"`, `"\r"` — are control characters below U+0020, and `json.dumps(..., ensure_ascii=False)` escapes every character in `\x00-\x1f` (`\b`,`\f`,`\n`,`\r`,`\t` and `\uXXXX` for the rest), so the bytes actually written to the shard for those cases are `\u001c`, `\u001d`, `\u001e`, `\u000b`, `\f`, `\r` (two-character escape sequences), never a raw separator. Consequently the unfixed `splitlines()` reader parses those lines whole and the test passes on the buggy code: e.g. with `sep="\x1c"` the shard contains `{"…","text":"before\u001cafter"}` and the old `for raw in …splitlines()` never breaks it. Only `U+2028`, `U+2029` and `U+0085` survive `ensure_ascii=False` raw and actually reproduce the bug; the file's docstring claim that "`U+2028`, `U+0085`, `\x1c` and friends land in a shard raw" is wrong for the control characters. The test therefore fails the change's own requirement ("watch it FAIL on the unfixed code") for those six cases and gives green coverage for inputs it cannot distinguish from correct code, so a re-introduction of the split for `\x1c`-class characters would go unnoticed.

chunk_findings.detail:
`_mask` assumes the whole matched secret is a `key<sep>value` pair and blindly splits on the first `:` or `=`. If a secret pattern matches a bare secret that itself contains those characters, everything after the separator is dropped but the part before it is emitted verbatim. Concrete case using the log profile, which always uses `secret_style="mask"`:

```python
cfg.session.redact_extra = [r"[A-Za-z0-9+/]{16,}={1,2}"]   # a base64-shaped secret
Redactor("log", cfg).text("c2VjcmV0IGtleQ==")
```

The pass matches the whole token `c2VjcmV0IGtleQ==`, `_mask` takes the `:`/`=` branch, `head = "c2VjcmV0IGtleQ"`, and the committed output becomes `c2VjcmV0IGtleQ= [REDACTED]` -- i.e. it leaks ~90% of the secret into the log it is supposed to sanitise. The same happens for any matched value containing `=` (base64/hex padding) or `:` (e.g. a `user:password` blob), and for a multi-word match, whose first word is likewise kept. The safe fallback (`[REDACTED]`) is only reached when the match contains neither separator and no whitespace.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/redact.py: `_mask`

chunk_findings.detail:
`_host_forms` builds `forms` as a `set` and returns `[f for f in forms ...]`, so the order in which the hostname and its first label are redacted depends on set iteration order, i.e. on `PYTHONHASHSEED`. That order is observable. Given `hostname="devbox.example.com"` and text `"devbox.example.com"` (the `_HOST` pattern does not fire here, since `example.com` is not lan/local/internal/home.arpa), the loop runs `p.sub(_term(h), "hostname")` for two forms, `"devbox.example.com"` and `"devbox"`, and the results differ:

* full form first -> `[REDACTED:hostname]`
* short label first -> `_term("devbox")` matches inside the FQDN (the following `.` satisfies `(?![A-Za-z0-9])`), yielding `[REDACTED:hostname].example.com`

So two runs of the same upstream/export Redactor on the same input on the same machine can produce different report text, defeating the reproducibility the profiles are described as guaranteeing. The same `set`-ordering applies to any two-form hostname whose short label occurs elsewhere/longer in the text (`host.corp`, `box.example.com`, ...).
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/redact.py: `_host_forms`

chunk_findings.detail: The old body was `redact_report(text, names=names_for(cfg), repo_root="", cfg=cfg)` — the empty `repo_root` was passed deliberately so that the repository's own directory name stays visible in exported text, and the docstring explaining exactly that is left untouched in the new version. The replacement `Redactor("export", cfg).text(text)` supplies no `repo_root` at all, so the value now comes from whatever default the `"export"` profile bakes in. The sibling caller in `bugreport.py` still passes `repo_root=scrub.repo_root` explicitly, showing that `repo_root` is a meaningful per-call input that profiles are not guaranteed to neutralize. Concrete failure: an export whose payload contains `<repo_root>/ddflow/services/export/safe.py` (or any path anchored at the project checkout). Previously the project directory name was preserved; if the `"export"` profile defaults `repo_root` to the config/repository root, the segment is now rewritten, so export output silently differs from what the retained docstring promises — a behaviour change that the stated intent ("behaviour of view/export ... unchanged") explicitly rules out. Either the empty `repo_root` must be passed explicitly, or the "export" profile must be shown to force it empty.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/export/safe.py:redact_text

chunk_findings.detail:
`_host_forms` builds a **set** of hostname forms and returns them in set iteration order:

```python
forms = {machine, machine.split(".")[0]} if machine else set()
return [f for f in forms if ...]
```

The short form is always a prefix of the FQDN form, and `_term`'s lookahead `(?![A-Za-z0-9])` makes the short form match *inside* the FQDN (the next char is `.`). So if the short form is applied first, the text becomes `"[REDACTED:hostname].corp"`, and because `_Pass.sub` splits on `_MARKER` and protects markers, the subsequent `_term("<full hostname>")` pass can no longer see the FQDN — the domain tail is never redacted. If the full form is applied first, the whole hostname is redacted. Since `str` hashing is randomized (`PYTHONHASHSEED`), the two orders alternate between processes.

Concrete demo: `redact_report("see devbox1.corp now", hostname="devbox1.corp")` (or any `export`/`upstream` `Redactor`, whose `hostname` defaults to the machine's). `_HOST` does not catch it because `corp` is not in the `lan|local|internal|home.arpa` list, so the output is nondeterministically either `"see [REDACTED:hostname] now"` or `"see [REDACTED:hostname].corp now"`, the latter leaking the domain and producing a different `counts`/output across runs. Contrast the `names` handling two functions above, which deliberately does `sorted(words, key=len, reverse=True)` for exactly this prefix case; `_host_forms` needs the same longest-first ordering.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/redact.py `_host_forms` (used in `redact_report`)

chunk_findings.detail:
The old call site explicitly forced the machine-dependent parameters off:

    redact_report(text, hostname="", home="", names=names_for(effective), repo_root="", cfg=effective)

The replacement passes only `("view", cfg or Config())` and drops `hostname=""`, `home=""`, `repo_root=""` and `names=...`. The comment immediately above the new call is retained verbatim and states exactly why those arguments existed: "a committed view must be byte-identical on every machine (roborev on 9b6db6bc); the rendering host's own name and $HOME are not inputs." Nothing in this diff shows the `"view"` profile hard-coding `hostname=""`/`home=""`/`repo_root=""` (that logic lived in `core/redact.py`, not in this diff), so unless the profile silently reproduces those overrides, a committed view rendered on machine A will contain A's hostname and `$HOME` and differ from the same view rendered on machine B, breaking the byte-identical invariant the comment documents. Given the stated intent that "behaviour of view/export/upstream/argv [is] unchanged", the call must either pass those empty overrides explicitly (as before) or the `"view"` profile must be shown to default them to empty; as written the parameters that enforced the invariant are gone. Input demonstrating it: `cfg.hostname`/`$HOME` set on the rendering host, a record citing `user@host:/home/user/...` — the old code emitted the record with host and home removed, the new call emits whatever the `"view"` profile does by default.

chunk_findings.detail: The two tests together pin the committed session log to a profile that the suite itself says never redacts hosts. `test_the_session_log_writes_through_the_log_profile` (lines 53-55) asserts `sessions.redact(LEAKY, Config())` equals `R.Redactor("log", Config()).text(LEAKY).text`, so the log is exactly the `"log"` profile. `test_log_and_view_do_not_read_the_machine` (lines 44-48) monkeypatches `socket.gethostname` to `"Zeta9.example.test"` and asserts `R.Redactor("log").text("ran on Zeta9 and zeta9.example.test").text == text`, i.e. the `"log"` profile deliberately leaves the machine hostname and the FQDN `zeta9.example.test` untouched (only `export`/`upstream` remove them, lines 49-50). But the stated intent is that the committed log now uses the full profile `(private addrs, hosts, home paths, emails, names; secrets keep context)` — hosts included. Given input `LEAKY`-style text containing the host the process is running on (e.g. any session run on `Zeta9.example.test`), `sessions.redact` writes `Zeta9`/`zeta9.example.test` into `sessions.redact` unredacted, which is exactly the leak the full-profile change was supposed to close. Either line 55 must select the full/host-redacting profile, or lines 47-48 must not assert host preservation; as committed, the test suite locks in hostname leakage in the committed log.

chunk_findings.detail: The log profile is changed to `Profile("log", None, None, "", secrets="mask")`: the first two machine-local inputs (hostname, `$HOME`) are switched from `""` to `None` so the Redactor resolves them, but the third machine-local input is left as `""` (disabled). Compare `Profile("upstream", None, None, None)` at line 341, where `None` is what makes the redactor pull names from the `[upstream]` section, and the README sentence edited in this very diff (README.md:3451) which promises the log removes "…and (once the `[upstream]` section exists) its `redact_extra` names from every NEW prompt and note." Input that demonstrates it: configure `redact_extra = ["acme-internal"]` under `[upstream]`, then write a note `deploy acme-internal service`. That name is stored verbatim in the *committed* log (and, from there, in anything derived from those events), contradicting the documented "full profile" behavior. The change intends the log to be the full profile, so the third positional should be `None` (as upstream) rather than `""`.

chunk_findings.detail:
`_host_forms` builds a **set** of hostname forms and returns them in set iteration order:

```python
forms = {machine, machine.split(".")[0]} if machine else set()
return [f for f in forms if ...]
```

The short form is always a prefix of the FQDN form, and `_term`'s lookahead `(?![A-Za-z0-9])` makes the short form match *inside* the FQDN (the next char is `.`). So if the short form is applied first, the text becomes `"[REDACTED:hostname].corp"`, and because `_Pass.sub` splits on `_MARKER` and protects markers, the subsequent `_term("<full hostname>")` pass can no longer see the FQDN — the domain tail is never redacted. If the full form is applied first, the whole hostname is redacted. Since `str` hashing is randomized (`PYTHONHASHSEED`), the two orders alternate between processes.

Concrete demo: `redact_report("see devbox1.corp now", hostname="devbox1.corp")` (or any `export`/`upstream` `Redactor`, whose `hostname` defaults to the machine's). `_HOST` does not catch it because `corp` is not in the `lan|local|internal|home.arpa` list, so the output is nondeterministically either `"see [REDACTED:hostname] now"` or `"see [REDACTED:hostname].corp now"`, the latter leaking the domain and producing a different `counts`/output across runs. Contrast the `names` handling two functions above, which deliberately does `sorted(words, key=len, reverse=True)` for exactly this prefix case; `_host_forms` needs the same longest-first ordering.

chunk_findings.detail:
The old call site explicitly forced the machine-dependent parameters off:

    redact_report(text, hostname="", home="", names=names_for(effective), repo_root="", cfg=effective)

The replacement passes only `("view", cfg or Config())` and drops `hostname=""`, `home=""`, `repo_root=""` and `names=...`. The comment immediately above the new call is retained verbatim and states exactly why those arguments existed: "a committed view must be byte-identical on every machine (roborev on 9b6db6bc); the rendering host's own name and $HOME are not inputs." Nothing in this diff shows the `"view"` profile hard-coding `hostname=""`/`home=""`/`repo_root=""` (that logic lived in `core/redact.py`, not in this diff), so unless the profile silently reproduces those overrides, a committed view rendered on machine A will contain A's hostname and `$HOME` and differ from the same view rendered on machine B, breaking the byte-identical invariant the comment documents. Given the stated intent that "behaviour of view/export/upstream/argv [is] unchanged", the call must either pass those empty overrides explicitly (as before) or the `"view"` profile must be shown to default them to empty; as written the parameters that enforced the invariant are gone. Input demonstrating it: `cfg.hostname`/`$HOME` set on the rendering host, a record citing `user@host:/home/user/...` — the old code emitted the record with host and home removed, the new call emits whatever the `"view"` profile does by default.

chunk_findings.detail: The two tests together pin the committed session log to a profile that the suite itself says never redacts hosts. `test_the_session_log_writes_through_the_log_profile` (lines 53-55) asserts `sessions.redact(LEAKY, Config())` equals `R.Redactor("log", Config()).text(LEAKY).text`, so the log is exactly the `"log"` profile. `test_log_and_view_do_not_read_the_machine` (lines 44-48) monkeypatches `socket.gethostname` to `"Zeta9.example.test"` and asserts `R.Redactor("log").text("ran on Zeta9 and zeta9.example.test").text == text`, i.e. the `"log"` profile deliberately leaves the machine hostname and the FQDN `zeta9.example.test` untouched (only `export`/`upstream` remove them, lines 49-50). But the stated intent is that the committed log now uses the full profile `(private addrs, hosts, home paths, emails, names; secrets keep context)` — hosts included. Given input `LEAKY`-style text containing the host the process is running on (e.g. any session run on `Zeta9.example.test`), `sessions.redact` writes `Zeta9`/`zeta9.example.test` into `sessions.redact` unredacted, which is exactly the leak the full-profile change was supposed to close. Either line 55 must select the full/host-redacting profile, or lines 47-48 must not assert host preservation; as committed, the test suite locks in hostname leakage in the committed log.

chunk_findings.detail: The `log` profile is constructed with `""` for the third `Profile` argument, which controls whether `[upstream].redact_extra` names are read. The README (lines 3452–3454) and the stated intent describe the log profile as the full one that removes those names. Concrete failure: with `[upstream] redact_extra = ["acme-secret"]`, a new prompt containing `acme-secret` is written to the committed event log unchanged, leaking the term; expected output is `[REDACTED]`. The `export`/`upstream` profiles show the intended `""` vs `None` distinction, and `log` should pass `None` for this slot as well.

chunk_findings.detail:
`_mask` assumes the whole matched secret is a `key<sep>value` pair and blindly splits on the first `:` or `=`. If a secret pattern matches a bare secret that itself contains those characters, everything after the separator is dropped but the part before it is emitted verbatim. Concrete case using the log profile, which always uses `secret_style="mask"`:

```python
cfg.session.redact_extra = [r"[A-Za-z0-9+/]{16,}={1,2}"]   # a base64-shaped secret
Redactor("log", cfg).text("c2VjcmV0IGtleQ==")
```

The pass matches the whole token `c2VjcmV0IGtleQ==`, `_mask` takes the `:`/`=` branch, `head = "c2VjcmV0IGtleQ"`, and the committed output becomes `c2VjcmV0IGtleQ= [REDACTED]` -- i.e. it leaks ~90% of the secret into the log it is supposed to sanitise. The same happens for any matched value containing `=` (base64/hex padding) or `:` (e.g. a `user:password` blob), and for a multi-word match, whose first word is likewise kept. The safe fallback (`[REDACTED]`) is only reached when the match contains neither separator and no whitespace.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/redact.py: `_mask`

chunk_findings.detail:
`_host_forms` builds `forms` as a `set` and returns `[f for f in forms ...]`, so the order in which the hostname and its first label are redacted depends on set iteration order, i.e. on `PYTHONHASHSEED`. That order is observable. Given `hostname="devbox.example.com"` and text `"devbox.example.com"` (the `_HOST` pattern does not fire here, since `example.com` is not lan/local/internal/home.arpa), the loop runs `p.sub(_term(h), "hostname")` for two forms, `"devbox.example.com"` and `"devbox"`, and the results differ:

* full form first -> `[REDACTED:hostname]`
* short label first -> `_term("devbox")` matches inside the FQDN (the following `.` satisfies `(?![A-Za-z0-9])`), yielding `[REDACTED:hostname].example.com`

So two runs of the same upstream/export Redactor on the same input on the same machine can produce different report text, defeating the reproducibility the profiles are described as guaranteeing. The same `set`-ordering applies to any two-form hostname whose short label occurs elsewhere/longer in the text (`host.corp`, `box.example.com`, ...).
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/redact.py: `_host_forms`

chunk_findings.detail: The old body was `redact_report(text, names=names_for(cfg), repo_root="", cfg=cfg)` — the empty `repo_root` was passed deliberately so that the repository's own directory name stays visible in exported text, and the docstring explaining exactly that is left untouched in the new version. The replacement `Redactor("export", cfg).text(text)` supplies no `repo_root` at all, so the value now comes from whatever default the `"export"` profile bakes in. The sibling caller in `bugreport.py` still passes `repo_root=scrub.repo_root` explicitly, showing that `repo_root` is a meaningful per-call input that profiles are not guaranteed to neutralize. Concrete failure: an export whose payload contains `<repo_root>/ddflow/services/export/safe.py` (or any path anchored at the project checkout). Previously the project directory name was preserved; if the `"export"` profile defaults `repo_root` to the config/repository root, the segment is now rewritten, so export output silently differs from what the retained docstring promises — a behaviour change that the stated intent ("behaviour of view/export ... unchanged") explicitly rules out. Either the empty `repo_root` must be passed explicitly, or the "export" profile must be shown to force it empty.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/export/safe.py:redact_text

chunk_findings.detail: The log profile is changed to `Profile("log", None, None, "", secrets="mask")`: the first two machine-local inputs (hostname, `$HOME`) are switched from `""` to `None` so the Redactor resolves them, but the third machine-local input is left as `""` (disabled). Compare `Profile("upstream", None, None, None)` at line 341, where `None` is what makes the redactor pull names from the `[upstream]` section, and the README sentence edited in this very diff (README.md:3451) which promises the log removes "…and (once the `[upstream]` section exists) its `redact_extra` names from every NEW prompt and note." Input that demonstrates it: configure `redact_extra = ["acme-internal"]` under `[upstream]`, then write a note `deploy acme-internal service`. That name is stored verbatim in the *committed* log (and, from there, in anything derived from those events), contradicting the documented "full profile" behavior. The change intends the log to be the full profile, so the third positional should be `None` (as upstream) rather than `""`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/redact.py:335 (`Profile("log", ...)`)

chunk_findings.detail: The assertion `out.endswith("x.py and myproj") and "REDACTED:name" not in out` passes even when the export profile performs no redaction at all: for input `see /tmp/pytest-.../myproj/x.py and myproj`, the unchanged text still ends with `x.py and myproj` and contains no `REDACTED:name`. Thus the test does not verify that the parent path components are redacted while the repository directory name is preserved, which is the behavior named by the test and implied by the export profile.

chunk_findings.detail:
The Jinja marker is written as `"{# ddflow-shipped: {digest} -#}
"`. The trailing `-#}` is Jinja's "strip all whitespace after this tag" operator, and it strips *through the newline and into the shipped text's first line*. The builtin file (no marker) preserves that leading whitespace, so for any shipped Jinja asset whose body begins with whitespace the ejected project copy renders differently from the builtin, even though `is_edited`/`drift` consider it pristine (they only compare `digest(body)` against `recorded`, and `split_mark` consumes just one `
`).

Concrete input: shipped `foo.jinja` = `"
  You are a helpful assistant.
"`. Builtin render → `"
  You are a helpful assistant.
"`. `eject` writes `"{# ddflow-shipped: <d> -#}

  You are a helpful assistant.
"`; rendering that file makes Jinja emit `"You are a helpful assistant.
"` (leading blank line and the two leading spaces are eaten by `-#}`). The copy is thus not render-equivalent to the layer it replaces, which contradicts the module's "the marker is a comment" invisibility premise. A marker written with no trailing newline (`"{# ddflow-shipped: {digest} #}"` + shipped, still matched by the `
?`-optional regex) would avoid the over-strip; the TOML side is unaffected because `#` is a line comment. The parity tests only pin the ejected file bytes, so they cannot catch this render-level divergence.

chunk_findings.detail:
The test asserts `problem.line == 2` for the template `"fine
{% if x %}
never closed
"`, i.e. it expects `validate` to report the line of the *opening* `{% if %}` tag. Jinja does not do that for an unclosed block: `Environment.parse` raises `TemplateSyntaxError: Unexpected end of template. Jinja was looking for the following tags: 'endif'` from `Parser.fail_eof`, whose `lineno` is `self.stream.current.lineno` at the EOF token — i.e. the *last* line of the template (line 3 here, since the body has 3 lines: `fine`, `{% if x %}`, `never closed`). A `validate` that propagates the caught exception's `lineno` therefore reports `3`, and both `problem.line == 2` and the `str(problem).startswith(f"{p}:2:")` assertion fail (or, if the assertion is made to pass by post-processing the error, the reported `file:line` for a real unclosed block points users at the wrong line). Note the sibling test `test_a_marked_copy_keeps_the_files_line_numbers` is consistent with the EOF semantics (marker + one body line = 2 lines → line 2), so only the raw three-line case carries the wrong expectation; the correct expected value is the last line of the template, not the line of the unclosed tag.

chunk_findings.detail: `_mask` picks the separator by fixed preference order (`":"` first, then `"="`) instead of picking the *first* separator that actually delimits key from value in the matched text, and it re-emits everything before that separator verbatim. Whenever the matched secret itself contains a `:` or `=` before its end, the prefix of the secret is written back into the output, so the log profile (the only profile using `secrets="mask"`) fails the stated invariant "a secret must not survive any profile." Concrete case: pattern `token\s*[:=]\s*\S+` (or just a value-shaped pattern like `\S+:\S+`) and input `token=abc:def` — `_mask` hits `":"`, partitions into head `"token=abc"` / tail `"def"`, and returns `"token=abc: [REDACTED]"`, so the token fragment `abc` (and the fact that the value had a colon) is committed to the event log. The same happens with an embedded `=`: `token=abc=def` → `"token=abc= [REDACTED]"`. The output contradicts `_mask`'s own docstring ("see WHAT was supplied **without the value**") and the change's secret-non-survival property; the replacement should split on the key/value separator (or blank the whole match) rather than preferring `":"` regardless of where it occurs in the match.

chunk_findings.detail:
`_mask` chooses the separator to split on by iterating `(":", "=")` and returning on the **first character present anywhere in the match**, not the first-occurring character. Because it checks `":"` before `"="` unconditionally, any secret whose *value* contains a colon but whose key/value separator is `=` leaks the portion of the value up to that colon. The `log` profile (the only one using `secrets="mask"`, per `PROFILES`) therefore writes part of the secret into the committed log, contradicting the stated invariant "a secret must not survive any profile".

Concrete reproduction: `mask_secrets("token=abc:def", [r"token=\S+"])` → `("token=abc: [REDACTED]", 1)`. The value is `abc:def`, but `_mask` partitions on the inner `":"` instead of the `"="` assignment, yielding `head="token=abc"`, and returns `f"{head}{sep} [REDACTED]"` = `token=abc: [REDACTED]` — so `abc` (part of the secret) survives. The same happens for the documented `Bearer` case: `_mask("Bearer abc:def")` returns `Bearer abc: [REDACTED]` rather than `Bearer [REDACTED]`. The fix is to split on whichever of `:`/`=` occurs *earliest* (or, when the `=`/`:` key form is present, always prefer the key separator), so the retained head is the key and never a prefix of the secret value.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/redact.py:_mask

chunk_findings.detail: `_safe` constructs its redactor without a config: `redactor("upstream").text(str(exc)).text`. The two other call sites migrated in this change (`sessions.redact` → `redactor("log", cfg)` and `markdown` → `redactor("view", cfg or Config())`) both pass `cfg`, which is the object that supplies the user's `session.redact_patterns` / `session.redact_extra` (and the name set) — the very rules the removed `sessions.redact` docstring calls the security control. With `cfg` omitted, exception text that reaches the upstream bug report is scrubbed only by whatever static rules the `"upstream"` profile hard-codes; any pattern the user configured is not applied. Demonstrable input: with `[session].redact_patterns = ["acme-[0-9]{4}"]` (or the env-var form `DDFLOW_SESSION_REDACT_PATTERNS='["acme-[0-9]{4}"]'`), an exception whose message contains `acme-1234` is returned verbatim by `_safe`, whereas the same string routed through `sessions.redact(text, cfg)` is masked to `acme-[REDACTED]`. Because this text is submitted upstream (public GitHub issue), a secret the user explicitly asked to redact leaks — the exact failure the change is meant to prevent. The fix is to thread `cfg` into `_safe` and call `redactor("upstream", cfg)`; if `redactor` has no default for its second parameter this is instead an immediate `TypeError` at every upstream-delivery failure path.

chunk_findings.detail:
The previous finding is only partially answered. The rewrite now picks the *first* separator (`min(cuts)`) and gates the key-preserving output on `_KEY.fullmatch(head.strip())`, which fixes the leak whenever the text before the separator contains anything other than `[A-Za-z0-9_. -]` (e.g. `P@ssw0rd:2024` now falls through to the full marker, and `Bearer abc:def` is now caught by the `_SCHEMES` branch). But when the matched text is the *entire* secret and its prefix before the first separator is word-like, that prefix is still re-emitted verbatim, so the stated invariant "a secret must not survive any profile" (and `secrets="mask"` is the profile that writes to the committed log) is still violated.

Concrete input: any secret pattern (including a user-supplied one via `DDFLOW_SESSION_REDACT_PATTERNS`) whose match is `MySecret:1234`. `cuts = [8]`, `head = "MySecret"`, `_KEY.fullmatch("MySecret")` succeeds, `"1234".strip("= \t")` is truthy, so `_mask` returns `"MySecret: [REDACTED]"` and `MySecret` is committed to the log.

This is also a regression relative to the pre-change function, not just an unfixed issue. `_mask("cGFzc3dvcmQ=:")` (base64 of `password`, with a trailing colon in the match):
- before: the `for sep in (":", "=")` loop hits `":"` first, its tail is empty, so it `break`s to `s.split(None, 1)`, which yields one part, and the whole match is replaced by the full marker;
- after: `find(":") = 13`, `find("=") = 11`, so `min(cuts) = 11`, `head = "cGFzc3dvcmQ"` matches `_KEY`, `tail = ":"` is truthy, and the function returns `"cGFzc3dvcmQ= [REDACTED]"`, leaking the base64 password value.

So the fix narrows the case but does not make the "first separator delimits key from value" assumption safe: a word-like prefix before the first separator is still treated as a key even when the redactor has already decided the whole match is a secret.

This is also a regression relative to the pre-change function, not just an unfixed issue. `_mask("cGFzc3dvcmQ=:")` (base64 of `password`, with a trailing colon in the match):
- before: the `for sep in (":", "=")` loop hits `":"` first, its tail is empty, so it `break`s to `s.split(None, 1)`, which yields one part, and the whole match is replaced by the full marker;
- after: `find(":") = 13`, `find("=") = 11`, so `min(cuts) = 11`, `head = "cGFzc3dvcmQ"` matches `_KEY`, `tail = ":"` is truthy, and the function returns `"cGFzc3dvcmQ= [REDACTED]"`, leaking the base64 password value.

So the fix narrows the case but does not make the "first separator delimits key from value" assumption safe: a word-like prefix before the first separator is still treated as a key even when the redactor has already decided the whole match is a secret.

chunk_findings.detail: The newer-schema branch does `int(raw.get("fmt", found))` with no guard. `fmt` is attacker/other-tool controlled and is never validated, unlike `schema` (which is checked with `isinstance(found, int) and not isinstance(found, bool)`). Given a document on disk that another tool wrote as `{"schema": 5, "ddflow": "9.9", "fmt": null, "data": {...}}` and a caller invoking `store.read(name, schema=1)`, `found (5) > schema (1)` is true, so the code evaluates `int(None)` and raises `TypeError` (or `ValueError` for `"fmt": "abc"`, or `TypeError` for `"fmt": [1]`) instead of the documented `fsio.NewerContent` (exit 3, "upgrade ddflow to >= X"). This is exactly the "torn by another tool" state the module claims to translate into a clean refusal, so the compatibility guarantee "a document written by a NEWER schema is refused" does not hold for these inputs. The `fmt` value should be validated (or `found` used when `fmt` is not an int) before being passed to `NewerContent`.
chunk_findings.title: `ddflow/infra/localstore.py: LocalStore._load` (the `NewerContent` raise)

chunk_findings.detail: `LocalStore.path(name)` is carefully validated ("a plain file name: no separators", rejects leading `.`, rejects anything where `Path(name).name != name`), but `sweep(subdir)` does no validation at all and just does `self.root / subdir`. Because `pathlib`'s `/` operator yields the right operand when it is absolute, `store.sweep("/tmp/victim", Retention(keep_n=0))` applies retention to `/tmp/victim`, not to a subdirectory of the store root, and `store.sweep("..", Retention(keep_n=0))` sweeps the root's parent. `Retention.sweep` with `keep_n=0` deletes every non-dotfile regular file it can unlink, so a caller that derives `subdir` from config (rather than a literal) can silently delete files anywhere the process can write, outside the machine-local directory the store is supposed to own.
chunk_findings.title: `ddflow/infra/localstore.py: LocalStore.sweep`

chunk_findings.detail: The coalescing timestamp is captured before the critical section: `now = self.clock()` runs, and only then does `self.update(...)` acquire the file lock and call `put`. Two agents putting the same key concurrently can therefore write `last_at` out of order. Concretely, with a clock returning 100.0, agent A enters `queue_put` and blocks on the lock for several seconds (another holder, up to `LOCK_TIMEOUT_S = 10`); agent B enters later with `now = 100.1`, acquires the lock first, records `last_at = 100.1`; A then acquires the lock and overwrites the entry with `last_at = 100.0`, i.e. *earlier* than the most recent put. With `debounce_s = 1`, a subsequent `queue_take` at wall time 101.0 sees `101.0 - 100.0 >= 1` and takes the key, even though the last put was recorded at 100.1 and the key had been quiet for only 0.9 s. Capturing `now` inside `put` (or otherwise ensuring `last_at` is monotonic per key) is needed for the stated "a key becomes due only after it has been quiet for `debounce_s`" contract to hold under contention.
chunk_findings.title: `ddflow/infra/localstore.py: LocalStore.queue_put`

chunk_findings.detail:
`_load` only guarantees that the document as a whole is a JSON object; it says nothing about the shape of the queue's *entries*. `queue_put` is written knowing this — it guards every access to the previous entry with `isinstance(old, dict)` (`old["first_at"] if isinstance(old, dict) else now`, `old["count"] if isinstance(old, dict) else 0`). But the read side is not guarded:

```python
return dict(sorted(items, key=lambda kv: (kv[1].get("first_at", 0), kv[0])))
...
order = sorted(q.items(), key=lambda kv: (kv[1].get("first_at", 0), kv[0]))
...
if now - entry.get("last_at", 0) >= entry.get("debounce_s", 0.0):
```

Concrete input: a schema-0 document (explicitly supported by the `if "schema" not in raw:` branch — "its whole value is the data") holding an old-style queue `{"job-a": {"task": 1}}` or even `{"job-a": "payload"}`, i.e. a value that is not a dict. `store.queue_pending("q")` then evaluates `kv[1].get(...)` on that value and raises `AttributeError: 'str' object has no attribute 'get'`, and `store.queue_take("q")` raises the same inside the `sorted` key. This is not a "missing document" (`default` does not apply) and not a torn/invalid JSON file (`json.loads` succeeds), so it is exactly the case the module promises to surface as `StoreUnreadable` ("Unreadable state is never silently an empty store"), yet it escapes as a raw `AttributeError` from the sort key. Because `_load` will happily return any schema-0 dict, and because `queue_put` itself demonstrates the author expects non-dict entries to be possible, `queue_pending`/`queue_take` need the same `isinstance(entry, dict)` guard (or `_load`/the queue helpers need to treat a non-dict entry as unreadable) before reading `first_at`/`last_at`/`debounce_s`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/localstore.py: LocalStore.queue_pending / LocalStore.queue_take

chunk_findings.detail:
`_gate_list_parser` is a module-level function, but it references the bare name `cmd_gate`. The module's own comment (immediately above `register` in the same hunk) states that the handlers "live in `cli.py`; imported at call time, when `cli` is loaded" — i.e. `cmd_gate` is bound only as a local inside `register()`. A function-local import in `register` is not visible to `_gate_list_parser`'s (module) scope, so evaluating `cmd_gate` there raises `NameError: name 'cmd_gate' is not defined`.

Because `register()` eagerly calls `_gate_list_parser(g_s)` while building the argument parser, this fires on *every* invocation, not just the new subcommand: running `ddflow gate list --refuted` (or `ddflow status`, or even `ddflow --help`) constructs the parser, enters `register`, calls `_gate_list_parser`, and hits the unresolved name before argparse ever dispatches. The fix is to make `_gate_list_parser` take the handler as a parameter (`glist.set_defaults(fn=handler)`) or bind `cmd_gate` at module scope, rather than relying on `register`'s local import.

chunk_findings.detail: `_gate_list_parser` is a module-level function that references the bare name `cmd_gate` in `glist.set_defaults(fn=cmd_gate)`. The lifecycle handlers are not imported into this module's globals: the comment inside `register` states "Handlers that live in `cli.py`; imported at call time, when `cli` is loaded", and the existing code depends on that local import (e.g. `gst.set_defaults(fn=cmd_gate, gate="")` inside `register`). When `register` executes `_gate_list_parser(g_s)`, name resolution for `cmd_gate` uses the module globals, where it is not bound, so parser construction raises `NameError: name 'cmd_gate' is not defined`. Since every `ddflow` invocation builds the parser (and therefore calls `register`), the whole CLI fails to start. Reproduction: run any `ddflow` command (or just call the lifecycle `register` function) with this change; the `NameError` is raised before argument parsing. The fix is to pass the handler into `_gate_list_parser`, define the parser inside `register`, or bind the import at module scope.

chunk_findings.detail: The new ceiling is internally inconsistent with the justification in its own comment. The comment states the previous list size was "94,5xx" and that the added `ddflow_gate_list` face is "~0.5 KB". "94,5xx" is at minimum 94,500 bytes, and 0.5 KB is ~512 bytes, so the post-change list is at minimum ~95,012 bytes — already above the new `TOOLS_LIST_BUDGET = 95_000`. Only if the old list was below 94,488 bytes does 95,000 leave headroom, which contradicts the stated "94,5xx". Concretely: if the list sat at 94,500 (the smallest value consistent with "94,5xx") and the new tool contributes 500 bytes, the assertion at the budget check fails; the constant needs to be ≥ 95,100 (ideally with real measured headroom) rather than 95,000. Because the figure is described as approximate, this may merely be a stale comment, but as written the constant does not demonstrably cover the documented growth.

Concretely, the new line `_gate_list_parser(g_s)` added to `register` (the `@@ -106,6 +119,7 @@` hunk) will raise `NameError: name 'cmd_gate' is not defined` every time `register` runs, i.e. on every `ddflow` CLI startup, before any subcommand can be parsed. chunk_findings.detail:
The leaf-level exemption list is matched against **data-supplied dict/list keys**, not against a fixed schema, and it contains very common prose-field names (`log`, `source`, `file`/`files`, `path`, `status`, `key`, `category`, `event`, `tests`, `regression_tests`, `output_file`, `output_log`, `base`, `head`, `id`, …). Any string leaf that happens to sit under such a key inside a declared text field is returned verbatim, so the fix silently fails exactly where the intent says it must work ("gate evidence and output tails").

Concrete trace with the code as written:

```
redact_event_data("gate.failed",
                  {"evidence": {"tests": "pytest tail: AWS_SECRET= [REDACTED] [REDACTED:path]"},
                   "reason": "boom"},
                  redactor)
```

`names == ("evidence", "reason")`, so `evidence` goes to `redact_leaves(..., "")`; it is a `Mapping`, so the value is recursed with `key="tests"`. `_KEEP_KEYS.search("tests")` matches (`(?:^|_)tests$`), so the branch `return value if key and _KEEP_KEYS.search(key)` returns the tail unchanged. Same for `{"output_log": "<actual log text>"}`, `{"source": "https://user:pw@host"}`, `{"files": ["<secret-bearing line>"]}` inside e.g. `research.recorded.probe_output` or `decision.recorded.alternatives`, and for `def.recorded`/`def.updated` where the keys of `fields` are literally user-chosen field names (`ddflow def --field path=…`). The exemption is only safe for keys the code itself produces; here the keys come from gate names, CI providers, def authors and file contents.

chunk_findings.detail: An event kind that is absent from `LOG_TEXT_FIELDS` is treated as text-free by default: `names` is `()`, the guard `if not names … return data` fires, and the payload is committed with **no** redaction and no error. `LOG_NO_TEXT` exists precisely because "a NEW kind must choose", but that choice is enforced only by `tests/test_log_redaction_all_kinds.py` against `tests/fixtures/event_kinds.json`; at runtime a renamed or newly introduced kind (e.g. any kind added after this table, or a typo such as `session.prompted`) yields empty `names` and leaks free text to git — the same failure mode as B5deba76d04, just on the kind axis. Given the stated goal ("the committed event log uses the full redaction profile … for NEW writes of everything"), the unknown-kind default should not be indistinguishable from a declared no-text kind.

chunk_findings.detail:
The regression test derives both *which kinds* to exercise and *which fields* to poison from the implementation under test, and its cross-checks are one-directional, so it passes even when the fix leaves free text unredacted.

- Field level: `test_no_text_field_leaks` builds `data = {name: _value(fields[name]) for name in R.LOG_TEXT_FIELDS[kind]}` — it only writes the probe into fields that are *already* declared. `test_declared_fields_exist_in_the_kind` only asserts `declared ⊆ actual` (`set(names) - set(KINDS[kind]["fields"])`), never the converse. So given a fixture kind, e.g. `X` with `fields = {"summary": ["str"], "body": ["str"]}` and a fix that declares `LOG_TEXT_FIELDS["X"] = ["summary"]`, no test ever puts a secret into `body`; the committed shard still contains `sk-...`/`[REDACTED:path]`, and the whole file is green.
- Kind level: `test_every_kind_is_declared` only requires each kind to be in `LOG_TEXT_FIELDS ∪ LOG_NO_TEXT`. A kind that actually carries free text but is (mis)listed in `LOG_NO_TEXT` is never parametrized into `test_no_text_field_leaks`, and nothing asserts that `LOG_NO_TEXT` kinds contain no `str`/`dict`/`list` fields.

Since the fix's entire mechanism is the per-kind/per-field declaration, an omitted field or a misclassified kind is the most likely way the original bug (secret/home-path in a gate tail, bug summary, lesson, … committed to git) survives — and this test cannot detect either case. The fixture already exposes field types (`KINDS[kind]["fields"]`), so the missing check (every non-id/digest/path field of a kind must be either declared text or explicitly justified as no-text) is available but not performed.

chunk_findings.detail: `_KEEP_KEYS` contains the bare alternative `key`, and it is applied with `re.search(...)`, not a full-key match, so the guard is `(?:^|_)key$` — any leaf whose enclosing dict key *ends in* `_key` is treated as a lookup value and returned verbatim. Those are exactly the names secrets are stored under: `api_key`, `access_key`, `secret_key`, `private_key`, `ssh_key`, `signing_key`. Concrete input: for the declared text kind `def.recorded` (field `fields`) the payload `{"fields": {"api_key": "[REDACTED]", "endpoint": "http://[REDACTED:ipv4]"}}` goes into `redact_leaves`; the recursion hits `key == "api_key"`, `_KEEP_KEYS.search("api_key")` matches, and the AWS key is written through untouched (the `endpoint` leaf is redacted, which makes the inconsistency obvious). The same holds for `research.recorded`/`def.updated`/any kind whose declared text field is a mapping — the mapping is free text by declaration, yet a credential under a `*_key` name escapes, so a secret is committed to the shard, which is the exact outcome this change is supposed to prevent. Note the docstring's own enumeration of what may be kept ("shas, digests, trees, paths, ids, branches, model and gate names") does not include credential names, and even under the charitable reading that `key` is meant for a `{"key": <name>, "value": <text>}` pair, the pattern should be anchored (`^key$`); the unanchored suffix is too broad.
