chunk_findings.detail: The redactor is built exactly once and memoized on `self._redactor`, and that one build is wrapped in `except Exception` around `Config.load(self.root)`. A single failure to load the project config is therefore swallowed *permanently*: the fallback redactor is cached for the lifetime of the `Log` instance and every later `append` reuses it, even after the config becomes readable, so `session.redact_patterns`/`session.redact_extra` are never re-applied. Note the catch-all also hides programming errors (e.g. `self.root` not actually being the attribute holding the project root → `AttributeError`, or any `Config`/`SessionConfig` API mismatch), which are indistinguishable from "unreadable config" here. Concretely: a project that advertises a customer-specific token format in `redact_extra`, where the first `append` after the `Log` is constructed hits a transient `Config.load` error (mid-write config file, validation error), will build the redactor from `SessionConfig().redact_patterns` only (the fallback also omits `redact_extra`), and every subsequent write — including long after the config is valid — commits that token to git. The proposed regression test would not catch this, because it only injects secrets, private IPs, hostname and home path, all of which the built-in patterns already cover, so the suite stays green while the custom pattern is silently dropped.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/log.py `_redact_data` (`red = self._redactor = R.Redactor(...)`)

chunk_findings.detail: The regression test derives the fields it probes from the very declaration it is supposed to validate: `TEXT_KINDS` is built from `R.LOG_TEXT_FIELDS`, and inside `test_no_text_field_leaks` the payload is built only from `R.LOG_TEXT_FIELDS[kind]`. Consequently a free-text field (or an entire text-bearing kind) that the fix fails to declare is never written, never probed, and the test stays green even though the bug B5deba76d04 leak persists. Concretely: suppose the vocabulary/fixture has a status-like kind such as `gate.finished` with a free-text field `output_tail`, and the implementation mistakenly classifies it via `LOG_NO_TEXT` (or declares a text kind but omits one of its fields, e.g. lists only `body` and not `summary`). Then: `test_every_kind_is_declared` passes because `gate.finished` is in `declared`; `test_declared_fields_exist_in_the_kind` passes because it only iterates `LOG_TEXT_FIELDS` entries; `test_no_text_field_leaks` is not even parametrized for that kind (it is not in `TEXT_KINDS`), so no secret/IP/host/home probe is ever written to `output_tail`; and the shard therefore contains no leak for the test to catch. The writer in production still serializes `output_tail` verbatim, so a secret in a gate's output tail is committed to git and the regression test that is supposed to lock the fix passes anyway. Nothing in the file cross-checks `LOG_NO_TEXT` kinds against the fixture's field types (e.g. asserting that no kind in `LOG_NO_TEXT` has a `str`/`dict`/`list` field that the writer would free-text, or that every non-id field of a text kind is declared), so this false-negative cannot be detected.

chunk_findings.detail: `_logged` runs the **entire** `fields` mapping through `R.redact_leaves(..., redactor("log", cfg))`, and it does this *before* `D.digest(fields)`. That is a per-caller redaction with no per-kind field list, whereas the stated design is "fix at the one choke point … declared per kind" and explicitly says "ids, digests or paths used for lookups stay as they are". Because the earlier triage removed the key-based exemption from `redact_leaves`, that function now rewrites *every* string leaf, so definition fields that are not free text are mangled and then hashed. Example: a definition written with `fields={"repo": "[REDACTED:path]", "target": "[REDACTED:ipv4]"}` is stored (and hashed) as `{"repo": "/home/[REDACTED]/work", "target": "[REDACTED]"}`. Two consequences: (a) the committed `def.recorded`/`def.updated` event for that definition no longer contains the value the caller supplied, and a field the design carves out as non-text (a path/host value carried as def data, possibly used to match the definition) is destroyed; (b) the digest cited in the event is now a function of the redacted value rather than of the supplied `fields`, so it cannot be reproduced by any consumer that hashes the logical fields, and if the same update is replayed over a pre-fix record (whose stored `fields` still hold the original string) `def.update`'s `merged = {**rec.fields, **fields}` silently replaces the stored original with the redacted form even though the caller passed the same value. The same redaction also runs before `chk.fields`/`source`/`provenance` are merged into `data`, so the "single choke point" guarantee is not actually delivered by this code path alone.

chunk_findings.detail:
The previous finding #1 was about the leaf-exemption list being matched against data-supplied dict/list keys inside a declared text field. The replacement `_PATH_KEYS` is still a *leaf-key* exemption applied inside declared text fields, and those keys come from data — the code's own comment one line above says so ("Every other leaf of a text field is redacted whatever its key, since keys come from data (gate names, `def` fields)"), then immediately exempts a data-keyed set (`path`, `worktree`, `source_tree`, `output_file`, `output_log`). The probe that closed #1 only exercises non-path "lookup-looking" keys (e.g. `log`/`source`), so it does not cover this list.

Nothing looks up leaves *inside* a text field, so the exemption buys nothing here and only drops redaction. Concrete inputs, all of which are committed verbatim (only `secret_patterns` are masked, so hosts/home paths/private addresses/emails survive):

- `def.recorded` / `def.updated` with `data = {"fields": {"path": "[REDACTED:path]"}}` → `redact_leaves` hits `key="path"` ∈ `_PATH_KEYS`, `mask_secrets` finds no secret pattern, returns the home path unchanged.
- `gate.passed` with `data = {"evidence": {"output_log": "connect to [REDACTED:ipv4] from [REDACTED:host] failed"}}` → `redact_leaves` is called with `key="output_log"`, only secrets masked, so the private address and machine hostname leak into the shard.

This is exactly the failure mode the intent calls out ("a secret or a home path in a gate's output tail or a bug's description is committed to git"): a home path or private IP under any leaf named `path`/`output_log`/`output_file`/`worktree`/`source_tree` in a declared text field is not redacted. chunk_findings.detail: The change moves the command resolver onto `OverlayLoader`, but the import hunk is missing from `prompts.py`. The parallel change in `help.py` explicitly adds `from .overlay import OverlayError, OverlayLoader`, whereas the `prompts.py` hunk (`@@ -266,14 +266,19 @@`) only adds `_command_loader()` and the `try/except OverlayError` block and adds no import line. As a result the new code references two names it never binds: `OverlayLoader` inside `_command_loader()` and `OverlayError` in `except OverlayError as exc:`. Concretely, any call that reaches the file-resolution path — e.g. `resolve_command("dev", repo)` with a valid command — first evaluates `_command_loader()`, which raises `NameError: name 'OverlayLoader' is not defined`. Because a `NameError` is not an `OverlayError`, it is not converted to `TemplateError` and escapes to the caller, so the resolver crashes for every input instead of returning a `Template` or the previous `TemplateError`. Add the `from .overlay import OverlayError, OverlayLoader` import to `prompts.py` (or confirm both names are already bound at module top; if only `OverlayError` is bound for the existing macro branch, `OverlayLoader` is still unbound).

chunk_findings.detail: `whole` decides whether an upper bound exists by truthiness (`hi and v > hi` / `f" and at most {hi}" if hi else " or more"`) rather than by `hi is not None`. Since `hi` is annotated `int | None`, `0` is a legal bound but is treated the same as `None`. Concretely, `whole("x", 0, 0)(5, [])` returns `5` with an empty `errors` list, i.e. a check that should accept only `0` silently accepts every non-negative integer (and its message would say "must be a whole number, 0 or more, got ..." instead of "and at most 0"). Any caller that passes `hi=0` — a range pinned at a single allowed value, e.g. a flag-like numeric field — gets no validation at all and no error string. Using `hi is not None` in both the comparison and the message construction fixes it. Note this is latent in the extracted module; whether a caller in the schedule/trigger code actually passes `hi=0` is in the parts of the diff not shown here, which is the only reason I rate it LOW rather than higher.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/fieldcheck.py:57-64 (`whole`)

chunk_findings.detail:
The rewritten `load_files` no longer uses the real file name to build the reported source; it reconstructs it from the parsed id: `(SCHEDULES_DIR / (jid + ".toml")).as_posix()`. `jid` is guaranteed only to equal `Path(f.name).stem`, which is *not* always `f.name` minus the literal suffix `.toml`. Two concrete divergences:

- Case-insensitive filesystems (macOS/Windows): `d.glob("*.toml")` matches a file stored as `job.TOML`, whose `stem` is `job`, so the check passes and the original code produced `file:.ddflow/schedules/job.TOML` (from `f.name`), but the new code produces `file:.ddflow/schedules/job.toml`. The `.TOML` file's source string silently changes, contradicting the stated "no behaviour change" / golden-pinned output.
- A dotfile literally named `.toml` (which `pathlib`'s glob matches, unlike the `glob` module): `Path(".toml").stem == ".toml"` (leading-dot names have no suffix), so `jid == f.stem` passes, but the reconstructed name is `.toml.toml` instead of `.toml`, i.e. the source becomes `file:.ddflow/schedules/.toml.toml`.

In both cases the pipeline emits a source string that does not correspond to any file on disk, so downstream references/dedup that key off `file:<rel>` differ from before. The fix is to have `load_toml_dir` return the actual file name (or `(jid, job, rel)`), rather than deriving the name from `jid + ".toml"`.

chunk_findings.detail:
The upper-bound test uses truthiness rather than a `None` check:

```python
if not isinstance(v, int) or isinstance(v, bool) or v < lo or (hi and v > hi):
```

When `hi == 0`, `hi` is falsy, so the `v > hi` clause is skipped and the bound is silently dropped; the message on line 61 (`top = f" and at most {hi}" if hi else " or more"`) likewise degrades to "or more". Concretely, `whole("count", 0, 0)(5, errors)` returns `5` and appends nothing, even though the declared range is exactly `0`. The helper's API reserves `None` as the "no upper bound" sentinel, so a caller that legitimately wants a zero ceiling (e.g. a value that must be `0`) gets an unbounded check instead — a validation bypass rather than a rejected input. The fix is to test `hi is not None and v > hi` (and `hi is not None` for the message).

chunk_findings.detail: The rewrite drops the explicit `candidates.sort(key=lambda c: -c["score"])` and now returns whatever order `similar(...)` yields, while the function's own docstring still promises "sorted by score descending". Previously the order was deterministic: candidates were appended in `existing_rules` iteration order and then stably sorted by `-score`, so for `existing_rules = [R_low, R_high]` with `R_low.similarity_score(content) == 0.5` and `R_high.similarity_score(content) == 0.9` (both `>= threshold`), the result was `[R_high(0.9), R_low(0.5)]`, and any caller using `candidates[0]` as the best match (the `rule_dedup_check_dry_run`/CLI path) reported `R_high`. The new code has no local ordering step and does not establish that `similar` sorts descending with the same stable tie-break, so if `similar` returns findings in record-iteration order (or with any other tie-break), the same input now yields `[R_low(0.5), R_high(0.9)]`, i.e. a different candidate list order and a different "closest existing rule" — directly contradicting the stated goal of byte-identical dedupe candidates/order. Ties are the clearest case: the old stable sort preserved `existing_rules` order for equal scores, a property that must be verified/restored rather than assumed of `similar`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/rules.py:rule_dedup_check

chunk_findings.detail: The parser builds the `Scope` sequence fields with `tuple(data.get("globs", ()))`, and likewise for `categories`/`gates`. Given an authored file that uses a single string value, e.g. `globs = "*.py"`, `tuple("*.py")` returns `('*', '.', 'p', 'y')`. The resolver then sees `*` as a glob matching every path, so a rule meant only for Python files applies globally (and the extra `.`/`p`/`y` patterns add further unintended matches). Even if a single string is considered schema-invalid, silently exploding it into character globs is a dangerous corruption; it should either be accepted as one pattern or rejected with a clear error.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/guidance/fileformat.py:64-66

chunk_findings.detail: In `render`, the condition `if rec.level or spec.default_level:` emits `scope = {rec.level}`. When a record’s level is empty (for example a record created without an explicit scope) and the kind has a non-empty default such as `"project"`, the rendered file contains `scope = ""`. Parsing that file back uses `level=data.get("scope", spec.default_level)`; because the `scope` key is present with an empty string, the result is `""`, not the kind’s default `"project"`. The condition indicates the intent was to record the effective level, so it should emit `rec.level or spec.default_level` (or omit the key when `rec.level` is empty).
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/guidance/fileformat.py:97-98

chunk_findings.detail: `decision_record` hardcodes `enforcement=DECISION.default_enforcement`, so every decision becomes `"warn"`, and `DECISION.extras` has no `enforcement` entry to preserve a per-decision value. The adjacent `DECISION` definition explicitly says “a decision warns by default; it may be set to block or advisory”, but this adapter never reads any such setting and the authored-file field list cannot round-trip it. Concrete input: a logged decision carrying `enforcement: "block"` (or a decision file with `enforcement: block` in front matter) is converted into a `GuidanceRecord` with `enforcement == "warn"`; `decision applicable`/`brief` then reports and ranks it as a warning instead of a block, and rendering/parsing the decision drops the `block`/`advisory` setting entirely.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/guidance/kinds.py decision_record (enforcement)

chunk_findings.detail: The two "allowed" checks in `over_limit` disagree about what an empty allow-list means. The tag check is guarded for the empty case — `if lim.tags_allowed and (bad := [t for t in rec.tags if t not in lim.tags_allowed])` — so an empty `tags_allowed` (the natural default when a project does not configure tags) accepts any tag. The scope check has no such guard: `if rec.level not in lim.scopes_allowed` will reject *every* record whenever `scopes_allowed` is the empty list, because no level value can be a member of `[]`. Given a config whose `[rules]` section leaves `scopes_allowed` at its default (empty list), a perfectly valid record with `level="project"` is refused with `scope 'project' is not in rules.scopes_allowed []`, even though the tag dimension is treated as unrestricted in exactly the same situation. Since the two lists are the same kind of concept, at least one of the two checks must be wrong; under the reading implied by the tag guard (empty = no restriction), the scope check wrongly rejects all records and `[rules]` limit messaging diverges for any project that does not set `scopes_allowed`. Add the same `if lim.scopes_allowed and ...` guard, or make the empty-list semantics explicit for both.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/guidance/limits.py :: over_limit (scope check)

chunk_findings.detail: For a `GuidanceRecord` whose `scope` has `always=False` and no gates, categories or globs (e.g. a rule/decision authored without any of those keys, which the module docstring explicitly says "applies always"), `_applies` falls through all three guards with `reason` still `""` and returns `Applies(rec, "", ())` at line 60. The documented contract for `Applies.reason` (lines 28-30) permits only `ALWAYS`, `GLOBS`, `CATEGORY`, or `GATE`, and the resolve docstring promises that "guidance with no restriction at all applies always." Since `Applies` is always truthy, `resolve` still includes the record, so applicability is unaffected, but any consumer that keys on `reason` (dedupe candidates, similarity scoring, or rendering the "why") now sees an empty/unknown reason and treats an unrestricted-but-not-flagged record differently from an identical `always: true` record. The fix is to set `reason = ALWAYS` for the empty case (or return `Applies(rec, ALWAYS, ())` after the guards).
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/guidance/resolve.py:45-60 (_applies)

chunk_findings.detail:
`names()` sorts ids with `key=lambda n: n + suffix`, i.e. it sorts the reconstructed *file names* rather than the ids. For any two ids where one is a prefix of the other and the next character of the longer id is below `'.'` (0x2E) — which includes the very common kebab-case `-` (0x2D) — the relative order flips versus sorting ids. With ids `commit` and `commit-message`:

- `sorted(["commit", "commit-message"])` → `["commit", "commit-message"]`
- `sorted(["commit", "commit-message"], key=lambda n: n + ".toml")` compares `"commit-message.toml"` vs `"commit.toml"`, and at index 6 `'-' < '.'`, giving `["commit-message", "commit"]`.

So the returned list is `commit-message, commit` where the id-ordered list (the usual `sorted(p.stem for p in dir.glob("*.toml"))`) is `commit, commit-message`. If the pre-change rule/decision listing ordered ids, `rules list` / `decisions list` now emits the pair in the opposite order, contradicting the "byte-identical CLI output" requirement; `all()` inherits the same order since it iterates `names()`. The same holds for dot-prefixed ids (`foo` vs `foo.bar`).
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/guidance/store.py: GuidanceFiles.names

chunk_findings.detail: `all()` is a read/listing entry point but calls `self.ensure_dir()`, so merely listing a kind's records now creates `.ddflow/<directory>/` on disk as a side effect (observed whenever `all()` is called in a repo that has no such directory yet). On a read-only checkout this turns a listing that should return an empty list into `PermissionError` from `mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)` instead of the documented "every record that loads" behavior.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/guidance/store.py: GuidanceFiles.all

chunk_findings.detail: The old `list()` wrapped the entire load-and-filter body in `except Exception: continue`, so any rule file that failed to load was silently skipped. The new implementation delegates only the *file* read to `self.files.all()` and then calls `Rule.from_record(rec)` unconditionally, outside any guard. `GuidanceFiles` is the shared, generic record store; it cannot perform the rule-specific `Record -> Rule` conversion (that is what `Rule.from_record` is for), so a file that parses as valid TOML/record but violates the `Rule` schema (e.g. `bad.toml` missing a field `Rule.from_record` requires such as `title`) is still handed back by `files.all()` and makes `from_record` raise. Result: given a directory containing one valid rule plus one schema-invalid-but-TOML-valid file, the old code returned the valid rule, while the new code raises out of `list()`, aborting the command. This directly contradicts the docstring added in this hunk ("a file that does not load is left out"): the file *does* load at the record layer, it only fails at the `Rule` layer, which is no longer protected. This is a behavioral change (regression), not a style issue.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/rules.py::RulesStorage.list

chunk_findings.detail: The old code iterated `sorted(self.rules_dir.glob("*.toml"))`, guaranteeing a deterministic, filename-ordered list. The new code iterates `self.files.all()` directly and no longer sorts anywhere in `rules.py`. If `GuidanceFiles.all()` yields records in directory-iteration order (e.g. `os.scandir`/`Path.glob` order, which is not sorted on most filesystems) rather than a sorted order, then given files `b.toml` and `a.toml` created in that order, the old `list()` returned `[a, b]` while the new one can return `[b, a]`. Since rule list output is required to be byte-identical, this ordering dependency on the unseen `files.all()` implementation is a real risk that the explicit `sorted(...)` previously ruled out.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/rules.py::RulesStorage.list

On a read-only checkout this turns a listing that should return `[]` into `PermissionError` from `mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)`, a behavior the previous read-only listing did not have.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/guidance/store.py::GuidanceFiles.all (side effect)

chunk_findings.detail:
The hunk deletes the explicit `candidates.sort(key=lambda c: -c["score"])` and now returns `found`-order directly:

```python
found = similar([r.to_record() for r in existing_rules], content, title=title, threshold=threshold)
candidates = [ ...for f in found ]
return bool(candidates), candidates
```

while the function's own docstring (unchanged in this hunk) still promises `"candidates: List of similar rules with scores and details, sorted by score descending"`. The previous implementation appended candidates in `existing_rules` iteration order and then stably sorted descending, so the order was deterministic and score-ordered independently of how the similarity engine emitted matches. The rewrite gives that guarantee away: nothing in this hunk (or in `api/rules.py`) establishes that `similar(...)` returns matches in descending-score order rather than in input order / a partial order of its own. Concretely, with `existing_rules = [R_low, R_high]`, `R_low.similarity_score(content)` scoring `0.5` and `R_high.similarity_score(content)` scoring `0.9`, both at or above `threshold`, the old code returned `[{R_high, 0.9}, {R_low, 0.5}]`, whereas the new code returns whatever position `similar` places them in; if the engine preserves input order (the natural way to build the list) the CLI/dry-run output prints the low-score candidate first, i.e. not byte-identical and not matching the documented "sorted by score descending" contract. Either the sort must be reinstated here, or `similar` must be shown to guarantee a stable descending sort over these inputs; the diff does neither.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/rules.py:rule_dedup_check

chunk_findings.detail:
The old body guarded the store read behind the tail of an `elif` chain:

```python
if len(rule.content.encode("utf-8")) > cfg.rules.max_size_bytes:
    problem = "..."
elif rule.scope not in cfg.rules.scopes_allowed:
    ...
elif ...:
    ...
elif len(RulesStorage(repo).list()) >= cfg.rules.max_rules:
    ...
```

so `RulesStorage(repo).list()` was evaluated *only* when size, scope and tags all passed. The new call passes `len(RulesStorage(repo).list())` as an ordinary argument, and Python evaluates arguments before the call, so the whole store listing now runs unconditionally on every `rule.add`, before `over_limit` can return the size/scope/tag refusal. Two concrete inputs make this observable and break the "byte-identical CLI output" contract:

1. `RulesStorage.list()` now delegates to `self.files.all()` and then calls `Rule.from_record(rec)` outside any guard, so a file such as `.ddflow/rules/broken.toml` that is valid TOML but whose record cannot be converted to a `Rule` raises. With that file present, `rule.add` on an oversized rule used to return `refused("rule.added", "content is over rules.max_size_bytes (...)")` (the size branch returned before the count branch ran); now the exception from `list()` propagates and no refusal message is produced at all.
2. `GuidanceFiles.all()` calls `ensure_dir()`, so merely evaluating this argument creates `.ddflow/rules/`. On a read-only checkout where `.ddflow/rules/` does not yet exist, adding an oversized rule now raises `PermissionError` from `mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)` instead of returning the size-limit refusal, and even on a writable checkout a *refused* add now leaves a newly created rules directory behind, which the previous code did not.

Both differences are caused solely by moving the store read from the condition to an eager argument.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/rules.py::_over_limits

chunk_findings.detail: This still holds; nothing in the diff answers it. `tuple()` on the value of a TOML key is only correct when the key is an array. Given an authored file with `globs = "*.py"`, `tuple("*.py")` yields `('*', '.', 'p', 'y')`; the resolver receives `*` as a glob that matches every path, so a rule written for Python files silently becomes global, and the stray `.`/`p`/`y` patterns add further unintended matches. The same construction is used for `categories` and `gates`, so `categories = "style"` likewise decomposes into `('s','t','y','l','e')`. The only guard is `lint(rec, spec)`, and an exploded string is still a tuple of strings, so a "globs must be strings" check would not catch it.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/guidance/fileformat.py:64-66 (`parse`, `scope=Scope(globs=tuple(data.get("globs", ()))...)`)

chunk_findings.detail: This still holds; the condition is unchanged. `if rec.level or spec.default_level:` writes `scope = {rec.level}` even when `rec.level` is the empty string. For a kind whose default level is non-empty (e.g. `"project"`), a record with `level == ""` is rendered as `scope = ""`. Any existing rule file that omits the `scope` key parses to `"project"` (`level=data.get("scope", spec.default_level)`); a file that the new writer produces for that same record instead pins `""`, so the file no longer expresses the kind's default and round-tripping through the new writer changes the on-disk rule text (the intent requires byte-identical rule files). The fix would be to also require `rec.level != spec.default_level` (or to omit the key when empty) rather than emitting an explicit empty scope.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/guidance/fileformat.py:97-98 (`render`)

chunk_findings.detail:
New issue: the frontmatter/content boundary is found by a literal `"

"` search, so a file written with CRLF line endings is misparsed. With `text = 'id = "r"
title = "T"

Body
'`, `split("

", 1)` matches nothing (the separator is `

`), `has_block` is `False`, and the whole file including the body is handed to `tomllib.loads`, which raises `ValueError: Invalid TOML in ... frontmatter` for a file that is valid TOML. A whitespace-only separator line (e.g. a line containing a single space) has the same effect, because the search only accepts exactly two consecutive newlines: an authored file edited on Windows or with a stray trailing space on the blank line is rejected (or, if the body happens to be valid TOML, silently treated as frontmatter). Splitting on the first line that is empty after stripping, or normalizing `
`, would make the documented "TOML frontmatter, a blank line, and the text" format actually parseable.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/guidance/fileformat.py:26-28 (`parse`, `parts = text.split("\n\n", 1)`)

chunk_findings.detail: `decision_record` maps a decision onto the shared record with `status=d.status or ACCEPTED` and stashes the supersession marker in `ext["superseded_by"]` (kinds.py lines 60-95), while `governing` relies on the generic resolver to decide liveness: `applied = resolve((decision_record(d) for d in state.decisions.values()), globs=globs)`. The generic resolver can only judge liveness from the fields it knows about — `GuidanceRecord.status` — because `superseded_by` is buried in the kind-specific `ext` dict and `KindSpec`/`resolve` carry no per-kind live predicate (the `KINDS` specs expose only kind/label/directory/limits/level/stamped/valid_id/enforcement/extras). So a superseded decision is still `status == "accepted"` (the docstring explicitly says it "stays accepted here with superseded_by set") and is treated as live. Concretely: the log holds `D1` (accepted, `superseded_by="D2"`) and `D2` (accepted, `supersedes=["D1"]`). The old path filtered on `Decision.live` (the docstring notes it "reads both", i.e. status and `superseded_by`) and returned only `D2`; the new `governing` hands `decision_record(D1)` to `resolve`, which sees `status == "accepted"` and no supersession signal, so both `D1` and `D2` are returned in the two output lists. `decision applicable now` therefore lists a withdrawn decision, differing from the previous output the change promises to keep byte-identical (and disagreeing with `brief`'s still-inline filter).
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/guidance/kinds.py:governing

chunk_findings.detail: The scope check `if rec.level not in lim.scopes_allowed:` has no empty-allow-list guard, while the very next check for tags is written defensively: `if lim.tags_allowed and (bad := [t for t in rec.tags if t not in lim.tags_allowed])`. The two "allowed" checks therefore disagree about what an empty allow-list means. If a project configures a kind's section (so `lim is not None`) without listing `scopes_allowed` — the natural "no restriction" default, matching how an omitted `tags_allowed` is treated — then `lim.scopes_allowed == []` and `rec.level not in []` is true for every possible level, so `over_limit` rejects every new record with `scope '...' is not in ...scopes_allowed []`. Concretely, with `scopes_allowed = []` and any record whose `level` is e.g. `"project"`, `over_limit` returns a limit-violation string (the second branch) even though the analogous tag list of `[]` would accept all tags, and even though a kind with no section at all (`lim is None`) accepts the same record unconditionally. This prior finding (#5) remains unaddressed here: the diff shows no `and lim.scopes_allowed`-style guard and no probe/comment establishing that `scopes_allowed` is ever non-empty when `lim` is not `None`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/guidance/limits.py:20 (over_limit, scope check)

chunk_findings.detail: `_applies` returns `Applies(rec, "", ())` whenever a record is not `scope.always` and sets none of `gates`/`categories`/`globs`: the `reason = ""` initializer at the top of the function is never overwritten and line 60 is reached with the empty string. The `Applies.reason` contract (lines ~28-30) allows only `ALWAYS`, `GLOBS`, `CATEGORY` or `GATE`, and `resolve`'s own docstring promises "Guidance with no restriction at all applies always". Concrete input: a `GuidanceRecord` with `scope.always == False` and `scope.gates == ()`, `scope.categories == ()`, `scope.globs == ()` (a rule/decision authored without any of those keys). `_applies` passes all three `if scope.*` guards, falls to the final `return Applies(rec, reason, pairs)`, and yields `reason == ""` instead of `ALWAYS`. Any consumer that branches on `Applies.reason` (e.g. to print why a rule/decision applies) sees an empty, undocumented value rather than the "applies always" the resolver documents. The diff adds no branch that maps the no-restriction case onto `ALWAYS`, so this prior finding is not answered.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/guidance/resolve.py:60 (`_applies` fall-through)

chunk_findings.detail: `all()` is a read/listing entry point, but its first statement is `self.ensure_dir()`, which performs `mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)` on `.ddflow/<spec.directory>/`. The previous `RulesStorage.list` only globbed `self.rules_dir.glob("*.toml")` and never created the directory. Consequences: (a) a pure listing now mutates the repository — `ddflow rules list` (or any caller using `all()`) creates `.ddflow/rules/` in a repo that had none; (b) on a read-only checkout, where the old code returned an empty list because the glob matched nothing, `ensure_dir()` raises `PermissionError` out of `all()`, and unlike the per-record errors it is outside the `try` block, so it is not swallowed and the documented "Every record that loads" behavior becomes an exception. `read()`/`names()` do not require the directory to exist (read raises `FileNotFoundError`, names globs an empty result), so the call is both unnecessary and observable. Input to demonstrate: a read-only checkout (or any repo without `.ddflow/rules/`) followed by `all()` → directory is created or `PermissionError` propagates; before the change `list()` returned `[]`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/guidance/store.py:92-93 (GuidanceFiles.all)

chunk_findings.detail: `decision_record` still hardcodes `enforcement=DECISION.default_enforcement` and `DECISION.extras` still has no `enforcement` entry, so a logged decision carrying `enforcement: "block"` (or a decision file with that field) is coerced to `"warn"` and cannot round-trip. The adjacent `DECISION` comment says a decision "may be set to block or advisory", so the adapter contradicts its own schema. Demonstrated input: parse a decision record whose source dict contains `{"enforcement": "block", ...}`; the produced `GuidanceRecord` comes back with `enforcement == "warn"`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/guidance/kinds.py :: decision_record

chunk_findings.detail: The parser builds `Scope` sequence fields with `tuple(data.get("globs", ()))` (same for `categories`/`gates`). Given an authored file with a single string value, `globs = "*.py"`, `tuple("*.py")` yields `('*', '.', 'p', 'y')`, so the resolver sees `*` and the rule applies to every path, with `.`/`p`/`y` adding further unintended matches. A one-value string should either be rejected loudly or wrapped as a one-element tuple; silently exploding it changes applicability.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/guidance/fileformat.py:64-66

chunk_findings.detail: `render` emits `scope = {rec.level}` under `if rec.level or spec.default_level:`. For a record whose level is empty and whose kind default is non-empty (e.g. `"project"`), the file contains `scope = ""`; parsing that back uses `level=data.get("scope", spec.default_level)` and, because the key is present with an empty string, returns `""` instead of `"project"`. Round-tripping a default-scoped record therefore loses its default.

chunk_findings.detail: The explicit `candidates.sort(key=lambda c: -c["score"])` was dropped and the function now returns whatever order `similar(...)` yields, while the docstring still promises score-descending order. With `existing_rules = [R_low, R_high]` where `R_low` scores 0.5 and `R_high` 0.9 (both `>= threshold`), the old result was `[R_high, R_low]`; if `similar` preserves input order the new result is `[R_low, R_high]`, changing CLI/dedup output.

chunk_findings.detail: The scope check `if rec.level not in lim.scopes_allowed` has no empty-list guard, unlike the tag check `if lim.tags_allowed and ...`. When `scopes_allowed` is the natural empty default for an unconfigured project, no level can satisfy `not in []`, so every record is reported over limit and the `[rules]` limit message fires for all rules.

chunk_findings.detail: For a record with `scope.always=False` and no gates/categories/globs (the module docstring says this "applies always"), `_applies` falls through all guards with `reason` still `""` and returns `Applies(rec, "", ())`. `Applies.reason` is documented to be one of `ALWAYS`/`GLOBS`/`CATEGORY`/`GATE`, so any consumer that switches on `reason` (or treats `""` as "not applicable") misclassifies an always-applicable record; an always-applicable rule/decision should report `ALWAYS`.

chunk_findings.detail: The old `list()` wrapped the whole load-and-filter body in `except Exception: continue`, silently skipping any file that failed to load. The new implementation delegates only the file read to `self.files.all()` and then calls `Rule.from_record(rec)` unguarded; a file that parses as valid TOML/record syntax but not as a valid rule makes `list()` raise instead of skipping, changing behavior for a corrupt/legacy rule file.

chunk_findings.detail:
`all()` is a read/listing entry point but calls `self.ensure_dir()`, so merely listing a kind's records now creates `.ddflow/<directory>/` on disk. In a repo without that directory, a listing that should return `[]` instead creates it, and on a read-only checkout it raises `PermissionError` from `mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)` rather than returning the documented "every record that loads" result.

Note on the two order findings (store.names sort key `n + suffix`, and "RulesStorage.list no longer sorts"): both compare the new ordering against id-sorting, but the previous implementation sorted `Path` objects from `glob("*.toml")`, i.e. by filename; filename order and `n + suffix` order coincide for the cited `commit`/`commit-message` case, so no before/after difference is demonstrated and I am not reporting them.

chunk_findings.detail: The rewrite drops `candidates.sort(key=lambda c: -c["score"])` and returns `similar(...)` order while the docstring still promises "sorted by score descending". With `existing_rules = [R_low, R_high]`, `R_low.similarity_score(content) == 0.5` and `R_high.similarity_score(content) == 0.9` (both `>= threshold`), the old code returned `[R_high, R_low]`; the new code returns whatever order `similar(...)` yields (input order, i.e. `[R_low, R_high]`), changing dedupe candidate order. The fenced diff contains no sort in this path.

chunk_findings.detail: The parser still builds the `Scope` sequence fields with `tuple(data.get("globs", ()))`. An authored rule `globs = "*.py"` becomes `('*', '.', 'p', 'y')`, so the resolver sees the `*` glob and applies the rule to every path (plus spurious `.`/`p`/`y` matches). `Rule.from_toml` now routes through this parser, so `from_toml('... globs = "*.py" ...')` yields a rule that matches everything. The fenced diff does not change the parser.

chunk_findings.detail: `render` still emits `scope = {rec.level}` whenever `rec.level or spec.default_level`, so a record with empty level and a non-empty kind default renders `scope = ""`; parsing back uses the present-but-empty key (`data.get("scope", spec.default_level)`), yielding `""` instead of the default. The new `Rule.to_toml` calls this renderer, so a rule with an empty `scope` does not round-trip to the kind default. Not addressed in this part.

The fenced diff does not change `_applies`.

For ids `commit` and `commit-message`, full-name order is `["commit-message", "commit"]` because `-` (0x2D) < `.` (0x2E), while id order is `["commit", "commit-message"]`, so listing order flips. Not touched here.

chunk_findings.detail: The new path calls `Rule.from_record(rec)` on every record returned by `GuidanceFiles.all()`. The old `list()` wrapped the load/filter body in `except Exception: continue`, silently skipping bad files; the fenced `from_record` has no guard (and does unguarded `rec.provenance["created"]`/`["updated"]` and `rec.scope.globs`), so a file that parses as a generic record but lacks rule-specific data now propagates an exception out of `list()` instead of being skipped. The fenced diff shows no compensating guard around this conversion.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/rules.py :: RulesStorage.list

chunk_findings.detail: The old `list()` iterated `sorted(self.rules_dir.glob("*.toml"))`; the new one iterates `self.files.all()` with no sort in `rules.py`. If `GuidanceFiles.all()` yields directory order (unsorted on most filesystems), files `b.toml`/`a.toml` created in that order make `list()` return `[b, a]` instead of the previous `[a, b]`. Not fixed by the fenced code.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/rules.py :: RulesStorage.list

chunk_findings.detail:
Prior finding 9 still holds. The old `list()` wrapped the whole per-file body (`self.get(...)` → `Rule.from_toml`, plus filtering) in `try/except Exception: continue`, so any rule file that failed to load was silently dropped. The rewritten body no longer has that guard:

```python
for rec in self.files.all():
    rule = Rule.from_record(rec)
    ...
```

The new docstring ("a file that does not load is left out") only covers failures inside `GuidanceFiles.all()` — i.e. a file that cannot be read or parsed into a generic `Record`. It does not cover failures in the rule-specific `Record -> Rule` conversion, because that call sits in `rules.py`, outside any guard. `GuidanceFiles` is the shared, kind-agnostic store, so its record schema cannot enforce Rule-specific invariants (e.g. a recognized `severity`, or a required rule field that the shared schema treats as optional). Concretely, an authored file such as a rule TOML carrying a plausible-but-invalid rule value (for example a `severity` string the `Rule` constructor/enum rejects, or a rule file missing a field that `from_record` dereferences but the shared schema defaults) parses cleanly into a `Record`, so `all()` yields it, and then `Rule.from_record(rec)` raises out of `list()` instead of being skipped. Old behaviour: `list()` returned the remaining valid rules; new behaviour: it raises, changing the CLI/API result for a directory whose only difference is one malformed rule file. The fix would be to restore a per-record guard around `Rule.from_record` (matching the docstring's "left out" promise), which the shown hunk does not do.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/rules.py :: RulesStorage.list

chunk_findings.detail: This test is the only probe added for score ordering, and it cannot detect the regression finding 1 describes. The input `[a, b, c]` has `a` scoring 1.0 and `c` scoring 0.75, and `a` precedes `c` in the input list; after `b` is filtered out, the expected result `[("a", 1.0), ("c", 0.75)]` is exactly what an implementation that returns `similar(...)` results in *input order* would also produce. So if `api/rules.py::rule_dedup_check` still returns whatever order `similar` yields (the dropped `candidates.sort(key=lambda c: -c["score"])`), this test passes and the docstring's "sorted by score descending" promise remains unverified. Concrete distinguishing input: call `similar([c, b, a], "", title="tests come first", threshold=0.5)`; an unsorted implementation yields `[("c", 0.75), ("a", 1.0)]` while a sorting one yields `[("a", 1.0), ("c", 0.75)]` — the current test data cannot separate these, so finding 1 is not answered.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_guidance_core.py::test_similar_compares_titles_for_title_only_guidance_and_orders_by_score (re-report of finding 1)

chunk_findings.detail: The only new test that renders a record with an unset `level` deliberately asserts nothing about the rendered text or the round-tripped level — it checks `got.provenance["created"]`/`["updated"]` only. Given the render condition `if rec.level or spec.default_level:` and a truthy `RULE.default_level` (the tests use `"project"` throughout, e.g. `_cfg(scopes_allowed=["project"])` and the `scope 'task' is not in ... ['project']` message), the empty-`level` branch is still taken and emits `scope = ""`. Parsing that back gives `level == ""` (the `scope` key is present), whereas before the key was omitted and the kind default applied, so a rule authored/saved without a scope gains a `scope = ""` line that changes its meaning on re-read. Concrete input: `RulesStorage.update("r-naming", priority=90)` on a file `r-naming.toml` with `id`/`title`/`priority` and no `scope` key (the test `test_editing_a_rule_keeps_the_keys_a_person_put_in_the_file` only uses a file that already contains `scope = "project"`), or `fileformat.parse(fileformat.render(GuidanceRecord(id="r-z", kind="rule", title="z", body="b"), RULE), RULE).level`, which is `""` rather than `"project"`. No test in this diff pins this case, so finding 3 still holds.

chunk_findings.detail: `tuple(data.get("globs", ()))` (and the `categories`/`gates` twins) explodes a scalar TOML value into characters. For an authored file with `globs = "*.py"`, the parsed `Scope.globs` becomes `('*', '.', 'p', 'y')`; the resolver then treats `*` as a pattern that matches every path, so a rule intended only for Python files silently applies globally, and `.`/`p`/`y` add further spurious matches. The visible test diff does not address this (it only exercises `Rule`-constructed records, never the file parser).

chunk_findings.detail: `if rec.level or spec.default_level:` emits `scope = {rec.level}` even when `rec.level == ""` and the kind default is non-empty. Given a record whose level is empty and a kind with `default_level = "project"`, `render` writes `scope = ""`; parsing that back runs `level = data.get("scope", spec.default_level)`, and because the `scope` key is present the result is `""` rather than `"project"`. A freshly parsed record (key absent) would get `"project"`, so the same logical record round-trips to two different scopes. Not covered by the test-only diff.

chunk_findings.detail: The adapter hardcodes `enforcement=DECISION.default_enforcement` and provides no `enforcement` entry in `DECISION.extras`, so every decision becomes `"warn"` and a per-decision value cannot round-trip. Given a decision logged/authored with `enforcement = "block"` (the adjacent `DECISION` definition says a decision "may be set to block or advisory"), it is read back as `"warn"`. The test diff does not exercise decision enforcement at all.

chunk_findings.detail: The scope check `if rec.level not in lim.scopes_allowed` is unguarded, unlike the tag check `if lim.tags_allowed and (...)`. With `scopes_allowed = []` (the natural default when a project configures no scopes), no level value satisfies membership, so every record is reported over-limit — whereas an empty `tags_allowed` accepts any tag. Input: a limits config with an empty scope allow-list and any record → spurious "[rules] limit" rejection. Not touched by the test diff.

chunk_findings.detail: For a record whose `scope.always` is `False` and which has no gates, categories or globs, all three guards fall through with `reason` still `""`, returning `Applies(rec, "", ())`. `Applies.reason` is documented to be one of `ALWAYS`/`GLOBS`/`CATEGORY`/`GATE`, and the module docstring says guidance with no restrictions "applies always". Any caller that switches on `reason` (e.g. treating only `ALWAYS` as unconditional) will misclassify such a record. The test diff asserts `hit.reason == "globs"` only for a globbed rule, so this path is untested.

chunk_findings.detail: `all()` calls `self.ensure_dir()` before listing, so a read-only operation creates `.ddflow/<directory>/` as a side effect. In a read-only checkout (or where the parent is not writable), `mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)` raises `PermissionError`, turning a listing that should return `[]` on a repo with no records into an exception. Not addressed by the test-only diff.

chunk_findings.detail: `decision_record` hardcodes `enforcement=DECISION.default_enforcement`, so every decision becomes `"warn"`, and `DECISION.extras` has no `enforcement` entry to preserve a per-decision value — contradicting the adjacent definition that says a decision may be set to block or advisory. Input: a logged/decision file carrying `enforcement: "block"` round-trips back as `"warn"`. Untriaged, unchanged here.

chunk_findings.detail: The parser builds sequence fields with `tuple(data.get("globs", ()))` (same for `categories`/`gates`). Given an authored file using a single string, e.g. `globs = "*.py"`, `tuple("*.py")` returns `('*', '.', 'p', 'y')`; the resolver then treats `*` as matching every path, so a Python-only rule applies globally (plus spurious `.`/`p`/`y` matches). Untriaged, unchanged here.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/guidance/fileformat.py:64-66

chunk_findings.detail: `render` emits `scope = {rec.level}` whenever `rec.level or spec.default_level`; when a record's level is empty and the kind's default is non-empty (e.g. `"project"`), the file gets `scope = ""`. Parsing it back takes `data.get("scope", spec.default_level)`, and because the `scope` key is present with `""`, the result is `""`, not the default — a round-trip that changes semantics. Untriaged, unchanged here.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/guidance/fileformat.py:97-98

chunk_findings.detail: The rewrite drops the explicit `candidates.sort(key=lambda c: -c["score"])` and returns whatever order `similar(...)` yields, while the docstring still promises "sorted by score descending". With `existing_rules = [R_low, R_high]`, `R_low.similarity_score(content)=0.5`, `R_high=0.9` (both `>= threshold`), a caller relying on the documented order can receive the low-score candidate first. Untriaged, unchanged here.

chunk_findings.detail: The two allow-list checks disagree on the empty case: the tag check is guarded (`if lim.tags_allowed and ...`) so an empty `tags_allowed` accepts any tag, but the scope check `if rec.level not in lim.scopes_allowed` rejects *every* record when `scopes_allowed` is the empty list (the natural default when a project configures no scopes), because no level value is in `[]`. Untriaged, unchanged here.

chunk_findings.detail: `names()` sorts with `key=lambda n: n + suffix`, i.e. by reconstructed file name rather than by id. For `commit` and `commit-message`, `sorted(ids)` gives `["commit", "commit-message"]`, but sorting `"commit.toml"` vs `"commit-message.toml"` flips (`'-'` 0x2D < `'.'` 0x2E), so the listing order differs from id order. Untriaged, unchanged here.

chunk_findings.detail: `all()` calls `self.ensure_dir()`, so merely listing a kind's records creates `.ddflow/<directory>/`; on a read-only checkout this turns a listing that should return `[]` into `PermissionError` from `mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)`. Untriaged, unchanged here.

chunk_findings.detail:
The old `list()` wrapped the load-and-filter body in `except Exception: continue`, silently skipping unloadable rule files. The new implementation delegates only the file read to `self.files.all()` and then calls `Rule.from_record(rec)` unconditionally, outside any guard; a file that parses as valid TOML/record but fails the rule-specific conversion now raises instead of being skipped. Untriaged, unchanged here.

I did not re-report the "RulesStorage.list loses filename ordering" item: `GuidanceFiles.names()` reconstructs and sorts file names, so if `all()` derives its listing from `names()` the order is already sorted-by-filename and the old `sorted(glob("*.toml"))` behavior is preserved.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/rules.py:RulesStorage.list

chunk_findings.detail:
The guard and the value disagree. `render` only writes the level when `rec.level` is truthy *or* the kind has a default level, but it always writes the raw `rec.level`:

    if rec.level or spec.default_level:
        lines.append(f"scope = {_toml_value(rec.level)}")

So for a kind with `spec.default_level = "project"` and a record whose `level` is the empty string, the guard passes and the output contains an explicit `scope = ""` (not the default). On the next read, `parse` does `level=data.get("scope", spec.default_level)` and, because the key is now present, returns `level=""` instead of falling back to `"project"`. The default is therefore never re-applied after a save/reload cycle: a rule that was meant to be project-scoped comes back with an empty scope, and any resolver/CLI logic that keys on the level (e.g. matching `"project"` rules) will treat it as unscoped. The guard indicates the intent was to persist the effective level (`rec.level or spec.default_level`); writing bare `rec.level` loses it.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/guidance/fileformat.py render (`if rec.level or spec.default_level`)

chunk_findings.detail: `decision_record` unconditionally sets `enforcement=DECISION.default_enforcement`, i.e. the hard-coded `"warn"`, and it never reads the decision's own enforcement setting. This directly contradicts the comment attached to the same KindSpec (`D-decision-management: a decision warns by default; it may be set to block or advisory.`) — if a decision can be set to `block` or `advisory`, the only place that value can enter the shared engine is this adapter, and the adapter maps every other optional Decision field (`context`, `consequences`, `alternatives`, `decided_by`, `item`, `supersedes`, `superseded_by`) into the record but silently drops enforcement. Concrete case: a decision recorded with enforcement `block` (e.g. an event whose payload carries `enforcement: "block"` per D-decision-management) is converted to a `GuidanceRecord` with `enforcement == "warn"`, so `resolve`/`governing` treat it as a mere warning. `decision applicable` and `brief` will then report it as warn (and not gate work) for input where the previous Decision-based path would have honored the decision's blocking enforcement — a behaviour change for `decision applicable now` of exactly the kind this change is supposed to preserve. Either `decision_record` must carry `d.enforcement or DECISION.default_enforcement`, or the KindSpec comment asserting configurability is false and the `block`/`advisory` path is unreachable.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/guidance/kinds.py :: decision_record

chunk_findings.detail:
The branch choice is driven by the *new* side's `title`, so the same pair of guidance can get two different scores depending on which member is the new one — and only one of those two directions preserves the old content-only score. Concretely, take A = `{title: "foo bar", body: ""}` (title-only) and B = `{title: "", body: "foo bar baz"}` (body-only, i.e. content but no title):

- With B already stored and A being added: `compared(B, title="foo bar", content="")` — `not title` is false, `content and rec.body` is `"" and "foo bar baz"` → falsy, `not content and not rec.body` is `True and False` → false, so it falls into the combined branch: `theirs = "foo bar baz"`, `mine = "foo bar"`, `jaccard(...) = 2/3 ≈ 0.667 ≥ 0.55` → A is refused as a duplicate.
- With A already stored and B being added: `compared(A, title="", content="foo bar baz")` — `not title` short-circuits, returning `jaccard(rec.body="", content) = 0.0` → B is accepted.

Before this change both directions scored `jaccard(body="", body)` = 0.0, so the pair could always coexist. Now duplicate detection for a title-only rule against a body-only rule is insertion-order dependent: one order rejects, the reverse accepts. So the "dedupe candidates/scores are byte-identical" claim does not hold, and more importantly the resolver's dedupe is non-deterministic for this input (a rule is treated as a duplicate of another that is not a duplicate of it).

The root cause is the `not title` short-circuit combined with the combined-text branch: a title on one side only is used for the score in the combined branch but ignored (content-only) in the other direction.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/guidance/similarity.py: `compared`

chunk_findings.detail: `read` treats a record that exists only in the shipped pack as existing (`if not (path.is_file() or self.loader.shipped_path(rid).is_file())` at store.py:57), but `write(..., new=True)` checks only the project path (`if new and path.exists()`). Concretely, with a shipped record `.ddflow/.../templates/guidance/<directory>/acl.toml` present and no project file, `read("acl")` returns the shipped record, yet `write(rec_for_acl, new=True)` does not raise — it silently creates `.ddflow/<directory>/acl.toml`, which then shadows the shipped record, contradicting the method's own contract ("``new`` refuses to replace one that exists"). The same asymmetry affects `delete` (it raises "not found" for a shipped-only record that `read` happily returns). Either `new`/`delete` should consult `shipped_path` too, or the shipped layer should not be considered a record for those operations.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/guidance/store.py:write

chunk_findings.detail: The old `list()` wrapped the per-file load in `try/except Exception` (`self.get(...)` + `Rule.from_toml`), so a `.toml` file that parses but fails rule validation was skipped and the remaining rules were still returned. The new body iterates `self.files.all()` and calls `Rule.from_record(rec)` with no exception guard. `GuidanceFiles.all()` only guarantees that files which "do not load" as records are dropped (`RULE`-typed records are returned as parsed dicts); rule-level validation still happens in `Rule.from_record`. Concrete input: `.ddflow/rules/r-bad.toml` containing valid TOML that lacks a required field (e.g. `title = "x"` with no `id`). Old behavior: `Rule.from_record`/`from_toml` raises, the `except` swallows it, and `list()` returns the other rules. New behavior: the exception propagates out of `list()`, so a single malformed rule file makes the whole `rules list` fail (and contradicts the newly added docstring "a file that does not load is left out"). This is a real behavior change for tolerant listing, not covered by the byte-identical-output claim.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/rules.py: RulesStorage.list

chunk_findings.detail: The expected value is recomputed with the same primitives the engine is being checked against (`d.live`, `conflicts(globs, d.globs)`) instead of calling the inline decision filter it is named after (`api/lifecycle/brief.py`, and the filter in `api/decisions.py`). So the test only proves `governing` equals a copy of itself; it cannot fail when `governing` and the retained inline filter disagree about applicability. The fixture shows this concretely: `_decisions()` deliberately includes `D-4` (`status="proposed"`, no globs) and `D-5` (`status="accepted"`, `superseded_by="D-next"`), which are exactly the rows that discriminate. If brief.py's filter admits only `status == "accepted"` decisions into the "always applicable" list (so `D-4` must not appear) while the new `live` predicate used by the engine counts `proposed`, then for `globs=["README.md"]` `governing` returns `D-4` in `wide` and the test still passes, because line `wide = [d for d in st.decisions.values() if d.live and not d.globs]` builds the expectation with `d.live` too. Same for `globs=[]`: whatever `governing` does with an empty incoming glob list is mirrored by the recomputation. The invariant "decision applicable now" is therefore pinned against nothing, and the discriminating inputs the author added never discriminate.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_guidance_core.py :: test_governing_answers_what_the_two_inline_filters_did

chunk_findings.detail: The ratchet only collects `Import`/`ImportFrom` alias `.name`s, `Name.id`, `Attribute.attr`, and `FunctionDef`/`ClassDef` names, so it can be satisfied while the deleted rule/decision-specific tokenizer is reintroduced. `from ddflow.core.textsim import words` records the alias name `words` and later a `Name(id='words')`; neither is in `{"fnmatch", "textsim", "_globs_match", "_tokenize", "matches_globs"}`, so the check passes even though `ddflow/services/rules.py` is tokenizing again. Likewise `import ddflow.core.textsim as ts` records alias name `ddflow.core.textsim` (the dotted path, not `textsim`) and `ts.words(...)` records only `Name(id='ts')` / `Attribute(attr='words')`. And because only `ast.FunctionDef`/`ast.ClassDef` are walked (not `ast.AsyncFunctionDef`), a re-added `async def _tokenize(...)` is invisible to the test as well.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_guidance_core.py :: test_no_rule_or_decision_specific_matcher_or_tokenizer_remains
