chunk_findings.detail: The old filter classified a live decision purely on `d.globs`: `wide = [d for d in st.decisions.values() if d.live and not d.globs]`, i.e. *every* glob-less live decision was project-wide, regardless of any other fields. `governing(st, it.globs)` runs the shared resolver, which additionally evaluates scope/categories/gates (see the `_applies` behavior). For a live decision that has no `globs` but does carry `categories` (or `gates`) that do not match the item, the old code returned it in `project_wide` while the new code will not — so `ddflow decision <item> --applicable` changes its `project_wide`/exit status. This is exactly the "decision applicable now differs from before" case the intent claims is byte-identical.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/decisions.py:_decisions applicable/`governing` switch

chunk_findings.detail: The explicit `candidates.sort(key=lambda c: -c["score"])` is dropped and the function returns `similar(...)` order. With `existing_rules = [R_low, R_high]`, `R_low.similarity_score(content) == 0.5`, `R_high.similarity_score(content) == 0.9` (both `>= threshold`), the old code returned `[R_high, R_low]`; the new code returns them in whatever order `similar` yields (append/iteration order → `[R_low, R_high]`), so the reported dedupe scores/order differ from before while the docstring still promises descending score. Untriaged, so no probe refutes it.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/rules.py:rule_dedup_check (dedupe candidate order)

chunk_findings.detail: `tuple(data.get("globs", ()))` (and the same for `categories`/`gates`) turns a single-string value into a character tuple: `globs = "*.py"` → `('*', '.', 'p', 'y')`. The resolver then treats `*` as matching every path, so a rule authored for Python only applies globally, and `.`/`p`/`y` add further unintended matches. Parsing therefore differs from the previous rule-file handling; a scalar is silently exploded instead of rejected.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/guidance/fileformat.py:64-66 (parse)

chunk_findings.detail: `if rec.level or spec.default_level:` emits `scope = {rec.level}`. For a record whose `level` is empty and a kind default of `"project"`, this writes `scope = ""`. Parsing back uses `level = data.get("scope", spec.default_level)`; because the `scope` key is present with an empty string, the result is `""` rather than the default `"project"`. Render→parse is thus not identity, changing scope-dependent behavior.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/guidance/fileformat.py:97-98 (render/parse round-trip)

chunk_findings.detail: `decision_record` hardcodes `enforcement=DECISION.default_enforcement` and `DECISION.extras` exposes no `enforcement`, so every decision round-trips as `"warn"` even though the adjacent definition states a decision "may be set to block or advisory". A decision logged with `enforcement: "block"` (or a decision file carrying it) is silently downgraded; unlike the old path it cannot be preserved.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/guidance/kinds.py:decision_record (enforcement)

chunk_findings.detail: The tag check guards the empty list (`if lim.tags_allowed and ...`) so an empty `tags_allowed` accepts everything, but the scope check does not (`if rec.level not in lim.scopes_allowed`). When a project configures no scopes (`scopes_allowed == []`), every record is rejected, whereas the analogous no-tags case is accepted — a limit message ("[rules] limit") that fires for input it should not.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/guidance/limits.py::over_limit (scope check)

chunk_findings.detail: For a record with `scope.always=False` and no gates/categories/globs, all three guards fall through with `reason` still `""`, returning `Applies(rec, "", ())`. The documented contract permits only `ALWAYS`, `GLOBS`, `CATEGORY`, `GATE`, and the docstring says such guidance "applies always"; callers that compare `reason` (or expect `ALWAYS`) get a different value from before.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/guidance/resolve.py:45-60 (_applies)

chunk_findings.detail: `names()` sorts with `key=lambda n: n + suffix`, sorting reconstructed file names rather than ids. For ids that are a prefix of one another and whose next char is below `'.'` (e.g. kebab-case `-`), the order flips: `commit` / `commit-message` sort `["commit", "commit-message"]` by id but `["commit-message.toml", "commit.toml"]` by key. Rule listing order therefore differs from the previous filename sort.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/guidance/store.py::GuidanceFiles.names (order)

chunk_findings.detail: The old `list()` wrapped the whole load-and-filter body in `except Exception: continue`, skipping any unreadable/unparsable rule file. The new implementation delegates only the file read to `self.files.all()` and calls `Rule.from_record(rec)` unguarded. A file that is a valid record but not a valid `Rule` now raises instead of being skipped, changing `rule list` from a partial listing to a failure.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/rules.py::RulesStorage.list (lost guard)

chunk_findings.detail: `all()` calls `self.ensure_dir()`, so merely listing a kind creates `.ddflow/<directory>/`. On a read-only checkout this turns a listing that should return `[]` into `PermissionError` from `mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)`, a behavior the previous read-only listing did not have.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/guidance/store.py::GuidanceFiles.all (side effect)

chunk_findings.detail:
The hunk deletes the explicit `candidates.sort(key=lambda c: -c["score"])` and now returns `found`-order directly:

```python
found = similar([r.to_record() for r in existing_rules], content, title=title, threshold=threshold)
candidates = [ ...for f in found ]
return bool(candidates), candidates
```

while the function's own docstring (unchanged in this hunk) still promises `"candidates: List of similar rules with scores and details, sorted by score descending"`. The previous implementation appended candidates in `existing_rules` iteration order and then stably sorted descending, so the order was deterministic and score-ordered independently of how the similarity engine emitted matches. The rewrite gives that guarantee away: nothing in this hunk (or in `api/rules.py`) establishes that `similar(...)` returns matches in descending-score order rather than in input order / a partial order of its own. Concretely, with `existing_rules = [R_low, R_high]`, `R_low.similarity_score(content)` scoring `0.5` and `R_high.similarity_score(content)` scoring `0.9`, both at or above `threshold`, the old code returned `[{R_high, 0.9}, {R_low, 0.5}]`, whereas the new code returns whatever position `similar` places them in; if the engine preserves input order (the natural way to build the list) the CLI/dry-run output prints the low-score candidate first, i.e. not byte-identical and not matching the documented "sorted by score descending" contract. Either the sort must be reinstated here, or `similar` must be shown to guarantee a stable descending sort over these inputs; the diff does neither.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/rules.py:rule_dedup_check

chunk_findings.detail:
The old body guarded the store read behind the tail of an `elif` chain:

```python
if len(rule.content.encode("utf-8")) > cfg.rules.max_size_bytes:
    problem = "..."
elif rule.scope not in cfg.rules.scopes_allowed:
    ...
elif ...:
    ...
elif len(RulesStorage(repo).list()) >= cfg.rules.max_rules:
    ...
```

so `RulesStorage(repo).list()` was evaluated *only* when size, scope and tags all passed. The new call passes `len(RulesStorage(repo).list())` as an ordinary argument, and Python evaluates arguments before the call, so the whole store listing now runs unconditionally on every `rule.add`, before `over_limit` can return the size/scope/tag refusal. Two concrete inputs make this observable and break the "byte-identical CLI output" contract:

1. `RulesStorage.list()` now delegates to `self.files.all()` and then calls `Rule.from_record(rec)` outside any guard, so a file such as `.ddflow/rules/broken.toml` that is valid TOML but whose record cannot be converted to a `Rule` raises. With that file present, `rule.add` on an oversized rule used to return `refused("rule.added", "content is over rules.max_size_bytes (...)")` (the size branch returned before the count branch ran); now the exception from `list()` propagates and no refusal message is produced at all.
2. `GuidanceFiles.all()` calls `ensure_dir()`, so merely evaluating this argument creates `.ddflow/rules/`. On a read-only checkout where `.ddflow/rules/` does not yet exist, adding an oversized rule now raises `PermissionError` from `mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)` instead of returning the size-limit refusal, and even on a writable checkout a *refused* add now leaves a newly created rules directory behind, which the previous code did not.

Both differences are caused solely by moving the store read from the condition to an eager argument.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/rules.py::_over_limits

chunk_findings.detail: This still holds; nothing in the diff answers it. `tuple()` on the value of a TOML key is only correct when the key is an array. Given an authored file with `globs = "*.py"`, `tuple("*.py")` yields `('*', '.', 'p', 'y')`; the resolver receives `*` as a glob that matches every path, so a rule written for Python files silently becomes global, and the stray `.`/`p`/`y` patterns add further unintended matches. The same construction is used for `categories` and `gates`, so `categories = "style"` likewise decomposes into `('s','t','y','l','e')`. The only guard is `lint(rec, spec)`, and an exploded string is still a tuple of strings, so a "globs must be strings" check would not catch it.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/guidance/fileformat.py:64-66 (`parse`, `scope=Scope(globs=tuple(data.get("globs", ()))...)`)

chunk_findings.detail: This still holds; the condition is unchanged. `if rec.level or spec.default_level:` writes `scope = {rec.level}` even when `rec.level` is the empty string. For a kind whose default level is non-empty (e.g. `"project"`), a record with `level == ""` is rendered as `scope = ""`. Any existing rule file that omits the `scope` key parses to `"project"` (`level=data.get("scope", spec.default_level)`); a file that the new writer produces for that same record instead pins `""`, so the file no longer expresses the kind's default and round-tripping through the new writer changes the on-disk rule text (the intent requires byte-identical rule files). The fix would be to also require `rec.level != spec.default_level` (or to omit the key when empty) rather than emitting an explicit empty scope.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/guidance/fileformat.py:97-98 (`render`)

chunk_findings.detail:
New issue: the frontmatter/content boundary is found by a literal `"

"` search, so a file written with CRLF line endings is misparsed. With `text = 'id = "r"
title = "T"

Body
'`, `split("

", 1)` matches nothing (the separator is `

`), `has_block` is `False`, and the whole file including the body is handed to `tomllib.loads`, which raises `ValueError: Invalid TOML in ... frontmatter` for a file that is valid TOML. A whitespace-only separator line (e.g. a line containing a single space) has the same effect, because the search only accepts exactly two consecutive newlines: an authored file edited on Windows or with a stray trailing space on the blank line is rejected (or, if the body happens to be valid TOML, silently treated as frontmatter). Splitting on the first line that is empty after stripping, or normalizing `
`, would make the documented "TOML frontmatter, a blank line, and the text" format actually parseable.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/guidance/fileformat.py:26-28 (`parse`, `parts = text.split("\n\n", 1)`)

chunk_findings.detail: `decision_record` maps a decision onto the shared record with `status=d.status or ACCEPTED` and stashes the supersession marker in `ext["superseded_by"]` (kinds.py lines 60-95), while `governing` relies on the generic resolver to decide liveness: `applied = resolve((decision_record(d) for d in state.decisions.values()), globs=globs)`. The generic resolver can only judge liveness from the fields it knows about — `GuidanceRecord.status` — because `superseded_by` is buried in the kind-specific `ext` dict and `KindSpec`/`resolve` carry no per-kind live predicate (the `KINDS` specs expose only kind/label/directory/limits/level/stamped/valid_id/enforcement/extras). So a superseded decision is still `status == "accepted"` (the docstring explicitly says it "stays accepted here with superseded_by set") and is treated as live. Concretely: the log holds `D1` (accepted, `superseded_by="D2"`) and `D2` (accepted, `supersedes=["D1"]`). The old path filtered on `Decision.live` (the docstring notes it "reads both", i.e. status and `superseded_by`) and returned only `D2`; the new `governing` hands `decision_record(D1)` to `resolve`, which sees `status == "accepted"` and no supersession signal, so both `D1` and `D2` are returned in the two output lists. `decision applicable now` therefore lists a withdrawn decision, differing from the previous output the change promises to keep byte-identical (and disagreeing with `brief`'s still-inline filter).
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/guidance/kinds.py:governing

chunk_findings.detail: The scope check `if rec.level not in lim.scopes_allowed:` has no empty-allow-list guard, while the very next check for tags is written defensively: `if lim.tags_allowed and (bad := [t for t in rec.tags if t not in lim.tags_allowed])`. The two "allowed" checks therefore disagree about what an empty allow-list means. If a project configures a kind's section (so `lim is not None`) without listing `scopes_allowed` — the natural "no restriction" default, matching how an omitted `tags_allowed` is treated — then `lim.scopes_allowed == []` and `rec.level not in []` is true for every possible level, so `over_limit` rejects every new record with `scope '...' is not in ...scopes_allowed []`. Concretely, with `scopes_allowed = []` and any record whose `level` is e.g. `"project"`, `over_limit` returns a limit-violation string (the second branch) even though the analogous tag list of `[]` would accept all tags, and even though a kind with no section at all (`lim is None`) accepts the same record unconditionally. This prior finding (#5) remains unaddressed here: the diff shows no `and lim.scopes_allowed`-style guard and no probe/comment establishing that `scopes_allowed` is ever non-empty when `lim` is not `None`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/guidance/limits.py:20 (over_limit, scope check)

chunk_findings.detail: `_applies` returns `Applies(rec, "", ())` whenever a record is not `scope.always` and sets none of `gates`/`categories`/`globs`: the `reason = ""` initializer at the top of the function is never overwritten and line 60 is reached with the empty string. The `Applies.reason` contract (lines ~28-30) allows only `ALWAYS`, `GLOBS`, `CATEGORY` or `GATE`, and `resolve`'s own docstring promises "Guidance with no restriction at all applies always". Concrete input: a `GuidanceRecord` with `scope.always == False` and `scope.gates == ()`, `scope.categories == ()`, `scope.globs == ()` (a rule/decision authored without any of those keys). `_applies` passes all three `if scope.*` guards, falls to the final `return Applies(rec, reason, pairs)`, and yields `reason == ""` instead of `ALWAYS`. Any consumer that branches on `Applies.reason` (e.g. to print why a rule/decision applies) sees an empty, undocumented value rather than the "applies always" the resolver documents. The diff adds no branch that maps the no-restriction case onto `ALWAYS`, so this prior finding is not answered.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/guidance/resolve.py:60 (`_applies` fall-through)

chunk_findings.detail: `all()` is a read/listing entry point, but its first statement is `self.ensure_dir()`, which performs `mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)` on `.ddflow/<spec.directory>/`. The previous `RulesStorage.list` only globbed `self.rules_dir.glob("*.toml")` and never created the directory. Consequences: (a) a pure listing now mutates the repository — `ddflow rules list` (or any caller using `all()`) creates `.ddflow/rules/` in a repo that had none; (b) on a read-only checkout, where the old code returned an empty list because the glob matched nothing, `ensure_dir()` raises `PermissionError` out of `all()`, and unlike the per-record errors it is outside the `try` block, so it is not swallowed and the documented "Every record that loads" behavior becomes an exception. `read()`/`names()` do not require the directory to exist (read raises `FileNotFoundError`, names globs an empty result), so the call is both unnecessary and observable. Input to demonstrate: a read-only checkout (or any repo without `.ddflow/rules/`) followed by `all()` → directory is created or `PermissionError` propagates; before the change `list()` returned `[]`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/guidance/store.py:92-93 (GuidanceFiles.all)

chunk_findings.detail: `decision_record` still hardcodes `enforcement=DECISION.default_enforcement` and `DECISION.extras` still has no `enforcement` entry, so a logged decision carrying `enforcement: "block"` (or a decision file with that field) is coerced to `"warn"` and cannot round-trip. The adjacent `DECISION` comment says a decision "may be set to block or advisory", so the adapter contradicts its own schema. Demonstrated input: parse a decision record whose source dict contains `{"enforcement": "block", ...}`; the produced `GuidanceRecord` comes back with `enforcement == "warn"`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/guidance/kinds.py :: decision_record

chunk_findings.detail: The parser builds `Scope` sequence fields with `tuple(data.get("globs", ()))` (same for `categories`/`gates`). Given an authored file with a single string value, `globs = "*.py"`, `tuple("*.py")` yields `('*', '.', 'p', 'y')`, so the resolver sees `*` and the rule applies to every path, with `.`/`p`/`y` adding further unintended matches. A one-value string should either be rejected loudly or wrapped as a one-element tuple; silently exploding it changes applicability.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/guidance/fileformat.py:64-66

chunk_findings.detail: `render` emits `scope = {rec.level}` under `if rec.level or spec.default_level:`. For a record whose level is empty and whose kind default is non-empty (e.g. `"project"`), the file contains `scope = ""`; parsing that back uses `level=data.get("scope", spec.default_level)` and, because the key is present with an empty string, returns `""` instead of `"project"`. Round-tripping a default-scoped record therefore loses its default.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/guidance/fileformat.py:97-98

chunk_findings.detail: The explicit `candidates.sort(key=lambda c: -c["score"])` was dropped and the function now returns whatever order `similar(...)` yields, while the docstring still promises score-descending order. With `existing_rules = [R_low, R_high]` where `R_low` scores 0.5 and `R_high` 0.9 (both `>= threshold`), the old result was `[R_high, R_low]`; if `similar` preserves input order the new result is `[R_low, R_high]`, changing CLI/dedup output.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/rules.py :: rule_dedup_check

chunk_findings.detail: The scope check `if rec.level not in lim.scopes_allowed` has no empty-list guard, unlike the tag check `if lim.tags_allowed and ...`. When `scopes_allowed` is the natural empty default for an unconfigured project, no level can satisfy `not in []`, so every record is reported over limit and the `[rules]` limit message fires for all rules.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/guidance/limits.py :: over_limit

chunk_findings.detail: For a record with `scope.always=False` and no gates/categories/globs (the module docstring says this "applies always"), `_applies` falls through all guards with `reason` still `""` and returns `Applies(rec, "", ())`. `Applies.reason` is documented to be one of `ALWAYS`/`GLOBS`/`CATEGORY`/`GATE`, so any consumer that switches on `reason` (or treats `""` as "not applicable") misclassifies an always-applicable record; an always-applicable rule/decision should report `ALWAYS`.

chunk_findings.detail: The old `list()` wrapped the whole load-and-filter body in `except Exception: continue`, silently skipping any file that failed to load. The new implementation delegates only the file read to `self.files.all()` and then calls `Rule.from_record(rec)` unguarded; a file that parses as valid TOML/record syntax but not as a valid rule makes `list()` raise instead of skipping, changing behavior for a corrupt/legacy rule file.

chunk_findings.detail:
`all()` is a read/listing entry point but calls `self.ensure_dir()`, so merely listing a kind's records now creates `.ddflow/<directory>/` on disk. In a repo without that directory, a listing that should return `[]` instead creates it, and on a read-only checkout it raises `PermissionError` from `mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)` rather than returning the documented "every record that loads" result.

Note on the two order findings (store.names sort key `n + suffix`, and "RulesStorage.list no longer sorts"): both compare the new ordering against id-sorting, but the previous implementation sorted `Path` objects from `glob("*.toml")`, i.e. by filename; filename order and `n + suffix` order coincide for the cited `commit`/`commit-message` case, so no before/after difference is demonstrated and I am not reporting them.

For ids `commit` and `commit-message`, full-name order is `["commit-message", "commit"]` because `-` (0x2D) < `.` (0x2E), while id order is `["commit", "commit-message"]`, so listing order flips. chunk_findings.detail:
Prior finding 9 still holds. The old `list()` wrapped the whole per-file body (`self.get(...)` → `Rule.from_toml`, plus filtering) in `try/except Exception: continue`, so any rule file that failed to load was silently dropped. The rewritten body no longer has that guard:

```python
for rec in self.files.all():
    rule = Rule.from_record(rec)
    ...
```

The new docstring ("a file that does not load is left out") only covers failures inside `GuidanceFiles.all()` — i.e. a file that cannot be read or parsed into a generic `Record`. It does not cover failures in the rule-specific `Record -> Rule` conversion, because that call sits in `rules.py`, outside any guard. `GuidanceFiles` is the shared, kind-agnostic store, so its record schema cannot enforce Rule-specific invariants (e.g. a recognized `severity`, or a required rule field that the shared schema treats as optional). Concretely, an authored file such as a rule TOML carrying a plausible-but-invalid rule value (for example a `severity` string the `Rule` constructor/enum rejects, or a rule file missing a field that `from_record` dereferences but the shared schema defaults) parses cleanly into a `Record`, so `all()` yields it, and then `Rule.from_record(rec)` raises out of `list()` instead of being skipped. Old behaviour: `list()` returned the remaining valid rules; new behaviour: it raises, changing the CLI/API result for a directory whose only difference is one malformed rule file. The fix would be to restore a per-record guard around `Rule.from_record` (matching the docstring's "left out" promise), which the shown hunk does not do.

chunk_findings.detail: This test is the only probe added for score ordering, and it cannot detect the regression finding 1 describes. The input `[a, b, c]` has `a` scoring 1.0 and `c` scoring 0.75, and `a` precedes `c` in the input list; after `b` is filtered out, the expected result `[("a", 1.0), ("c", 0.75)]` is exactly what an implementation that returns `similar(...)` results in *input order* would also produce. So if `api/rules.py::rule_dedup_check` still returns whatever order `similar` yields (the dropped `candidates.sort(key=lambda c: -c["score"])`), this test passes and the docstring's "sorted by score descending" promise remains unverified. Concrete distinguishing input: call `similar([c, b, a], "", title="tests come first", threshold=0.5)`; an unsorted implementation yields `[("c", 0.75), ("a", 1.0)]` while a sorting one yields `[("a", 1.0), ("c", 0.75)]` — the current test data cannot separate these, so finding 1 is not answered.

chunk_findings.detail: The only new test that renders a record with an unset `level` deliberately asserts nothing about the rendered text or the round-tripped level — it checks `got.provenance["created"]`/`["updated"]` only. Given the render condition `if rec.level or spec.default_level:` and a truthy `RULE.default_level` (the tests use `"project"` throughout, e.g. `_cfg(scopes_allowed=["project"])` and the `scope 'task' is not in ... ['project']` message), the empty-`level` branch is still taken and emits `scope = ""`. Parsing that back gives `level == ""` (the `scope` key is present), whereas before the key was omitted and the kind default applied, so a rule authored/saved without a scope gains a `scope = ""` line that changes its meaning on re-read. Concrete input: `RulesStorage.update("r-naming", priority=90)` on a file `r-naming.toml` with `id`/`title`/`priority` and no `scope` key (the test `test_editing_a_rule_keeps_the_keys_a_person_put_in_the_file` only uses a file that already contains `scope = "project"`), or `fileformat.parse(fileformat.render(GuidanceRecord(id="r-z", kind="rule", title="z", body="b"), RULE), RULE).level`, which is `""` rather than `"project"`. No test in this diff pins this case, so finding 3 still holds.

chunk_findings.detail: `tuple(data.get("globs", ()))` (and the `categories`/`gates` twins) explodes a scalar TOML value into characters. For an authored file with `globs = "*.py"`, the parsed `Scope.globs` becomes `('*', '.', 'p', 'y')`; the resolver then treats `*` as a pattern that matches every path, so a rule intended only for Python files silently applies globally, and `.`/`p`/`y` add further spurious matches. chunk_findings.detail: `parse` reads `checks` straight through as `checks=data.get("checks", [])`, with none of the coercion every other list field gets (`globs`, `categories`, `gates`, `tags`, `sources`, `links` all go through `_strings`). `render`, however, serializes it as `("checks", list(rec.checks), [])`. So a TOML file that authors a single check as a bare string — exactly the form `_strings` exists to support ("a bare string is the one pattern it says (never its characters)") — parses into a `str`, and the next write explodes it per character. Concretely, a rule file containing `checks = "pytest -q"` parses to `rec.checks == "pytest -q"`; on render, `list("pytest -q")` is `['p', 'y', 't', 's', 't', ' ', '-', 'q']` and the frontmatter is rewritten as `checks = ["p", "y", "t", "s", "t", " ", "-", "q"]`, destroying the check on a plain read/write cycle. Because `lint` is applied to the record after construction and (from this diff) is not shown to type-check `checks`, nothing forces `checks` to be a list before `render` runs; making `parse` use `_strings(data, "checks")` (or making `render` reject a non-list) would remove the asymmetry.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/guidance/fileformat.py — `parse` (checks=) / `render` (checks entry)

chunk_findings.detail: The scope check is the only cap that is not guarded against an "unset" value, and it disagrees with the semantics the very next line uses. The tags check reads `if lim.tags_allowed and (bad := [...])`, i.e. an empty `tags_allowed` means "no tag restriction"; the scope check is written `if rec.level not in lim.scopes_allowed:` with no such guard. Take a project whose rules limits section sets `max_rules` (and/or `max_size_bytes`) but omits `scopes_allowed`, so `Limits.scopes_allowed` defaults to the empty collection. Then calling `over_limit(rec, lim, existing)` for a perfectly ordinary new rule with `rec.level == "project"` evaluates `"project" not in ()` → True and returns `scope 'project' is not in rules.scopes_allowed ()`, rejecting a valid record (and, if the default were `None`, the same expression raises `TypeError` instead). Before the refactor an empty `scopes_allowed` meant "any scope allowed", matching the `tags_allowed` branch that was copied from it; the missing `lim.scopes_allowed and ...` guard changes behaviour for exactly the config that leaves the scope list unset.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/guidance/limits.py :: over_limit (scope check)

chunk_findings.detail: `all()` deliberately tolerates read failures (`except (OSError, OverlayError, ValueError): continue`), but `problems()` only catches `OverlayError` around the overlay read/validate call. Given a `.ddflow/<directory>/acl.toml` whose mode is `000` (still listed by `names()` because listing the directory does not require permission on the file), `all()` skips it, whereas `problems()` calls `self.loader.resolve(name, self.repo)` / `validate(...)`, the underlying file read raises `PermissionError` (an `OSError`, not an `OverlayError`), and the exception propagates out of `problems()` instead of being reported as a `Problem`. The error-reporting path therefore crashes exactly on a file it is meant to report, instead of returning `file:line: why` like it does for parse failures.

chunk_findings.detail: The previous finding on this method still holds: the triage probe only demonstrates the *kind* filter (`test_listing_rules_skips_a_file_that_is_not_one_and_creates_the_directory`), i.e. it covers a file that is not a rule at all, while the finding is about a file that *is* a `RULE`-typed record but fails rule‑level validation inside `Rule.from_record`. `GuidanceFiles.all()` only promises that "files which do not load" as *records* are dropped — it returns `RULE`-typed records as parsed dicts, and the rule-specific validation (id format, required fields, globs) still happens later in `Rule.from_record(rec)`, which the new `list()` calls with no `try/except`. Concretely, put a syntactically valid TOML file such as `.ddflow/rules/bad.toml` containing `id = "not-a-rule-id"` (or a rule missing a required field) in the rules directory: `fileformat.parse` succeeds, `all()` yields it, `Rule.from_record` raises `ValueError`, and `list()` propagates instead of returning the remaining rules. The old body wrapped `self.get(...)` / `Rule.from_toml` in `except Exception` and skipped that file, so the caller-visible behaviour differs (an exception vs. a shorter list). The probe does not exercise that path, so it does not answer the finding.

chunk_findings.detail:
The refactor drops the per-file `try/except Exception` that surrounded the load in the old `list()` (`self.get(...)` + `Rule.from_toml`, with `# Skip invalid rules`). The old loop therefore skipped any `.toml` file that parsed but failed *rule-level* validation and still returned the remaining rules; the new loop calls `Rule.from_record(rec)` unguarded, so such a file now aborts the whole listing. Concretely, with `.ddflow/rules/ok.toml` (valid) and `.ddflow/rules/broken.toml` containing a record that `GuidanceFiles.all()` returns as a parsed dict but whose rule fields `Rule.from_record` rejects (e.g. a missing/again invalid `title`/`scope`), old `RulesStorage(repo).list()` returned `[ok]`, while the new one raises out of `list()` instead of returning the valid rules.

The cited refutation probe (`test_listing_rules_skips_a_file_that_is_not_one_and_creates_the_directory`) does not answer this: it exercises a file that is *not a rule record at all*, which `GuidanceFiles.all()` drops during record loading, before `Rule.from_record` is ever reached. The finding is about a file that loads fine as a generic record but fails the RULE-specific validation that only happens in `Rule.from_record` — exactly the case the deleted `except Exception` guarded and the kind-filtering in `all()` cannot catch.

chunk_findings.detail:
The triage keeps this refuted with `test_enforcement_is_carried_by_the_file_not_dropped`, but that test only ever calls `fileformat.parse` / `fileformat.render` on a DECISION-kind file (see the diff: `text = 'id = "D-b"\ntitle = "t"\nenforcement = "block"\n\nbody'` → `rec.enforcement == "block"`). It never constructs a `Decision` and never calls `decision_record`, so it cannot show that the *adapter* preserves a decision's own enforcement. The only test in this diff that goes through the adapter is `test_a_decision_as_guidance`:

    d = Decision(id="D-1", title="T", decision="do x", globs=["a/*"], context="why", tags=["t"])
    rec = decision_record(d)
    ...
    assert rec.enforcement == "warn"

which asserts exactly the hard-coded `DECISION.default_enforcement` value and never supplies a non-default one, so it passes whether or not the adapter reads `d.enforcement`. Since the finding was triaged `refuted` (i.e. no change was made to the adapter), `decision_record` still writes `enforcement=DECISION.default_enforcement` while the file format it is converting from can carry `enforcement = "block"` (proven by the very probe cited). Input: a decision whose file says `enforcement = "block"` routed back through `decision_record` (the path used to build in-memory decisions) yields a record with `enforcement == "warn"`, i.e. the block is silently downgraded. The cited probe exercises a different function than the one the finding faults, so the refutation is not established and the finding stands.

So a TOML file that authors a single check as a bare string — exactly the form `_strings` exists to support ("a bare string is the one pattern it says (never its characters)") — parses into a `str`, and the next write explodes it per character. Because `lint` is applied to the record after construction and (from this diff) is not shown to type-check `checks`, nothing forces `checks` to be a list before `render` runs; making `parse` use `_strings(data, "checks")` (or making `render` reject a non-list) would remove the asymmetry.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/guidance/fileformat.py — `parse` (checks=) / `render` (checks entry)

chunk_findings.detail: The scope check is the only cap that is not guarded against an "unset" value, and it disagrees with the semantics the very next line uses. The tags check reads `if lim.tags_allowed and (bad := [...])`, i.e. an empty `tags_allowed` means "no tag restriction"; the scope check is written `if rec.level not in lim.scopes_allowed:` with no such guard. Take a project whose rules limits section sets `max_rules` (and/or `max_size_bytes`) but omits `scopes_allowed`, so `Limits.scopes_allowed` defaults to the empty collection. Then calling `over_limit(rec, lim, existing)` for a perfectly ordinary new rule with `rec.level == "project"` evaluates `"project" not in ()` → True and returns `scope 'project' is not in rules.scopes_allowed ()`, rejecting a valid record (and, if the default were `None`, the same expression raises `TypeError` instead). Before the refactor an empty `scopes_allowed` meant "any scope allowed", matching the `tags_allowed` branch that was copied from it; the missing `lim.scopes_allowed and ...` guard changes behaviour for exactly the config that leaves the scope list unset.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/guidance/limits.py :: over_limit (scope check)

chunk_findings.detail: `all()` deliberately tolerates read failures (`except (OSError, OverlayError, ValueError): continue`), but `problems()` only catches `OverlayError` around the overlay read/validate call. Given a `.ddflow/<directory>/acl.toml` whose mode is `000` (still listed by `names()` because listing the directory does not require permission on the file), `all()` skips it, whereas `problems()` calls `self.loader.resolve(name, self.repo)` / `validate(...)`, the underlying file read raises `PermissionError` (an `OSError`, not an `OverlayError`), and the exception propagates out of `problems()` instead of being reported as a `Problem`. The error-reporting path therefore crashes exactly on a file it is meant to report, instead of returning `file:line: why` like it does for parse failures.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/guidance/store.py :: GuidanceFiles.problems

chunk_findings.detail: The previous finding on this method still holds: the triage probe only demonstrates the *kind* filter (`test_listing_rules_skips_a_file_that_is_not_one_and_creates_the_directory`), i.e. it covers a file that is not a rule at all, while the finding is about a file that *is* a `RULE`-typed record but fails rule‑level validation inside `Rule.from_record`. `GuidanceFiles.all()` only promises that "files which do not load" as *records* are dropped — it returns `RULE`-typed records as parsed dicts, and the rule-specific validation (id format, required fields, globs) still happens later in `Rule.from_record(rec)`, which the new `list()` calls with no `try/except`. Concretely, put a syntactically valid TOML file such as `.ddflow/rules/bad.toml` containing `id = "not-a-rule-id"` (or a rule missing a required field) in the rules directory: `fileformat.parse` succeeds, `all()` yields it, `Rule.from_record` raises `ValueError`, and `list()` propagates instead of returning the remaining rules. The old body wrapped `self.get(...)` / `Rule.from_toml` in `except Exception` and skipped that file, so the caller-visible behaviour differs (an exception vs. a shorter list). The probe does not exercise that path, so it does not answer the finding.

chunk_findings.detail:
The refactor drops the per-file `try/except Exception` that surrounded the load in the old `list()` (`self.get(...)` + `Rule.from_toml`, with `# Skip invalid rules`). The old loop therefore skipped any `.toml` file that parsed but failed *rule-level* validation and still returned the remaining rules; the new loop calls `Rule.from_record(rec)` unguarded, so such a file now aborts the whole listing. Concretely, with `.ddflow/rules/ok.toml` (valid) and `.ddflow/rules/broken.toml` containing a record that `GuidanceFiles.all()` returns as a parsed dict but whose rule fields `Rule.from_record` rejects (e.g. a missing/again invalid `title`/`scope`), old `RulesStorage(repo).list()` returned `[ok]`, while the new one raises out of `list()` instead of returning the valid rules.

The cited refutation probe (`test_listing_rules_skips_a_file_that_is_not_one_and_creates_the_directory`) does not answer this: it exercises a file that is *not a rule record at all*, which `GuidanceFiles.all()` drops during record loading, before `Rule.from_record` is ever reached. The finding is about a file that loads fine as a generic record but fails the RULE-specific validation that only happens in `Rule.from_record` — exactly the case the deleted `except Exception` guarded and the kind-filtering in `all()` cannot catch.

chunk_findings.detail:
The triage keeps this refuted with `test_enforcement_is_carried_by_the_file_not_dropped`, but that test only ever calls `fileformat.parse` / `fileformat.render` on a DECISION-kind file (see the diff: `text = 'id = "D-b"\ntitle = "t"\nenforcement = "block"\n\nbody'` → `rec.enforcement == "block"`). It never constructs a `Decision` and never calls `decision_record`, so it cannot show that the *adapter* preserves a decision's own enforcement. The only test in this diff that goes through the adapter is `test_a_decision_as_guidance`:

    d = Decision(id="D-1", title="T", decision="do x", globs=["a/*"], context="why", tags=["t"])
    rec = decision_record(d)
    ...
    assert rec.enforcement == "warn"

which asserts exactly the hard-coded `DECISION.default_enforcement` value and never supplies a non-default one, so it passes whether or not the adapter reads `d.enforcement`. Since the finding was triaged `refuted` (i.e. no change was made to the adapter), `decision_record` still writes `enforcement=DECISION.default_enforcement` while the file format it is converting from can carry `enforcement = "block"` (proven by the very probe cited). Input: a decision whose file says `enforcement = "block"` routed back through `decision_record` (the path used to build in-memory decisions) yields a record with `enforcement == "warn"`, i.e. the block is silently downgraded. The cited probe exercises a different function than the one the finding faults, so the refutation is not established and the finding stands.

chunk_findings.detail: `body = {"name": label, **entry, ...}` unpacks the preset-derived `entry` after the caller-controlled `name`, so any `name` field declared by the preset shadows the user's override. Given `reviewers_add(repo, preset="claude", name="my-reviewer", person=True)` where `RV.PRESETS["claude"]` contains `{"name": "Claude", "model": ...}`, the appended block is written as `name = "Claude"` while the returned Outcome and the user-facing text report `author=my-reviewer`/`added reviewer 'my-reviewer'`. The explicit `name` argument is supposed to win (that is why `label` is derived from it and reported back), so the unpack order is reversed: it should build `{**entry, "name": label, ...}`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/review.py reviewers_add (body construction)

chunk_findings.detail: The diff deletes `FormatRefused`, whose entire purpose was to carry `exit_code = 3` (`"...exit 3, refused (core.outcome.exit_for)"`), while introducing `EditResult`/`apply_edit` as the single write path. But the `EditResult` docstring added in this same hunk enumerates exactly three outcomes for a non-empty `error`: "a `KeyRefused` is a refusal (exit 3), a `ReviewerRefusal` an agent's refused reviewer, any other string a failure." The `Guards` docstring in the same hunk also states the format guard is *not* optional ("The key, human-gate, format, schema, range and gate-table guards are not optional"), so a format mismatch is still detected and surfaced — but it is neither a D-plain-keys `KeyRefused` nor a reviewer refusal, so it necessarily falls into "any other string a failure", i.e. exit 1. Concrete input: a layer's `config.toml` whose `format` is newer than this ddflow understands, written through `apply_edit` (e.g. `config --set ...`, or a committed `Block`). Previously `append_block` raised `FormatRefused`, `core.outcome.exit_for` read its `exit_code`, and the process exited 3 (refused); now the same refusal is an ordinary error string and exits 1, so callers/scripts that branch on the refused-vs-failed distinction (the same distinction `KeyRefused`'s docstring says the caller is careful about: "answers exit 3 (refused), not 1") silently change behavior. If format refusal is meant to keep its "refused" semantics, the new result type needs an equivalent marker (e.g. an `exit_code = 3`-bearing refusal) rather than a bare string.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/configwrite.py (`FormatRefused` removal / `EditResult`)

chunk_findings.detail: The new `_text_refusal` helper calls `tomllib.loads(text)` and references `tomllib.TOMLDecodeError`, but the diff removes the function-local `import tomllib` that used to sit at the top of both `_write_config` and `_append_config` and adds no module-level import in its place. In the code shown, nothing brings the name `tomllib` into `configwrite.py`'s namespace, so `_text_refusal` raises `NameError: name 'tomllib' is not defined` on the first statement that needs it. Concrete reproducer: any `config --append-toml <valid TOML>` (or `ddflow_configure` with an `AppendText` edit) routes through `_text_refusal`; instead of returning `""` for a valid block, it raises `NameError` before `appended_key_problem`/`_human_cleared` are reached. The old functions worked only because each carried its own `import tomllib`; extracting the TOML parsing into a free function without carrying the import across is the regression. (If a module-level `import tomllib` is introduced elsewhere in the 18-part change, this does not apply — but within this diff no such import exists.)
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/configwrite.py:_text_refusal

chunk_findings.detail: Inside `apply_edit`, every guard except the reviewer-trust guard runs unconditionally: `_key_refusal`/`_text_refusal` run before the lock, and `_schema_problem`, `_gate_problem`, `_human_removed` and `_workflow_refusal` are called from `_result_problem` regardless of `dry_run`. The reviewer-trust guard (decision D-reviewer-trust) lives solely in `RT.write`, which is now wrapped in `if not dry_run:`, so on a dry run it is never consulted. Concretely, `apply_edit(repo, Block(text='[[reviewer]]\nkind = "command"\n...'), layer="local", dry_run=True, agent="a")` returns `EditResult("", ...)` with no error, while the identical call with `dry_run=False` returns `EditResult(ReviewerRefusal(...))`. A surface like `ddflow config ... --dry-run` therefore reports an agent-authored command reviewer as acceptable and only the subsequent real write fails, which contradicts the docstring's claim that anything refused comes back as `EditResult.error` (the wrap conflates RT.write's side effect of recording `reviewer.configured` with its validation role, so the validation is skipped along with the side effect).
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/configwrite.py `apply_edit` (the `if not dry_run:` guard around `RT.write`)

chunk_findings.detail: The refactor drops the explicit `sync_attributes(Path(repo))` call and replaces it with a comment asserting that "The committed write also brings `.gitattributes` up to date (`merge=union`)". Nothing in the change description supports that claim: the unified pipeline is described as providing one layer/path definition, typed values, the human-gate/policy guards and agent context — `.gitattributes` maintenance is not part of it, and `configure` still performs the attribute sync as a separate caller step ("does both": writes the local layer *and* syncs attributes). So for this caller the attribute update is simply lost. Concrete scenario: call `register_append_only(repo, "data/foo.bin")` for a glob that is not yet in the committed `[lease].append_only_globs`. The committed config now lists `data/foo.bin`, but `.gitattributes` never gains the corresponding `data/foo.bin merge=union` line, so subsequent merges of that file no longer use union merge and will conflict. If `apply_edit` genuinely does perform the sync, this needs to be demonstrated; otherwise the explicit `sync_attributes(repo)` must be restored after a successful edit.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/export/write.py:register_append_only

chunk_findings.detail:
The test previously pinned the refusal contract for a too-new config format:

```python
with pytest.raises(CW.FormatRefused) as exc:
    CW.append_block(repo, block, shared=True)
assert exc.value.exit_code == 3 and "format" in str(exc.value)
```

It is now:

```python
res = CW.apply_edit(repo, CW.Block(block), layer="file")
assert isinstance(res.error, CW.KeyRefused) and "format" in res.error
```

Two guarantees are dropped. First, the specific type: the sibling assertion at line 228 (for the append path) already shows that this project distinguishes `KeyRefused` from `FormatRefused`, and the format path was previously surfaced as `FormatRefused.with exit_code == 3`. If the unified `apply_edit` still returns `FormatRefused` and `FormatRefused` is not a `KeyRefused` subclass, the new assertion fails; if it returns a plain `KeyRefused` (or any subclass), the test passes even though the format-specific behavior changed. Second, the CLI-visible `exit_code == 3` is no longer checked at all. Concretely: given a repo whose `.ddflow/config.toml` is `format = CONFIG_FORMAT + 1`, if `apply_edit` reports the refusal as a generic `KeyRefused` whose exit code is 1, this test still passes, masking a regression in the documented format-refusal exit status. The file-unchanged assertion cannot distinguish the two cases because a correct `FormatRefused` and a wrong `KeyRefused` both leave the file untouched.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_compat_config.py : test_append_block_refuses_a_newer_format_too

chunk_findings.detail: The second half of this test does not actually verify the D-org-config agent guard it claims to cover. The assertion is wrapped in `if out.exit != 0:`, so when the guard is absent and the call succeeds (exit 0), the body is skipped and the test goes green. This is not protecting against "preset missing": if `claude-cli` were an unknown preset, `reviewers_add` would return nonzero with an "unknown preset" reason and `out.data["reviewer_refused"]` would be missing/false, so the assertion `out.exit == 3 and out.data["reviewer_refused"]` would itself fail — the only case the `if` skips is the one where the agent guard failed to fire. Concrete scenario: delete the guard that refuses an agent command reviewer (or flip it off); `AR.reviewers_add(repo, name="c", preset="claude-cli", person=False, agent="a1")` returns exit 0, the `if` body is skipped, and this test still passes, so a regression in the very guard the intent says must "live in one place" is undetectable. The test should assert the refusal unconditionally (e.g. `assert out.exit == 3 and out.data["reviewer_refused"]`).
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_config_writes.py::test_reviewers_add_refuses_an_unknown_preset_and_an_agent_command_reviewer
ddflow/services/configwrite.py — `_text_refusal`

chunk_findings.detail: `apply_edit` skips `RT.write` entirely when `dry_run=True`, and `RT.write` is the *only* place the reviewer-trust guard runs (the `_check_reviewer_fields` call in `_schema_problem`/`_result_problem` is a reviewer-key allowlist check, as the retained `TC._check(raw, set(Reviewer.__dataclass_fields__), ...)` shows, not the D-reviewer-trust guard). So a dry run is not a faithful preview of what the real write does: given an agent caller, `apply_edit(repo, Block('[[reviewer]]\nkind = "command"\n...'), layer="local", person=False, agent="bot", dry_run=True)` reaches `return EditResult("", text, path, [])` with an empty error, while the identical call with `dry_run=False` returns `EditResult(ReviewerRefusal(...), text)`. Every other guard (schema, range, gate, human-gate, workflow) is evaluated before this branch and therefore also on dry runs, so the dry run reports success for exactly the one edit (an agent's command reviewer) that the real run refuses; the `apply_edit` docstring, which promises refusals as `EditResult.error` and treats "nothing is written" as the only dry-run effect, is violated. Fix by running the trust check in the `_result_problem`/compose path (or by calling a no-write variant of `RT.write`) so `dry_run` yields the same verdict as the write.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/configwrite.py:apply_edit (the `if not dry_run:` branch)

chunk_findings.detail: The refactor deletes the explicit `sync_attributes(Path(repo))` call (and the `sync_attributes` import) that the previous implementation ran after every successful write of `lease.append_only_globs`, replacing it with only a comment asserting that "the committed write also brings `.gitattributes` up to date (`merge=union`)". The change intent enumerates what the new unified `apply_edit` owns — the D-plain-keys / human-gate / D-org-config guards and the layer/typed-value handling — and describes the `.gitattributes` regeneration as a separate step that `configure` performs around the write ("never sync `.gitattributes`, while configure … does both"). So the side effect that previously kept `.gitattributes` in sync is no longer performed on this path. Concrete scenario: call `register_append_only(repo, "SHARED_EXPORTS.csv")` on a repo whose `.ddflow/config.toml` lacks that glob and whose `.gitattributes` has no `merge=union` line for it; the config is written and `True` is returned, but the `merge=union` line is never added, so a later git merge of the append-only file produces conflicts instead of a union merge. If `apply_edit` actually does call `sync_attributes` internally this finding is void, but nothing in the diff or intent attributes that responsibility to it, whereas the deleted call is directly visible.

chunk_findings.detail:
`_value` wraps *every* string plan value in `CW.Spelled`, i.e. it asserts that the string is already the verbatim TOML literal. That is only valid if upgrade plans always store pre-serialised literal text. But upgrade-plan items carry typed values: the deleted `_value_text` (`value if isinstance(value, str) else TC.value(value)`) has a `TC.value` branch precisely because `item["new"]` can be a typed bool/int/list, and for a *string* it deliberately returned the string **unquoted**, leaving `_write_config`'s `_toml_literal` re-guessing (which the intent calls out explicitly) to decide between "already a literal" and "plain value that must be quoted". A plan entry for a genuine string value therefore arrives as a raw Python string, e.g. `{"new": "claude"}` for `workflow.default_agent`.

With this change, `_value("claude")` returns `Spelled("claude")`, and `apply_edit` emits the spelled text verbatim, producing `default_agent = claude` — an unquoted bare word, which is not a legal TOML value, so the resulting `config.toml`/`config.local.toml` fails to parse (or, for values that happen to look like literals, e.g. the string `"true"`, silently writes a boolean instead of a string). The old path produced `default_agent = "claude"` because `_write_config`/`_toml_literal` quoted the raw string. Note the asymmetry: non-strings take the `else value` branch and are still serialised by `apply_edit`, so only string-valued config keys regress.

chunk_findings.detail:
The second half of this test only asserts anything when `out.exit != 0`:
```python
out = AR.reviewers_add(repo, name="c", preset="claude-cli", person=False, agent="a1")
if out.exit != 0:  # the preset exists and is a command reviewer
    assert out.exit == 3 and out.data["reviewer_refused"], out.reason
```
If the D-org-config agent guard is removed, weakened, or simply fails to fire, `reviewers_add` for a command preset with `person=False, agent="a1"` returns success (exit 0), the `if` body is skipped, and the test passes — so the very behavior the test name claims to verify ("refuses ... an agent command reviewer") is untested and a regression here would go undetected. Conversely, in an environment where the `claude-cli` preset is not registered, `out.exit` is also nonzero for the "unknown preset" reason, and `assert out.exit == 3` (or `out.data["reviewer_refused"]`) will fail, contradicting the comment that assumes "the preset exists". The condition should be an unconditional assertion after establishing the preset is available (e.g. skip explicitly if the preset is absent), not a guard that silently swallows the success path.

chunk_findings.detail: The write path hands the person's raw input straight to `CW.apply_edit` as a literal (`CW.Spelled(edit.value)`), but the `literal` field of the returned `Outcome` and the user-facing `text` are produced by serialising `edit.value` a second time with `TC.literal(edit.value)`. Because `Spelled` treats the typed text as the literal (the diff's own comment: "`5` and `true` are the literals they spell"), while `TC.literal` is the value→literal serialiser (the same family as `tomlcfg.value` used by the other callers to pre-serialise), the two disagree whenever the typed literal is not a string. Concrete input: `compute --set workers 4` writes `workers = 4` (raw `Spelled`) but the returned `literal`/`text` are computed from the Python-ish value and report a quoted string, i.e. `workers = "4"  (<path>)`. API consumers reading `out.data["literal"]` and users reading the message are then told a value different from what is on disk. Since the whole point of the refactor is that the caller/person already supplies the literal (which is why `Spelled` is used for the write), the display must be `literal = edit.value` (the literal actually written), not a re-serialisation of it.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/setup.py, `configure` set branch (`literal = TC.literal(edit.value)`)

chunk_findings.detail: The two halves of this test disagree about which file `reviewers_add` writes reviewers to, so one of them must fail. The first half asserts the local write lands in the side file `repo/".ddflow"/"local"/"reviewers.toml"`, and `test_layer_paths_are_defined_once` pins `TC.layer_path(tmp, "local", "reviewers.toml")` as the reviewers path for the local layer — i.e. reviewers are written through the per-group side file `reviewers.toml`, not the layer's `config.toml` (in fact, this same file proves `CW.config_file(repo, local=True)` is `layer_path(repo, "local")` == `.ddflow/local/config.toml`, which is *not* where the local reviewers were just written). For `shared=True` the analogous path is `layer_path(repo, "file", "reviewers.toml")` == `.ddflow/reviewers.toml`, but the assertion reads `_committed(repo)` which is `tomllib.loads((repo/".ddflow"/"config.toml").read_text())`. Since the preceding non-shared call wrote only `.ddflow/local/reviewers.toml`, `.ddflow/config.toml` does not exist (or contains no `[[reviewer]]`), so `_committed(repo)["reviewer"]` raises `FileNotFoundError`/`KeyError` and the test never exercises the quoting behavior (`Bb11e7a8186`) it claims to cover. Fixing the test requires reading the shared file (`tomllib.loads((repo/".ddflow"/"reviewers.toml").read_text())["reviewer"]`) or using the path returned in `out.data["path"]`, as the sibling `test_a_name_given_wins_over_the_preset_and_a_newer_format_is_a_refusal` does.

chunk_findings.detail: `_upgrade_vocabulary["provided"]` is flipped to `True` *before* `api.refs.provide_upgrade_vocabulary(...)` is actually executed, so a single failure of the provision permanently and silently disables it for the rest of the process. Concretely: `_api()` is called by every tool; on the first `ddflow_upgrade` invocation the flag is set, then `provide_upgrade_vocabulary` runs `services.migrations.refs.provide`, which imports the migration module. If that import/call raises once (e.g. a partially-initialized environment or a transient import failure), the exception propagates to the first tool caller, but the guard is already `True`. Every later `_api()` call — including a retry of `ddflow upgrade --apply` — short-circuits the `if`, so the tool table is never handed to the stale-references migration and `ddflow upgrade` reports nothing/does not rewrite the deprecated command in `AGENTS.md`. The assignment should occur only after `provide_upgrade_vocabulary` returns (or on success), matching the stated meaning "whether this process has handed the tool table to `ddflow_upgrade` yet".
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/tools/_common.py:137 (`_api`)

chunk_findings.detail:
`_upgrade_vocabulary["provided"]` is flipped to `True` *before* `api.refs.provide_upgrade_vocabulary(None, sources()[1])` is actually invoked:

    _upgrade_vocabulary["provided"] = True
    api.refs.provide_upgrade_vocabulary(None, sources()[1])

That latches "registered" on the mere intent to register. In the long-lived MCP server process, if the `provide` call raises for any environment reason (e.g. a transient import/registry error while `sources()` or `services.migrations.refs` is being wired up), the first tool call surfaces the exception, but the flag has already been persisted as `True`. On the next `ddflow_upgrade` invocation the guard short-circuits, `_api()` returns the module normally, and the stale-references migration is handed no Vocabulary — so it finds nothing and leaves deprecated command names in the project's managed `AGENTS.md` region untouched, with no error. The failure only appears on the retry, which is exactly the "silently does nothing" symptom this change exists to remove, and it is unrecoverable until the process restarts. Setting the flag only after `provide_upgrade_vocabulary` returns (or resetting it on exception) removes the masking.

chunk_findings.detail:
The previous command normalized the internal filter key `agent` to the public `owner` before emitting JSON: `"filters": {("owner" if k == "agent" else k): v for k, v in res.filters.items()}`. The new code deleted that transformation and now emits `out.data` verbatim, so the JSON body's `filters` object is whatever the shared `view_read` returns.

Concretely: `ddflow search foo --owner alice --json`. Before this change the body contained `"filters": {"owner": "alice"}`; after the change, if `view_read` returns the viewer's raw filter dict (the same key the human-readable branch consumes with `d['filters']`, i.e. `agent`), consumers get `"filters": {"agent": "alice"}`. Any script parsing `.filters.owner` (the documented/normalized name that the removed line existed to guarantee) now silently reads a missing key. The human path only prints the dict, so this asymmetry is invisible without a JSON consumer, which is exactly why the normalization was there. Either `view_read` must be verified to re-apply the `agent`→`owner` mapping, or the mapping must be restored in the JSON branch.

data.body:
~12 planned hand-written CRUD surfaces and ~8 new verb tools against a nearly full tools/list budget. The descriptor reuses B-view-list-core (done), mcp_bound, api/_dedupe and search-core. Settles the naming decided in B-uni-decide. Then rules move onto it and onto def-records (the rules subsystem re-implements dedupe Answer at api/rules.py:29, its own tokenizer, Jaccard, regex search and manifest writes: ~500 lines). Re-point B-rules-cli, B-skills-events, B-skills-author, B-sub-events, B-sched-author, B-dt-surfaces, B-ds-surfaces, B-docs-check-command, B-quota-surfaces, B-hx-cli, B-id-surfaces, B-af-surface, B-coh-resolve, B199, B-rw-revise, B-rules-inventory.

D-unify (operator 2026-10-06): Rules become recorded events on the definition-record model (B-uni-def-records): one-time import of today's .ddflow/rules/*.toml as events; the files stay as a generated view checked like other views; a hand edit is detected by digest and imported as an event. Names: 'ddflow rule' singular with 'rules' alias; 'ddflow docs' is the single docs group; schedules are 'schedules'; process jobs keep 'job'.

Rules and decisions are both GuidanceRecord kinds (B-uni-guidance-core): one descriptor family, two user-facing names ('ddflow rule', 'ddflow decision').

Widened 2026-10-06 (unification survey): the RecordKind descriptor also serves the knowledge kinds: items, decisions, bugs, research, lessons and the viewers. Evidence of duplication: api/decisions.py:90 vs api/items.py:507, and api/knowledge/bugs.py:68 vs research.py:76.

Split into: B-uni-record-surface.1-api, B-uni-record-surface.2-surface.

chunk_findings.detail: `_limit` implements "0 or None is the default" as `raw in (None, 0)`. Because `False == 0` and `0.0 == 0`, that membership test is also true for `False` and for the float `0.0`, so the two non-count values that the very next line tries to reject (`isinstance(raw, bool)` and the `not isinstance(raw, int)` check) never reach it. Given `record_list(repo, RULE, limit=False)` (or `limit=0.0`, e.g. a JSON `false`/`0.0` limit arriving from an MCP client), `_limit` returns `(DEFAULT_LIMIT, "")` and the call silently lists 25 rows instead of refusing with "limit must be a whole number, 0 or more". The bool guard only ever fires for `True`, so the explicit refusal contract documented on `_limit` is bypassed for the most plausible bad inputs.

chunk_findings.detail: `record_add` builds and passes the definition-level `title` and `body` (`title=str(stored.get(kind.title,""))`, `body=_text(...)`), but `record_revise` calls `DEFS.def_record(repo, kind.def_kind, rid, stored, source=prev.source, provenance=..., agent=agent)` with neither, so a revise overwrites the definition recorded for that id with the parameter defaults. `def_record` only receives `def_kind` (a plain string) and therefore cannot rebuild the descriptor's text itself — that is exactly why `add` computes `_text`/title for it. Revise even preserves `source` from `prev` but not `title`/`body`, i.e. it is an overwrite, not a merge. Input: `record_revise(repo, RULE, "r1", {"title": "New rule", "content": "New text"}, reason="fix")` stores the new `fields` but leaves the definition's `title`/`body` empty, which are "what the duplicate check and the search read" per `RecordKind`'s docstring, so the record's dedup text/digest no longer reflect its content.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/records.py:record_revise

chunk_findings.detail: The required-field check is `[s.name for s in kind.fields if s.required and not out.get(s.name)]`, which uses truthiness rather than presence. `out.get(...)` is `0`/`False`/`""`/`[]` for a legitimately supplied value, so the add/revise is refused as if the field were absent. Input: a kind declaring `FieldSpec("count", "integer", required=True)` with `record_add(repo, kind, "x", {"count": 0, ...})` returns "a kind needs count" although `count` was given; likewise a required boolean `False` or a required array `[]` (an empty list is a valid value for `FIELD_TYPES` `"array"`). The check should test membership (`s.name not in out`), not the value's truthiness.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/records.py:_checked (whole branch)

chunk_findings.detail: `MAX_SCAN` is documented as "Characters of one record a regex or an exact search looks at", and the regex branch honours it (`if rx.search(t[:MAX_SCAN])`), but the exact branch does `if needle in " ".join(t.lower().split())` over the *full* text. Since `content` is unbounded, `record_search(repo, RULE, "x", mode="exact")` builds a full normalized copy of every candidate's entire text, so the documented bound does not hold for exact search. It should slice `t[:MAX_SCAN]` (or scale it) like the regex and ranked branches do.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/records.py:_scored (exact branch)

chunk_findings.detail: The required-field check is `missing := [s.name for s in kind.fields if s.required and not out.get(s.name)]`. It tests *truthiness*, not presence, so a required field whose supplied value is legitimately falsy is reported as absent. Concretely, given a `RecordKind` with `FieldSpec("priority", "integer", required=True)` and a call `record_add(repo, kind, "r1", {"title": "x", "priority": 0})`, `out` contains `{"priority": 0}`, but `not out.get("priority")` is `True`, so the call returns `O.failed(..., "a <kind> needs priority")` even though `priority` was supplied. The same happens for a required boolean supplied as `False`, and worse, for a required field whose declared `default` is `0`/`False`/`""`: the default is inserted (`spec.default is not None`) and then immediately flagged missing, so such a record can *never* be added. `FIELD_TYPES` explicitly allows `integer`/`boolean` and `FieldSpec.required` is a supported option, so this is reachable; the check should distinguish "key absent / None" from "value is falsy".
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/records.py — `_checked` (the `whole=True` branch)

chunk_findings.detail: The constant is documented as "Characters of one record a regex or an exact search looks at" (`MAX_SCAN`), and the regex branch honours it (`rx.search(t[:MAX_SCAN])`), but the exact branch uses the full, unsliced text: `if needle in " ".join(t.lower().split())`. For a record whose `_text` exceeds `MAX_SCAN` and whose query phrase occurs only past character 2000, `record_search(..., mode="exact")` returns the record while `record_search(..., mode="regex")` for a matching pattern does not — the two modes disagree on the same record, and the documented cap does not apply to exact. Given the module's "Every payload is bounded" premise and the `(as services.search)` note, the exact branch should slice `t` like the regex branch.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/records.py — `_scored`, `mode == "exact"`

chunk_findings.detail: `_cell` bounds each individual string to `CELL_MAX` but places no bound on the *number* of elements in an array field, and `_row` emits the whole clipped list. A definition record can be added with an arbitrarily long array (`_field_problem` only requires "a list of strings"), so `record_add(repo, RULE-kind, "r1", {"title": "x", "tags": ["t"] * 1_000_000})` followed by `record_list` returns a single row carrying all million elements, contradicting the module's "Every payload is bounded" claim; `tags` is even one of `RULE.columns`, so this path is on the default list surface.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/records.py — `_cell`

chunk_findings.detail: The edit path validates named fields only with `_field_problem`, and for a partial record (`whole=False`) the required-field check (`_absent`) is never run — that block is guarded by `if whole:`. `_field_problem` accepts *any* string for a `string` field, including `""`/whitespace, so a required string field can be blanked through an edit even though `record_add`/`record_revise` reject exactly the same value (whole mode's `_absent` treats a blank string as missing: `value is None or (spec.type == "string" and not value.strip())`). Concretely, after `record_add(repo, RULE, "r1", {"title": "x"})` succeeds, `record_edit(repo, RULE, "r1", {"title": "   "})` returns OK with `title` stored blank: `fields` is non-empty so the `if not fields` guard does not fire, `value is None` is false so the removal branch does not fire, and `_field_problem(FieldSpec("title", required=True), "   ")` returns `""`. The record then violates the "must carry every required field" invariant that the add and revise verbs enforce, and its blank title flows into `_text`/`_body` (duplicate check and search) and into list rows.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/records.py — `_checked`/`record_edit`

chunk_findings.detail: The assertion `assert a.fn is p.parse_args(["note", "list"]).fn or callable(a.fn)` is a tautology: the right-hand operand `callable(a.fn)` is true for every subcommand handler that `parse_args` can produce (the fixture itself later invokes `a.fn(...)`, so it must be callable). Because of the `or`, the whole expression is `True` regardless of whether the `notes` alias actually routes to the same handler as `note`. Concretely: if `add_commands`/`record_group_aliases` wired the `notes` alias to a distinct or wrong handler, or returned some other callable stored in `a.fn`, this line would still pass, so the part of the test named "the old group word still works" is not actually verified by this check. The `is`-comparison that was presumably intended (identity of the handler for `notes list` and `note list`) is effectively dead code; dropping the trailing `or callable(a.fn)` (and asserting directly) would make the test able to fail.

chunk_findings.detail: The sequential `str.replace` calls operate on the whole reason string, including the caller-supplied `rid`, so a swap trigger that appears inside the record id is silently rewritten. Concretely, with `kind.def_kind == "skill"`, `kind.name == "note"`, `rid == "record it again to bring it back"`, and `out.reason == "skill 'record it again to bring it back' was deleted"`, the second swap produces `"note 'record it again to bring it back' was deleted"`; then the final generic swap fires inside the quoted id and returns `"note 'revise it to bring it back' was deleted"`. The error message names the wrong record id. Similarly, a `rid` containing `"skill definition"` is corrupted by the first swap before the later kind-specific swap runs, leaving the storage kind in the output. These swaps need to apply only to the template text around the id, or the message must be rebuilt from structured data instead of blind `str.replace`.

chunk_findings.detail: The test does not verify what its name asserts. It iterates `R.VERBS`, calls `_parser().parse_args(["note", verb, "--help"])`, and only asserts `stop.value.code == 0`. It never inspects the rendered help text (the `capsys` fixture is not even requested), so the assertion only proves each verb's subparser exists and accepts `--help`. If a verb's help omitted some or all of its flag names, the test would still pass, so it provides no protection for the "help names its flags" behavior it is named for. Given a change that drops a flag from a verb's help formatting, this test stays green.

chunk_findings.detail: `_named` builds the dk-specific substitutions as `[("skill definition", "note"), ("skill 'r1'", "note 'r1'"), ("skill r1:", "note r1:")]` (with `dk="skill"`, `name="note"`, `rid="r1"`) and then applies them in that order with `str.replace`. The first pattern is a prefix of the third whenever the record id begins with `definition`, so it fires first and eats the id. Concretely, for a record whose id is `definition` (a perfectly legal user-chosen id) and the `api.defs` reason that the third pattern was written to handle, `"skill definition: already exists"` becomes `"note: already exists"` instead of `"note definition: already exists"` — the id is dropped and the user is told to use a name that does not exist. Same for any id with the prefix, e.g. `rid="definitions-v2"`: `"skill definitions-v2: ..."` → `"notes-v2: ..."` (correct would be `"note definitions-v2: ..."`). The general defect is that the dk-specific patterns are matched in a fixed order over a string that may re-contain another pattern (and the first pattern is not anchored on the right, so it also matches inside the quoted id form, e.g. `rid="'skill definition'"`), so the substitution can rewrite part of an id or of another pattern's match instead of only the kind wording.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/records.py:412 `_named` (swap ordering / overlapping patterns)

chunk_findings.detail: The function is documented as producing the kind's *group* aliases ("The old words of the kind's group (`add_commands`' `group_aliases`)"), yet every alias it builds is stamped as a command alias: `Alias("command", old, kind.name, since)`. If `Alias`'s first field discriminates the kind of entity being aliased (which is why a separate `group_aliases` input exists on `add_commands`), then for a kind with `aliases=("rules",)` this registers `rules` as a hidden *command* alias of the group name rather than a *group* alias, so the old group spelling (`ddflow rules ...`) will not resolve to the group's subcommands (or will be rejected as an unknown command) instead of being an always-callable hidden group alias. The literal should be `"group"` for the aliases returned by `record_group_aliases`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/records.py `record_group_aliases`

chunk_findings.detail: `_tool_params` deliberately marks every parameter `required=False` on the tool and states "which are needed depends on the verb, and `dispatch` says", and `_common("reason")` is `required=True` on the CLI for both `remove` and `revise` ("Needs a reason."). But `dispatch` only enforces `id` (show/add/edit/remove/revise) and `query` (search); it never requires `reason` for `remove`/`revise`. So the MCP call `{"verb": "remove", "id": "X"}` (or `{"verb":"revise","id":"X", ...}`) passes validation and reaches `R.record_remove(..., reason="")` / `R.record_revise(..., reason="")`, a call the corresponding CLI command rejects at argument-parse time because `--reason` is required. The two surfaces of the same dispatch therefore disagree on whether a reason is mandatory.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/records.py `dispatch` / `_tool_params`

chunk_findings.detail: The `check` parameter is declared with `exclusive=_ONE`, placing the dry-run flag into the same mutually exclusive “answer” group as `--new`, `--extends`, `--duplicate-of`, and `--related`. `--check` is not an answer: its help begins “dry run”, and the MCP half keeps the equivalent `check_only` independent of `relation` rather than exclusive with it. With this declaration, a formerly valid invocation such as `add --check --extends ID` (or `--check --new`, `--check --related ID`, etc.) now fails with argparse’s `argument --extends: not allowed with argument --check`, and the generated usage line changes from the answer alternation plus a separate `[--check]` to `[--new | --extends ID | --duplicate-of ID | --related ID | --check]`. That violates the stated requirement that `--help` remain byte-identical and changes CLI behaviour beyond the intended `skip_verify` destination rename. Remove `exclusive=_ONE` from the `check` `Param`; the group should contain only the four answer flags.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/declared/answer.py:62 (`Param("check", ...)`)

chunk_findings.detail:
The `limit` param of `decision list` is declared with `type="integer"` but no `default`:

```python
Param(
    "limit",
    type="integer",
    help="Newest decisions returned (default 25; 0 = all).",
    cli_help="the newest N (0 = all)",
),
```

while its handler is `limit=int(a["limit"]) if a.get("limit") else None`. The handler always passes `limit=` explicitly and maps a falsy value to `None`, which the API interprets as "no limit" (that is the whole reason `0` can mean "all"). The documented default of 25 therefore has to be supplied by the *parser/schema* (the original hand-written `decision list` had an argparse `default=25`: omitted ⇒ `25`; `--limit 0` ⇒ `0` ⇒ `None` ⇒ all). Because the registry Param carries no `default`:

- `ddflow decision list` with no `--limit` now yields `None` → the API returns **all** decisions instead of the newest 25 (on a project with many decisions this changes both the result set and its size).
- The generated CLI help and MCP inputSchema no longer carry `default: 25`, so `--help` / `tools/list` are not byte-identical to the previous output (the MCP `help` text even still claims "default 25").

Contrast with the sibling declarations that got this right: `recall`'s limit has `default=3`, `dupes`'s limit has `default=0` (also documented as "0 = all"), and `lesson search`'s limit deliberately omits a literal default because its default is config-driven (`"default: [lessons].max_results"`). `decision list` has a literal default of 25 and must declare `default=25`.

chunk_findings.detail: The whole change to this file is six added import lines and ten deleted `Command(...)` entries; nothing that reads the six new names is added, and no replacement entry is emitted for any deleted path. So within this file the coverage metadata for `("task","list")`, `("phase","list")`, `("bug","list")`, `("lesson","list")`, `("session","list")`, `("session","show")`, `("search",)`, `("bug","reopen")`, `("decision","search")` and `("session","adopt-orphans")` is simply gone: there is no code that rebuilds them from `_KNOWLEDGE`/`_RECORDS`/`_lists`/`_search`/`_sessions`/`ANSWER_FLAG_EXEMPT` and no comprehension/unpacking (the second hunk is a pure deletion — old 18 lines → new 10, exactly the two removed four-line `Command`s). Unless some other module independently re-registers each of these exact paths and its `via`/`reason`, the consumer of this list (`covering_tools`, already imported here) now reports a path such as `covering_tools(("task","list")) == ()` instead of `("ddflow_list",)`, i.e. the CLI/MCP parity check flags these previously-covered commands as uncovered. If the intent was to derive these exemptions from the declared workspaces, the derivation call is missing from this diff.
