chunk_findings.detail: The guard `if self.positional and not self.required and self.nargs is None` equates "has a non-None `nargs`" with "optional positional", but argparse only treats `"?"` and `"*"` as optional; a positional with `nargs="+"` is still mandatory (`parse_args([])` raises "the following arguments are required"). Nothing in the new validation restricts `nargs` to `"?"`/`"*"` (the only new check merely forbids it on non-positionals), so `Param("terms", positional=True, nargs="+")` passes `__post_init__`, leaves `required` as `False`, and therefore `mcp_required` returns `False`: the generated MCP schema omits `terms` from the `required` list while the generated argparse parser refuses an invocation without it. (The same root cause makes the other direction wrong too: `self.nargs != "?"` in the default check rejects `nargs="*"` with a default, which argparse accepts.) If only `"?"` is intended to be supported, `nargs` should be constrained to it; otherwise requiredness must be derived from the specific nargs value.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/registry.py (Param.__post_init__, `required` derivation)

chunk_findings.detail: `add_to` sets `kwargs["required"] = True` on the action (line 376–377) *before* the action is handed to the named mutually exclusive group created at line 384 (`groups[self.exclusive] = parser.add_mutually_exclusive_group()`), and the group is created with no `required=` argument. argparse's `_MutuallyExclusiveGroup._add_action` refuses any action whose `required` is truthy (`ValueError: mutually exclusive arguments must be optional`). So any declaration that both names a group and marks the param required — which is the only way the registry can express "exactly one of `--id`/`--last` must be given", e.g. `Param(name="id", option="--id", exclusive="sel", required=True)` — blows up while the CLI parser is being built instead of producing `add_mutually_exclusive_group(required=...)` with an optional member. The same ValueError is hit by a positional that names a group, since argparse marks positionals `required=True` by default. `_check_params` validates duplicate names and `tool_order` but not this combination, so nothing rejects it earlier; the failure surfaces only at parser construction.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/registry.py:376 (`Param.add_to`)

chunk_findings.detail: The hunk deletes the two guards that used to sit at this spot — `if not self.path and not self.tool: raise ValueError(...)` and `if len(self.via) > MAX_VIA: raise ValueError(...)` — and replaces them with an unrelated `tool_order` check. Nothing in the visible new code re-establishes those invariants: `add_commands` now only does `if not declared.path: continue`, so a declaration such as `Command(path=(), tool="", params=())` (or any declaration where the CLI path and the MCP tool name are both unset/default) constructs without error and is then silently dropped by the CLI registration loop (and has no tool name for the MCP TOOLS entry), instead of failing at construction as it did before. Demonstrating input: build a `Command` whose `path` is empty and whose `tool` is falsy, then run it through `add_commands`; before this change `__post_init__` raised, now the command simply vanishes from every surface with no diagnostic. The same deletion also drops the `via` length constraint, so `Command(via=("a", "b", "c"))` is accepted even though the removed message documents `via` as `(tool,)` or `(tool, selector)`; any consumer that unpacks or indexes `via` will now fail at run time rather than at declaration time.

chunk_findings.detail: The old code always passed a `help` kwarg (`help=(groups or {}).get(group, "")`), whereas the new code omits the kwarg entirely when `groups` is falsy or does not contain the group. `argparse._SubParsersAction.add_parser` only creates a `_ChoicesPseudoAction` when the literal key `'help'` is present in `**kwargs`, so `help=""` still registers a pseudo-action (the subcommand name is printed as a line under the group, with no description), while omitting `help` registers nothing (`_choices_actions` stays empty) and the subcommand/alias name line disappears from `--help`. Concrete input: `add_commands(subparsers, COMMANDS, groups=None)`, or a `groups` dict missing the command's top-level group; before this change `--help` showed the `foo` name line under the group, now it does not, so `--help` is not byte-identical (the only intended difference is the `skip_verify` → `skip_regression_verify` dest rename). Note the `group_aliases` loop still uses the old `help=(groups or {}).get(group, "")` form, so alias-only groups keep the name line while command groups silently lose it, making the two paths inconsistent.

chunk_findings.detail:
When `_group_subparsers` returns an existing group, the function sets `made[group] = existing` but never sets `parsers[group]`. The later `group_aliases` loop is guarded by `if group not in made:` and then unconditionally calls `add_command_alias(subparsers, parsers[group], alias.old, alias)`. For a group that already exists (the new “existing group” path added in this change), `group in made` is true, the creation branch that would populate `parsers[group]` is skipped, and `parsers[group]` raises `KeyError`. Concrete input: 
a first `add_commands(...)` that creates group `decisions`, followed by a second `add_commands(..., existing group)` that also passes `group_aliases={"decisions": [...]}` — the second call crashes instead of attaching the alias. The old code maintained the invariant that every group in `made` also has a `parsers[group]` entry; the new `existing` branch breaks that invariant without updating the alias loop.

chunk_findings.detail: The changed line replaces the binding of the constant `RECALL_MAX_CHARS` with a module alias `K`, but no use of `RECALL_MAX_CHARS` in this module is rewritten by the change (the diff for reporting.py contains only this one hunk). `RECALL_MAX_CHARS` was previously imported precisely because the module body used it — the fact that this import had to be updated at all when the constant moved to `surfaces/declared` proves the name was live — so every remaining reference in `TOOLS` (the dict beginning on the following line) is now an unbound name. chunk_findings.detail: The command declares `max_chars` with the literal default `4000`, but the module imports `RECALL_MAX_CHARS` from `...core.budget` and the same command's handler reads the value back as `max_chars=int(a.get("max_chars") or RECALL_MAX_CHARS)`. The declared default is what gets put into the argparse namespace (and into every MCP invocation that does not supply the field), so `ddflow recall QUERY` — with no `--max-chars` — always feeds the handler the truthy literal `4000`, the `or RECALL_MAX_CHARS` fallback is never reached on the CLI, and the effective answer budget is pinned to the hard-coded number instead of the project's budget constant. On the MCP side the same omission falls through to `RECALL_MAX_CHARS`. Unless `RECALL_MAX_CHARS` happens to equal `4000` exactly, the two surfaces of this one declaration return differently sized recall answers, and the `tools/list` schema is no longer the "byte-identical" output the change claims (the recall input schema's `max_chars` default changed from the constant's value to `4000`). The declaration should use `default=RECALL_MAX_CHARS`, which is exactly what the handler's own fallback shows was intended; contrast the sibling `limit` param, which duplicates its literal (`default=3` / `or 3`) consistently.

chunk_findings.detail:
The added guard only rejects `nargs` on a *non*-positional:
```python
if self.nargs is not None and not self.positional:
    raise ValueError(f"param {self.name!r}: nargs is for a positional")
```
and the required-derivation was changed to skip every positional that has a non-`None` `nargs`:
```python
if self.positional and not self.required and self.nargs is None:
    object.__setattr__(self, "required", True)
```
Nothing restricts a positional's `nargs` to `"?"`/`"*"`. So `Param("terms", positional=True, nargs="+")` passes `__post_init__` unmodified: the default check is skipped (`default is _UNSET`), the new check is skipped (`positional` is true), and the required check is skipped (`nargs is not None`), leaving `required == False`. Via `mcp_required` the tool schema then advertises the property as optional, while argparse treats a `nargs="+"` positional as mandatory (`parse_args([])` raises "the following arguments are required: terms") — the CLI and MCP surfaces disagree about the same parameter.

The triage's probe does not answer this: `Param(positional, nargs='+')` is `Param("positional", nargs="+")`, i.e. a parameter whose *name* is `"positional"` with `positional=False`, which is exactly the non-positional case the new guard rejects. It never exercises `positional=True`, so the original defect (`Param("terms", positional=True, nargs="+")` being silently accepted and marked optional) is still present; a `nargs` whitelist (`"?"`/`"*"`) or forcing `required=True` for `"+"` is still required.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/registry.py:288 (`Param.__post_init__`, the new `nargs` validation)

chunk_findings.detail: The hunk only does `made[group] = existing` when `_group_subparsers(subparsers, group)` returns a pre-existing group; it never populates the local `parsers` dict for that group (`parsers[group] = ...` is only executed in the `else` branch that actually calls `subparsers.add_parser`). The unchanged `group_aliases` loop below it still resolves aliases with `add_command_alias(subparsers, parsers[group], alias.old, alias)` in its `else` arm, so for a joined group this raises `KeyError: <group>`. Concretely, a second `build(...)`/`add_commands(...)` call that joins a group created by an earlier call while passing `group_aliases={"lesson": [...]}` hits `parsers["lesson"]` before any assignment. The prior triage marked this finding `confirmed` (its probe `tests/test_command_registry.py::test_a_group_is_listed_only_when_it_has_help_and_an_existing_group_is_joined` appends `group_aliases` to a joined group); this diff does not add the missing `parsers[group] = existing` assignment (or any equivalent), so the fix the confirmation implies is absent and the probe’s scenario still fails.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/registry.py build (the joined-group branch)

chunk_findings.detail: `Command(path=("decision","add"), ...)` declares `tool_order=("id","title","decision","context","consequences","alternatives","globs","by","supersedes","item","tags","status","sources","relation","check_only")`, but none of this command's params is named `relation`: its params are exactly `id, title, decision, context, consequences, alternatives, globs, tags, sources, item, by, status, supersedes` plus whatever `ANSWER_PARAMS` supplies. `relation` is the property of the *link* tool, not of `decision_add`. When the registry builds the MCP inputSchema for `ddflow_decision_add` and resolves each `tool_order` entry against the command's params, `relation` has no match: either the lookup raises (KeyError while generating the tool, so the tool/CLI cannot even be constructed) or the unknown name is ignored and the declared ordering is not reproduced (any `answer`/`check_only` param supplied by `ANSWER_PARAMS` is emitted after the ordered block instead of at its original position), so the `tools/list` golden cannot be byte-identical as the intent states. The same copy/paste is what makes `answer` (if it is one of `ANSWER_PARAMS`) absent from `tool_order` while `check_only` is present, i.e. the tail of the schema order is wrong regardless of how the registry treats an unresolved name. A concrete check: for this `Command`, `{p.name for p in cmd.params}` does not contain `"relation"`.

chunk_findings.detail: Every `Param` in this file carries a `help` (and generally a `cli_help`), including the positional `id` of the two sibling bug commands (`bug invalid` and `bug fixed` both use `help="Bug id."`), the `verb` positional (`help="optional: \`research add\` = \`research\`"`) and both `session` positionals. The `bug reopen` command is the single exception: its `id` is declared with `positional=True` and nothing else, even though the same command's `reason` param does carry the CLI text (`help="why the closure was wrong"`), confirming that for this tool-less command `help` is the CLI help source. This command has no `tool` (it is dispatched through `via=("ddflow_bug_invalid", "reopen")`), so its parser is built from these params; with `help` absent, `ddflow bug reopen --help` renders the `id` positional with no description instead of the "Bug id." line the pre-refactor parser had, so the `--help` output for `bug reopen` is *not* byte-identical to the golden and any argument-metadata dump/parser-equivalence test fails. (If `Param.help` has no default on the dataclass, the omission is worse than cosmetic: constructing this `Param` raises `TypeError` at import.)

chunk_findings.detail: The patch deletes ten exemption entries from the module's `Command(...)` tuple — `task/phase/bug/lesson list`, `session list`, `session show`, `search`, `bug reopen`, `decision search` and `session adopt-orphans` — which are the only places those CLI commands' MCP coverage is recorded. It replaces them with imports of the declared command modules (`viewers_lists`, `viewers_search`, `viewers_sessions`, `declared.knowledge`, `declared.records`) that were supposed to supply the replacements, but no statement anywhere in the file ever references `_lists`, `_search`, `_sessions`, `_KNOWLEDGE`, `_RECORDS` or `ANSWER_FLAG_EXEMPT` (they are under aliases, which strongly implies intended later use, and no `noqa` is present). The exemption tuple is therefore simply short by ten entries. Demonstrating input: run the MCP-coverage audit (`ddflow doctor` or the test asserting that each CLI command is either surfaced as an MCP tool or listed as exempt) — `task list` (via `ddflow_list task`), `bug reopen` (via `ddflow_bug_invalid reopen`) and `decision search` (via `ddflow_recall`) now come back uncovered, a regression that neither the `--help` nor the `tools/list` golden exercises, which is exactly why the stated golden checks pass while the behavior is wrong.

chunk_findings.detail: The diff deletes the `ddflow_link` `Command` and adds no replacement for it in this file. Unlike the other removals (`ddflow_bug_found`, `ddflow_lesson_add`, `ddflow_decision_add`, `ddflow_research_add`), which the stated intent covers by moving "knowledge … onto the declarative registry", `ddflow_link` is a relation command and its `flag_exempt` is semantically different from the consolidation constant: it exempted `--extends`, `--duplicate-of`, `--related`, **and `--distinct`** with the reason "the relation is MCP `relation` + `target`, not one flag per relation". `ANSWER_FLAG_EXEMPT` (now used for `ddflow_phase_add`, `ddflow_task_add`, `ddflow_memory_add`) only carries the duplicate-check answer flags (`--new`, `--extends`, `--duplicate-of`, `--related`, `--check`) under the "duplicate-check answer" reason, so it does not cover `--distinct` and would attach the wrong rationale to the other three flags anyway. Given the input `ddflow link --distinct …`, if the actual `ddflow_link` declaration elsewhere does not re-supply this exemption, the MCP-parity check will treat `--distinct` as an unexempted CLI flag with no MCP counterpart, changing the `tools/list` golden. If `ddflow_link` was in fact meant to be redeclared outside the stated knowledge/records/viewer move set, that redeclaration (including its distinct `flag_exempt`) is required here to keep the golden byte-identical.

chunk_findings.detail:
The removed code deliberately pinned the argparse destination to `skip_verify`:

```python
bx.add_argument("--skip-regression-verify", dest="skip_verify", action="store_true", ...)
```

An explicit `dest=` that differs from the default (`skip_regression_verify`) is only written when something reads `args.skip_verify`; the handler for this subcommand here is `cmd_bug` (imported unchanged from `..commands.knowledge`, mapped as `("bug","fixed"): cmd_bug`), and nothing in this change moves the read to the new name. The intent states the dest is now `skip_regression_verify`, i.e. the default dest of the flag. Consequently the parsed namespace gets `args.skip_regression_verify`, while `cmd_bug` still consults `args.skip_verify` (whether via direct attribute access or `getattr(args, "skip_verify", False)`). Given the input

```
ddflow bug fixed BUG-1 --skip-regression-verify --verify-reason "flaky pre-fix tree"
```

the flag no longer sets the attribute the handler reads: the "skip the pre-fix regression run" request is silently ignored (or, on direct attribute access, raises), so the pre-fix test is executed anyway and the command fails/blocks exactly in the case the flag was added for. The golden `--help`/`tools/list` checks cannot catch this because the dest is not rendered; only an end-to-end invocation of `bug fixed` with the flag does. Any MCP tool argument that was derived from the same dest name (`skip_verify`) is likewise renamed, changing the tool's accepted parameter set beyond what "byte-identical tools/list" claims.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/parsers/records.py (bug fixed registration / `HANDLERS[("bug","fixed")]`)

chunk_findings.detail: The forced-required guard was narrowed to `self.nargs is None`, but the comment it guards ("argparse refuses a missing positional, so the schema must say it is required") applies to every `nargs` value for which argparse rejects an omitted argument — notably `"+"` (one-or-more) and fixed-count nargs. Only `"?"` (and `"*"`) are genuinely optional to argparse. Given a declaration such as `Param("paths", positional=True, nargs="+")`, `required` is never forced to `True`, so `mcp_required` returns `False` and the generated MCP schema marks `paths` as not required. An MCP call omitting `paths` is therefore accepted, even though the same command on the CLI (`add_argument("paths", nargs="+")`) fails with "the following arguments are required: paths", and the handler (expecting a non-empty list) is invoked with an absent argument. The condition should treat all nargs except `"?"`/`"*"` as required, e.g. `self.nargs not in ("?", "*")`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/registry.py:292

chunk_findings.detail:
The change is supposed to introduce `Param.tool_required` as the field that records whether a
parameter is required in the generated MCP tool declaration ("Registry gains
Param.nargs/metavar/exclusive/tool_required"). The diff, however, makes both MCP-side reads go
through a different name: `spec()` now returns `self.mcp_required`
(registry.py:400) and `params_schema()` builds its `required` list from
`p.mcp_required` (registry.py:413). With the declaration's field named `tool_required`,
`Param` has no `mcp_required` attribute, so the very first command that has any parameter blows
up with `AttributeError: 'Param' object has no attribute 'mcp_required'` — `spec()` is called
by the MCP engine when it builds its tool table, and `params_schema()` when it builds the
tool's input schema. Demonstrating input: declare any command with a parameter (e.g. the
viewers' positional) and ask for `tools/list`; the MCP engine iterates the params, calls
`spec()`/`params_schema()`, and raises instead of emitting the schema. Both reads must use
`self.tool_required`, the field the change actually adds; the rename from `required` is only
correct if it names that new field.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/registry.py (Param.spec and params_schema)

chunk_findings.detail:
The hunk deletes two construction-time guards from `Command.__post_init__` without replacement in this class:

```python
if not self.path and not self.tool:
    raise ValueError("a command needs a CLI path or an MCP tool name")
if len(self.via) > MAX_VIA:
    raise ValueError(f"{'/'.join(self.path)}: via is (tool,) or (tool, selector)")
```

The new `tool_order` permutation check does not subsume either. Concretely, `Command(path=(), tool="", params=(Param("x", ...),))` used to fail at construction; it now passes `__post_init__`. `add_commands` then silently drops it (`if not declared.path: continue`), and the MCP-TOOLS side — which is generated from the same declaration and keys the tool entry off `cmd.tool` — will publish an entry whose tool name is `""` (invalid MCP) rather than failing fast on the typo'd declaration; the fact that the new error message falls back to `self.tool or '/'.join(self.path)` shows the both-empty case is no longer considered anywhere in this method. Likewise a `via` tuple longer than `MAX_VIA` (a value the field's contract, and `MAX_VIA` itself, say is illegal) is now accepted and flows into the MCP routing code instead of being rejected at declaration time. If these checks were intended to move into the new `surfaces/declared/` loader, that replacement is not visible here and the registry no longer enforces the invariant for any other constructor of `Command`.
chunk_findings.location: ddflow/surfaces/registry.py — `Command.__post_init__` (the block that used to end with the alias check)

chunk_findings.detail: In the new reuse path the code only records the group's subparsers action (`made[group] = existing`) and never populates `parsers[group]`; the creation path still does `parsers[group] = gp`. The alias loop that runs a few lines later in the same function unconditionally dereferences `parsers[group]` for every group that ended up in `made` (`add_command_alias(subparsers, parsers[group], alias.old, alias)`). Since `made` now also contains joined groups, any call that joins a pre-existing group *and* supplies `group_aliases` for that group skips the intended `if group not in made: raise ValueError(...)` and instead dies with `KeyError: 'viewer'` at parser-build/import time. Concrete trigger: call `add_commands(sub, [Command(path=("viewer",))], groups={"viewer": "..."})` and then `add_commands(sub, [Command(path=("viewer","list"))], group_aliases={"viewer": [Alias("v", "viewer")]})` — the second call takes the `existing is not None` branch, then `parsers["viewer"]` raises. The join path needs the group's parser recorded (e.g. have `_group_subparsers` return the parser as well, or fall back to it), otherwise the `parsers` invariant the alias loop relies on is broken.

chunk_findings.detail: The change removes the module's only binding for `RECALL_MAX_CHARS` (`-from ...core.budget import RECALL_MAX_CHARS`) and substitutes an unrelated alias import (`+from ..declared import knowledge as K`), but no other line in this file is touched — no use site is rewritten and none is deleted. The constant was imported because this module references it (it is consumed by the module-level `TOOLS` entry, which is built at import time and whose start is visible unchanged just below the import), so after this change the name is unbound. Concretely, `import ddflow.surfaces.tools.reporting` (which the CLI/MCP surface does at startup, and which the stated `tools/list` golden exercises) now raises `NameError: name 'RECALL_MAX_CHARS' is not defined` instead of producing the tool schema. The use site must be updated to `K.RECALL_MAX_CHARS` (or the constant re-imported from the new location); the lone import swap leaves the module inconsistent and `K` with no consumer.

chunk_findings.detail: The `Param("verb", positional=True, nargs="?", choices=("add",), cli_only=True)` declaration has no default, so argparse uses `None` as the default. For a positional with `nargs='?'`, argparse validates the default against `choices` even when the argument is omitted (`_get_values` calls `_check_value` unconditionally for `OPTIONAL`). Since `None` is not in `("add",)`, `root.parse_args(["x"])` raises `SystemExit` with “invalid choice: None” before any of the assertions after that line can run. The test therefore cannot pass without either giving `verb` a default that belongs to `choices` or not using `choices` in the omitted-argument case.

chunk_findings.detail: The command declares `max_chars` with the literal default `4000`, but the module imports `RECALL_MAX_CHARS` from `...core.budget` and the same command's handler reads the value back as `max_chars=int(a.get("max_chars") or RECALL_MAX_CHARS)`. The declared default is what gets put into the argparse namespace (and into every MCP invocation that does not supply the field), so `ddflow recall QUERY` — with no `--max-chars` — always feeds the handler the truthy literal `4000`, the `or RECALL_MAX_CHARS` fallback is never reached on the CLI, and the effective answer budget is pinned to the hard-coded number instead of the project's budget constant. On the MCP side the same omission falls through to `RECALL_MAX_CHARS`. Unless `RECALL_MAX_CHARS` happens to equal `4000` exactly, the two surfaces of this one declaration return differently sized recall answers, and the `tools/list` schema is no longer the "byte-identical" output the change claims (the recall input schema's `max_chars` default changed from the constant's value to `4000`). The declaration should use `default=RECALL_MAX_CHARS`, which is exactly what the handler's own fallback shows was intended; contrast the sibling `limit` param, which duplicates its literal (`default=3` / `or 3`) consistently.

chunk_findings.detail:
The added guard only rejects `nargs` on a *non*-positional:
```python
if self.nargs is not None and not self.positional:
    raise ValueError(f"param {self.name!r}: nargs is for a positional")
```
and the required-derivation was changed to skip every positional that has a non-`None` `nargs`:
```python
if self.positional and not self.required and self.nargs is None:
    object.__setattr__(self, "required", True)
```
Nothing restricts a positional's `nargs` to `"?"`/`"*"`. So `Param("terms", positional=True, nargs="+")` passes `__post_init__` unmodified: the default check is skipped (`default is _UNSET`), the new check is skipped (`positional` is true), and the required check is skipped (`nargs is not None`), leaving `required == False`. Via `mcp_required` the tool schema then advertises the property as optional, while argparse treats a `nargs="+"` positional as mandatory (`parse_args([])` raises "the following arguments are required: terms") — the CLI and MCP surfaces disagree about the same parameter.

The triage's probe does not answer this: `Param(positional, nargs='+')` is `Param("positional", nargs="+")`, i.e. a parameter whose *name* is `"positional"` with `positional=False`, which is exactly the non-positional case the new guard rejects. It never exercises `positional=True`, so the original defect (`Param("terms", positional=True, nargs="+")` being silently accepted and marked optional) is still present; a `nargs` whitelist (`"?"`/`"*"`) or forcing `required=True` for `"+"` is still required.

chunk_findings.detail: The refactor throws away the declarative answer flags that used to be produced here and replaces them with `tuple(dataclasses.replace(p, exclusive=None) for p in ANSWER_CLI_PARAMS)`, forcibly clearing the parser-level grouping that `ANSWER_CLI_PARAMS` declares for these exact five flags (they are the shared CLI answer params, which is why the registry had to grow `Param.exclusive` in the first place). The only justification offered for dropping the group is the new docstring sentence “Not exclusive on the parser: `_handler` refuses two with a message that names them,” but no handler is added or changed in this diff, so the mutually-exclusive argument check that the records CLI previously had (the flags were added through `dedupe_flags.add_flags`, which is the very helper the old docstring says these params “spell”) is simply gone. Concretely, `ddflow bug add --new --extends 5 …` (likewise `lesson add`/`research add`) now parses successfully with two contradictory answer flags set instead of being rejected at argument-parsing time; nothing in this hunk demonstrates that `_handler` rejects the combination, and any test or caller that relied on the argparse error/exit-2 path now observes different behavior. This is a silent behavior change that the `--help`/`tools/list` goldens cannot catch, because mutual exclusion is not part of the help text.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/records.py `_answer_params()`

chunk_findings.detail:
`add_to` implements `exclusive` by lazily creating a group with `parser.add_mutually_exclusive_group()` and then calling `groups[self.exclusive].add_argument(*args, **kwargs)`, where the optional branch has already put `required=True` into `kwargs` whenever `self.required` is set. argparse refuses exactly that: `_MutuallyExclusiveGroup._add_action` raises `ValueError('mutually exclusive arguments must be optional')` as soon as it is handed an action whose `required` is true. So a declaration such as

    Param("relation", flag="--extends", exclusive="relation", required=True)   # sibling: --duplicate-of/--related/--distinct, same exclusive

makes `add_to` execute `group.add_argument("--extends", required=True, ...)`, which raises from inside argparse at registration/import time with an internal message, instead of being rejected by the new `_check_params()` construction-time validation or expressed as a group-level requirement. The same rejection fires for a *positional* carrying `exclusive`, because `_get_positional_kwargs` sets `required=True` for every positional whose `nargs` is not one of `?`/`*`, so `Param("x", positional=True, exclusive="g")` also dies in `_MutuallyExclusiveGroup._add_action`. Because the group is created with the default `required=False` and the only lever the registry gives a declaration is the per-parameter `required` flag, the new `exclusive` field cannot express the common "exactly one of these flags must be supplied" pattern: the declaration either crashes as above or, if the author drops `required=True`, silently stops enforcing it.

chunk_findings.detail: The `split` `Param("into", …, action="append", default=[])` makes the command-line parser collect repeated `--into` values into a **list** (e.g. `["login=add login", "logout=add logout"]`), while the MCP entry passes one comma-separated string. The shared `call` does `into=[x.strip() for x in str(a.get("into", "")).split(",") if x.strip()]` unconditionally. Ran from the CLI, `str(["login=add login", "logout=add logout"])` yields the literal `"['login=add login', 'logout=add logout']"`, which splits into `["['login=add login'", "'logout=add logout']"]`; the api then parses each element as `sub-id=title`, producing sub-ids like `['login` and titles like `add login'`. Every CLI `ddflow split` invocation files garbage children. That the sibling `update` command explicitly branches on `isinstance(a["globs"], list)` (same shared-lambda mechanics) confirms the `call` receives lists from the CLI, so the missing `list` branch here is the defect: it should pass a list through unchanged and only split the MCP string.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/declared/queue.py — `Command(path=("split",))`, the `call` lambda's `into` conversion

chunk_findings.detail: Both `call` lambdas compute `priority=int(a.get("priority") or _api().DEFAULT_PRIORITY)`. Because `0` is falsy, `ddflow phase add P1 --priority 0` (or `task add`) does not file priority 0; it silently files `DEFAULT_PRIORITY` (100). The help text ("Lower is offered first (default 100)") states no minimum, so 0 is an expressible priority and the user's value is discarded. The `or` is only needed for the case where the key is absent (`a.get(...)` is `None`), so it should test for `None` rather than truthiness — note `update` already passes priority 0 through unmangled, making the two paths inconsistent.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/declared/queue.py — `phase add` / `task add` priority handling

chunk_findings.detail: `cli_type` is only consulted in the final `elif`, i.e. after the `type == "integer"` and `type == "number"` branches have already claimed `kwargs["type"]`. Any `Param` whose schema type is numeric therefore has its declared CLI type silently discarded and argparse receives `int`/`float` instead. Concretely, `Param(name="timeout", type="number", cli_type=_wait_timeout)` (the wait-timeout parameter this change is relocating, whose helper was imported into the old inline tool definitions) produces `kwargs["type"] = float`, so `--timeout 30s` is now rejected with `argument --timeout: invalid float value: '30s'`, and any clamping/validation done inside `_wait_timeout` (e.g. against `MCP_WAIT_MAX_S`) is bypassed. The field's own contract — "argparse's `type` when the tool's JSON type differs" — is two-directional; the `--exit-code` example in the comment only works because its schema type is `"string"`, so it falls into the `elif` by luck. The `--help` and `tools/list` goldens cannot catch this because neither exercises the parser's `type` callable. The check needs to come before the numeric branches (`if self.cli_type is not None: … elif integer … elif number …`), or the numeric branches must not preempt an explicitly supplied `cli_type`.

chunk_findings.detail: `approve` is the only command in `COMMANDS` that declares `params` but no `call`. The module docstring and the `reason=(...)` text justify why it has no **tool** (an agent must not be able to clear a human checkpoint), but they say nothing about the **call**, and the change's own intent is that "parser and MCP TOOLS entry generated" from these declarations. Every other lifecycle command — including `gate skip`, whose `outcome`/`evidence`/`command`/`exit_code`/`model`/`output_file` params are `cli_only=True` and are never forwarded by its `call` — still provides a `call` so the generated parser has something to dispatch to. `approve` does not, so its generated subparser will have no implementation attached: invoking `ddflow approve <id> <gate> --note "looked at it"` (or the `--reject --reason ...` form) has no function to run, and the human-approval gate cannot be cleared or rejected from the CLI at all. This is exactly the kind of defect the stated goldens cannot catch: `--help` is built from `params` alone, and `tools/list` is unaffected because there is no tool; only actual invocation fails. Note also that `reason` is a conditional flag here (only required with `--reject`), so unlike `abandon`/`block` it cannot rely on `required=True` to enforce it — the enforcement has to live in the missing implementation.

chunk_findings.detail: The declaration says `Param("into", ..., tool_required=True, action="append", default=[])`, and the code comment itself states "the CLI takes repeated `--into`". When the generated CLI parser fills the args dict for `ddflow split P1 --into a=Alpha --into b=Beta`, `a["into"]` is the list `["a=Alpha", "b=Beta"]`, so `str(...)` produces the literal `"['a=Alpha', 'b=Beta']"`, `.split(",")` yields `["['a=Alpha'", " 'b=Beta']"]`, and after `strip()` the api receives child specs whose ids are `"['a"` / `"'b"` — i.e. the split either creates children with garbage ids or fails parsing `sub-id=title`. The same `str()` conversion also breaks the empty case: because the param declares `default=[]`, an invocation without `--into` puts `[]` in the dict, `str([])` is `"[]"`, and the comprehension yields `["[]"]` (a truthy one-element list) instead of `[]`, so instead of the api's clean "at least two" validation the api is handed a bogus single spec `"[]"`. Contrast the `update` command's `globs` handling in the same file, which explicitly branches on `isinstance(a["globs"], list)` precisely because CLI values arrive as lists; `split`'s `into` has no such branch.

chunk_findings.detail: `DEFAULT_PRIORITY` is 100 per the help text, so the `or` fallback turns a legitimate explicit priority of `0` into `100`. Input: `ddflow phase add P2 --priority 0` (or `ddflow task add ... --priority 0`, or an MCP call with `"priority": 0`) — the arg dict contains `0`, which is falsy, so the api is called with `priority=100` and the item is offered last instead of first. The program itself treats 0 as valid (it is "lower", and the sibling `update` command passes `priority=a.get("priority")` with no fallback), so this silently rewrites a caller's value. Since `Param("priority", ..., default=DEFAULT_PRIORITY)` already supplies 100 when the argument is omitted, the `or _api().DEFAULT_PRIORITY` is unnecessary and is the only thing that corrupts 0.

chunk_findings.detail: The new `cli_type` branch is placed at the end of the mutually-exclusive `if/elif` chain that maps the declared JSON type to argparse's `type`, after the `string → str`, `integer → int` and `number → float` branches. It is therefore unreachable for exactly the case its own comment documents: `--exit-code`, described as "an int on the command line and a string in the tool's schema". Because the declared type is `string`, the earlier `self.type == "string"` arm fires first and sets `kwargs["type"] = str`, so `cli_type=int` is silently ignored. Concretely, parsing `--exit-code 3` yields the string `"3"` rather than the int `3`, defeating the only reason `cli_type` was added. Note that a `--help` golden would not catch this (argparse/`--help` shows the metavar, not the `type` callable), so the regression can pass the byte-identical help/tools-list checks while changing parse behavior.

chunk_findings.detail: Both handlers apply Python truthiness (`or 50`) to a value whose declared range, per the help string, is "Priority 0-100 (default 50)". `0` is therefore treated as "unset" and silently rewritten to `50`. Demonstrated input (MCP): call `ddflow_rule_add` with `{"id": "r-x", "title": "t", "priority": 0}`. `a.get("priority", 50)` yields `0`, `0 or 50` yields `50`, so the persisted rule gets priority 50 instead of the requested 0. The same happens on `ddflow_rule_edit` with `{"id": "r-x", "priority": 0}`: the guard `if a.get("priority") is not None` correctly decides that priority *was* supplied, but the value expression `int(a.get("priority") or 50)` then throws it away and passes 50. Any client that legitimately uses 0 (the bottom of the documented 0-100 range) cannot set or reset a rule's priority; it is transmuted to the default.

chunk_findings.detail: The `rule add` handler computes `priority=int(a.get("priority", 50) or 50)`. When the user supplies a priority of `0`, `a.get("priority", 50)` yields `0`, and `0 or 50` evaluates to `50`, so `ddflow rule add --priority 0 ...` silently creates the rule with priority 50 instead of 0. The declared semantics for this parameter are "Priority 0-100 (default 50)", i.e. 0 is an explicitly valid value, not a sentinel for "unset", so the `or 50` fallback is wrong for the boundary value.

chunk_findings.detail: The `rule edit` handler guards the field with `if a.get("priority") is not None` (correct: it distinguishes "not supplied" from 0), but then converts with `int(a.get("priority") or 50)`, which maps the supplied value `0` to `50`. So `ddflow rule edit <id> --priority 0` does not clear the priority to 0; it writes 50. The guard admits 0 as "present" while the conversion discards it — the same `or 50` bug as in `rule add`, but here it contradicts the explicit `is not None` intent.

chunk_findings.detail: `_rule_answer` decides whether a relation was supplied with a truthiness test, `a.get(r)` (and `bool(a.get("new"))` for the `new` flag), so a relation that is present but carries a falsy value is treated as "not supplied". This contradicts the function's own contract and the CLI parity it claims to restore. The CLI's dedup flags are in an argparse mutually-exclusive group, which refuses on *presence* of the flags regardless of the value: `ddflow rule add --duplicate "" --supersedes R7` errors out. Over MCP the same payload `{"duplicate": "", "supersedes": "R7"}` produces `given == ["supersedes"]`, so the `len(given) > 1` guard does not fire, no `ValueError` is raised, and `RuleDedupAnswer("supersedes", "R7")` is returned — i.e. it *silently keeps one and drops the other*, which is exactly the failure the docstring says this helper was written to prevent ("silently keeping one dropped the other"). The same happens for a single supplied-but-falsy target (e.g. `{"duplicate": ""}` or a numeric rule id `{"duplicate": 0}`), where the call is converted to `None` ("no dedup answer") rather than an answer with the given target. Detection should be on key presence (`r in a` / `a.get(r) is not None`) for the non-`new` relations, mirroring the `is not None` guard the author already adopted for the priority-0 fix.

chunk_findings.detail: The `rule search` handler wraps the limit in Python truthiness (`or 10`), so an explicitly requested limit of `0` is silently replaced by the default of 10. The declared contract is "Maximum results to return (default 10)"; a maximum of 0 is a valid integer request, but the falsy `0` is treated as "unset". Demonstrated input (MCP): call `ddflow_rule_search` with `{"query": "naming", "limit": 0}`. `a.get("limit", 10)` yields `0`, `0 or 10` yields `10`, so `rule_search` is invoked with `limit=10` and up to ten rows are returned instead of zero. This is the same truthiness-on-a-numeric-parameter pattern that the earlier review flagged for `priority` (where `0` is in the declared 0-100 range) and that was fixed for `priority` in this diff; it was not fixed here. The correct form is the one used for priority: substitute the default only when the key is absent/`None`, e.g. `10 if a.get("limit") is None else int(a["limit"])`.

chunk_findings.detail: `results` is rebound from "every source the search returned" to "only the tables that survived `CP.pack`", and it is rebound *before* the `if not results:` guard is evaluated. Consequently the guard no longer means "the search found nothing"; it means "the pack kept nothing". Given a query that does match records but whose candidates are all removed by textsim/textcut (e.g. a `max_chars` small enough that the `Budget` cuts every candidate), `cut.kept` yields no table keys, the comprehension produces `{}`, `not results` is true, and the function returns the stale "…Searched: …" outcome whose `reason` is the fixed no-match text rather than `cut.note()`. So the MCP second block reports "no matches" instead of the truncation/duplicate note the change explicitly says it is introducing, and `data["results"]`/`_render["results"]` are left empty even though candidates existed (the very information `pack.truncated`/`pack.duplicates` was added to convey). Even in the non-empty case, any source whose candidates are all deduped disappears from `data["results"]` and `_render["results"]` while still being listed in `searched`, so consumers keyed on `searched` see a missing key. The guard/early return needed to be based on the original search results (or removed in favour of the pack `shown == 0` path with `cut.note()`).

chunk_findings.detail: `bound_recall` no longer reads `args["max_chars"]` and no longer measures anything against the returned JSON, so the MCP `ddflow_recall` payload is now unbounded by this boundary. The docstring claims "the budget ... is enforced once, in the API's context pack, so what arrives here is already within it," but the context pack cuts the rendered *text* (textcut under a text Budget, as the CLI in `knowledge.py` now relies on), whereas the budget this function documented and previously enforced was the serialized JSON actually handed to the model. Concrete input: `body = {"lessons": [{"id": f"L{i}", "headline": "h", "body": "b"*20} for i in range(300)]}` with `args = {"max_chars": 100}`. The pack's 100-char text budget is easily satisfied by 300 short hits, but the JSON returned here is ~300 * (keys + quotes + punctuation) ≈ 10 KB — ~100x `max_chars` — and nothing trims it because the only surviving code is the field-stripping comprehension. Previously this call returned a small set plus a note. Two secondary consequences fall out of the same removal: the `max_chars` argument (and `RECALL_BUDGET` default) is silently ignored for any caller that does not route through the context pack, and the returned note is now the constant "each hit's raw record is left out ...", so when the pack *did* drop hits the caller is told nothing about the truncation (the docstring's "the outcome's reason says what that left out" is not implemented here — the returned dict drops every non-list field, including any reason/pack field it might carry).

chunk_findings.detail: The change removes the payload bound entirely and keeps only raw-record stripping. The new test pins this in place: with `{"max_chars": 1}` and three hits whose bodies are 300 chars each, it now asserts `[len(v) for v in out.values()] == [2, 1]` (all hits kept), whereas the old contract returned `[1, 0]` so that "the first hit survives any budget". The consequence is that `max_chars` is accepted and silently ignored for any hit that does not carry a `raw` key: `bound_recall({"a": [{"id": 1, "kind": "K", "headline": "h", "body": "b" * 100_000}]}, {"max_chars": 10})` returns the 100 kB body unchanged with no truncation note. Recall is migrated to `ContextPack`, so its own path is covered, but this function is the generic MCP payload bound and is not recall-specific; every other caller that still relies on it, and every recall hit that reaches this layer without a `raw` field (the common case once `raw` has already been stripped upstream), now produces a response that can vastly exceed the requested `max_chars`. Because the pack measures `text + body + 1` while the MCP payload also carries `id`/`kind`/`headline` JSON overhead, the two budgets are not even in the same units, so the pack budget does not restore the guarantee this function used to provide.

chunk_findings.detail:
The empty-results guard now tests the pack output instead of the search output. `results` is overwritten with `{t: [c.row for c in cs] for t, cs in cut.kept.items()}`, i.e. a dict keyed by whatever `CP.pack` put in `kept`, whereas before it held the raw search rows. Either key policy breaks the guard:

- If `CP.pack` preserves an entry for every table it was given (the usual shape, since the input `{table: [...] for table, rows in results.items()}` includes every searched table, empty or not), then `results` is always a non-empty dict, so `if not results:` can never be true. A query that genuinely matches nothing now falls through to `return O.Outcome(kind="recall", ...)` and reports success with zero records, instead of the no-results warning.
- If `CP.pack` instead drops tables whose candidates were all removed, then the guard fires whenever the budget (or the textsim dedupe) eliminates every hit, which is a different condition from "search found nothing." With e.g. `max_chars` smaller than the shortest hit, a query that did match returns the `O.warn(f"Searched: ...", **data)` path whose message/reason says nothing about truncation, and the `cut.note()` that the rest of the change is built to surface is never passed as the outcome reason.

In both cases the condition being tested was changed from "the search returned no rows" to "the pack kept no candidates," so the no-match warning and the budget-truncation reporting are conflated; whichever way `Pack.kept` handles empty tables, one of the two behaviors is wrong.

chunk_findings.detail: Given a recall whose pack removed duplicates but did not truncate (e.g. the search core returned two hits with near-identical text, both fitting the budget), this branch prints `pack['note']`. The JSON path in the same function treats `pack["note"]` as strictly the truncation explanation and only touches it under `pack["truncated"]`, implying it is populated/meaningful for a cut and not for a dedupe. So this branch either raises `KeyError` if the API only sets `note` when truncated (the JSON guard exists precisely because it can be absent), or, if `note` is present, prints a truncation-flavoured message ("… N over budget …") for a result that was never truncated — a reader is told the answer was cut when only duplicates were dropped. The test input is a duplicate-yielding query with a budget large enough that truncation is False: the command should report the dedupe reason, but instead crashes or lies about truncation.

chunk_findings.detail: The docstring justifies removing the truncation logic by saying "the outcome's reason says what that left out", but this function's second return value — the outcome's reason/note — is now the hard-coded string `"each hit's raw record is left out (its id is in the hit)"`, and the body projection keeps only list-valued keys (`for k, hits in body.items() if isinstance(hits, list)`). So a truncation reason the context pack hands back is not carried through: if the API returns the per-kind hit lists plus a non-list `reason` field, that field is filtered out by the comprehension, and the constant note replaces the old `"truncated: showing X of Y hits within max_chars=…; … Raise max_chars for more."` message. A caller of `ddflow_recall` whose hits were cut by the budget therefore gets the full-looking set of remaining hits with no indication anything was dropped, contrary to what the docstring promises this layer delivers.

chunk_findings.detail: The `ci` command declares its CLI verb as a `cli_only` parameter named `verb` (`choices=("run","status","record")`) and its MCP verb as a `mcp_only` parameter named `action`, but the shared `call` reads only `a["action"]` and never `a["verb"]`. `cli_only` means `verb` is present only in the CLI arg mapping and `action` only in the MCP mapping, so on the command line `a.get("action")` is always `None` and the fallback `or "status"` wins. Evidence that `a` is keyed by the declared parameter names (not some canonical name) is in the same file: `bisect`'s `call=lambda repo, a, agent: _bisect(repo, a)` must read the `cli_only` `glob`/`repeat`/`max_runs` from that same dict, and `export`'s `export_tool(repo, a, agent)` must read `target`/`local`/`lock` from it. Consequences: `ddflow ci run --ref <sha> --base main` silently reports status instead of running the merge-result check, and worse, `ddflow ci record --stage pre-push --result failed --report out.txt --sha <sha>` also folds to `action="status"`, so the pre-push hook's record invocation is discarded rather than recorded. The command works only over MCP; its generated command-line half is a no-op for every verb. Contradicts the stated intent ("Declare ... ci once and generate their command-line halves") and the pattern of the other four commands, whose `call`s read shared/`cli_only` names from `a`.

The intent lists five areas to be declared once (export, bisect, tests, precommit, ci), so the `bisect` and `ci` declarations must be pulled in separately; this hunk supplies no import for them. chunk_findings.detail:
The `ci` command declares its command-line verb as the positional parameter `verb` (`positional=True`, `cli_only=True`, `choices=("run", "status", "record")`) and its MCP-side equivalent as the separate parameter `action` (`mcp_only=True`). But the call lambda bridges to the API using only `action`:

```
call=lambda repo, a, agent: _api().ci_tool(
    repo,
    action=a.get("action", "status") or "status",
    ...
)
```

On a CLI invocation the argparse namespace contains `verb` (e.g. `{"verb": "run", ...}`), never `action`, because `action` is `mcp_only`. So `a.get("action", "status")` always falls back to `"status"`. Concretely, running `ddflow ci run` (or `ddflow ci run --ref X --base main`) executes the *status* code path — it prints what would run and exits 0 — instead of running the pre-push checks on the merge result. Likewise `ddflow ci record --stage pre-push --result passed --sha ...`, which the `flag_exempt` entries say is invoked by the pre-push hook script ("which has a shell and no MCP session"), never records anything: the verb is discarded and `ci_tool` runs the default `status`, so the pre-push hook silently no-ops. The lambda needs to consult the CLI verb (e.g. `action=a.get("action") or a.get("verb") or "status"`); as written the CLI half of `ci` cannot select `run` or `record` at all. No other code in the change maps `verb` onto `action`.

chunk_findings.detail: This diff removes three `Command(...)` exemption entries — `ddflow_ci`, `ddflow_export`, and `ddflow_bisect` — but only one replacement source is wired back in: `*_EXPORT` is added to the aggregate tuple. chunk_findings.detail:
The `tests` Param is declared with `default=""` and the handler converts that straight into a tuple:

```python
tests=tuple(t.strip() for t in (a.get("tests") or "").split(",") if t.strip()),
```

When the user omits `--tests`, the parser hands back the declared default `""`, the split yields `[""]`, the `if t.strip()` filter removes it, and the api is called with `tests=()` — never the documented `("tests", "test")` and never `None`. The declared `help`/`cli_help` both promise "(default: tests,test)", but that value is not expressible through this declaration. Contrast the sibling parameters, which deliberately carry the api's default through: `min_needle` passes `None` so the api can apply its 12, and `top` passes `10`. For `tests` the empty tuple short-circuits that mechanism: if the api's fallback is keyed on `None` (the pattern the rest of the lambda assumes), running `ddflow_pins AGENTS.md` in a repo that does have `tests/` and `test/` scans no directories at all, so the command reports the whole document as unpinned — or exits 2 with "no Python suite to read pins from", which its own description says means "treat ALL of it as pinned". Either way the user gets the opposite of the documented default. Setting `default="tests,test"` (or collapsing an empty result to `None` so the api default applies) fixes it.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/declared/cadence.py — `pins` / `tests` Param and its `call` lambda

chunk_findings.detail:
The declaration contradicts itself and the documented behavior. Both `help` ("Comma-separated test dirs (default: tests,test).") and `cli_help` ("comma-separated test dirs (default: tests,test)") state that the default test dirs are `tests,test`, but the declared `default` is `""`. The call lambda then does `tests=tuple(t.strip() for t in (a.get("tests") or "").split(",") if t.strip())`, which turns an absent/empty value into an empty tuple and hands `tests=()` to `_api().pins(...)`. So the concrete input `ddflow pins AGENTS.md` (no `--tests`) parses to `tests == ""` and calls `pins(..., tests=(), ...)` instead of the pinned `("tests", "test")`.

Note the asymmetry with the neighbouring `min_needle` param: there the code deliberately passes `None` through (`min_chars=None if a.get("min_needle") is None else int(...)`) so the API-level default (12) can still apply. An empty *tuple* is not `None`, so it overrides any `tests` default rather than falling back to it. This breaks the stated goal (the generated help and the parsed namespace must reproduce the pinned hand-written parser): the CLI help promises `tests,test` while the namespace yields empty, and if `pins` has a real default of `("tests", "test")` the command silently scans no test directories — exactly the failure mode this command exists to prevent (a user concluding text is unpinned when it is not).

chunk_findings.detail: `_def_docs` builds the search text as `_join(rec.id, *(v for v in rec.fields.values() if isinstance(v, str | int | float)))`, so every list-valued frontmatter field is silently dropped from the text. For a rule the `tags` (and `scope`) field is exactly such a list — the rule format is "TOML with frontmatter block (id, title, tags, scope, priority)" [D-rules-format]. `_rule_docs` then does `have = {d.id for d in out}` and `if r.id in have: continue`, so once a rule is recorded as a definition (the normal case), the file copy that *would* have contributed `" ".join(r.tags)` is skipped. Net effect: searching `--source rules` for a tag (e.g. a rule with `tags = ["security"]` that is recorded in `State.defs`) returns no hit for a recorded rule, while the identical unrecorded rule on disk does hit. The recorded-rule path loses tags/scope that the file path explicitly includes.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/search.py `_def_docs` / `_rule_docs`

chunk_findings.detail: `_rule_docs` deliberately deduplicates the two sources of truth ("a file not (yet) recorded as a definition": `have = {d.id for d in out}` … `if r.id in have: continue`). `_skill_docs` and `_agent_docs` read the *same* kind of overlap (`_def_docs(c.st, "skill", …)` plus `SK.inventory`, and `_def_docs(c.st, "agent", …)` plus `.claude/agents/*.md`) but never deduplicate. Given a skill that is both recorded in `State.defs` and present in the repo inventory (or an agent recorded as a definition and also on disk as `.claude/agents/<id>.md`), both builders emit a row with the same `(kind, id)` — two identical hits for one entity, whereas the rules source emits one. Either the rules dedup is redundant or the skill/agent sources are returning duplicates for every recorded entity.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/search.py `_skill_docs` / `_agent_docs`

chunk_findings.detail:
The added keyword does not match the field the new code reads. `Filters` gains the attribute `sources` (`+    sources: str = ""` in search.py) and `_source_names` parses `f.sources`; `given()` also emits `"source": self.sources`. The handler, however, builds the filter object with `source=a.source` (singular) while the pre-existing `sources=a.kind` line is left in place. So the value of the CLI `--source` argument never lands in `Filters.sources`; instead that field is populated from the `--kind` argument, and the `source` name is not a declared field at all.

Concrete failures:

- `ddflow search foo --source rules`: `a.source == "rules"` is passed as `source="rules"`. If `Filters` is a normal dataclass/model without a `source` field this is `TypeError: __init__() got an unexpected keyword argument 'source'`, i.e. every search invocation raises. If the model silently drops unknown keys, the source filter is simply ignored (`sources` stays `""`), so `--source` has no effect and all sources are searched, contradicting the documented behaviour.
- `ddflow search foo --kind task`: `a.kind == "task"` is passed as `sources="task"`. `_source_names` then does `wanted = {"task"}` and `bad = sorted(wanted - set(source_names()))`, which yields `SearchError("unknown source task: one of ...")` because `task` is a kind, not a registered source name. The kind filter is therefore unusable, and kinds like `rule`/`skill`/`agent` that are only valid as kinds would also be rejected as "unknown source".

The two keywords need to be `kinds=a.kind` and `sources=a.source` for the `--kind` / `--source` split introduced in this change to work at all.

chunk_findings.detail: The `SOURCES` tuple is the module's declared list of accepted source tokens: before this change it read exactly `("task", "phase", "bug", "research", "decision", "lesson", "session", "prompt", "log")` and the module docstring enumerated those same tokens one-for-one. This change replaces that enumeration in the docstring with the group vocabulary pinned by the intent (`records`, `sessions`, `prompts`, `log`, `rules`, `skills`, `agents`, `jobs`, `schedules`) but updates `SOURCES` with per-row/registry names instead: `"rule"`, `"skill"`, `"command"`, `"agent"`, `"job"`, `"schedule"`. Not a single token from the pinned `--source` list (`records`, `sessions`, `prompts`, `rules`, `skills`, `agents`, `schedules`) appears in the tuple. Concretely, if the token is validated against `SOURCES` in the request path, `ddflow search --source rules` and `--source records` are rejected as unknown sources while the undocumented singular `--source rule`, `--source command` and `--source job` are accepted — exactly inverted from the interface the intent and this file's own docstring describe. Note also that `"command"` and `"job"` have no counterpart in the documented group list at all (the docstring folds commands into `skills` and jobs into `schedules`), so either the docstring or `SOURCES` is wrong here regardless of where validation happens.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/search.py:SOURCES

chunk_findings.detail: The rules path immediately above explicitly defends against the same entity being present both as a recorded definition in `State.defs` and as a file on disk (`have = {d.id for d in out}` … `if r.id in have: continue`, with the comment "a file not (yet) recorded as a definition"). `_skill_docs` and `_agent_docs` drop that guard: they append every `SK.inventory(c.repo)` entry / every `.claude/agents/*.md` file without checking the ids already produced by `_def_docs(c.st, "skill", "skill")` / `_def_docs(c.st, "agent", "agent")`. So for a skill (or agent) that is recorded as a definition and also exists as a file — exactly the case the rule comment documents as possible — `ddflow search --source skills <q>` returns two Docs with the same `(kind, id)` and identical text: the same hit is listed twice and is double-weighted in ranking. `_schedule_docs` has the same shape and is arguably worse: `_def_docs(c.st, "schedule", "schedule")` is concatenated with `SCH.definitions(c.repo, c.cfg, c.st)`, which is given the state, so recorded schedule definitions that `SCH.definitions` resolves from `c.st` will also be emitted twice. Fix: extend the `have` id set used in `_rule_docs` to these three builders before appending the file/config-derived rows.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/search.py `_skill_docs` / `_agent_docs` / `_schedule_docs`

chunk_findings.detail: The `Filters(...)` call that backs `ddflow search` does not bind the values to the filter attributes that the service reads. In this same diff, `Filters` gets a new attribute `sources` (`+    sources: str = ""`), `_source_names(f)` parses `f.sources.split(",")`, and `Filters.given()` maps the CLI param `source` to `self.sources`; the kind filter is read as `f.kinds` in `_sources(f)`. But the viewer passes the `--kind` value into `sources=a.kind` and passes the new `--source` value as `source=a.source`, and never passes `kinds` at all. So (a) `kinds` stays `""`, and `--kind` no longer restricts anything; (b) `--kind task` is instead interpreted as a source name and `_source_names` raises `SearchError: unknown source task: one of ...`; and (c) `--source rules` / any invocation hits `Filters(..., source=a.source, ...)`, where `source` is not an attribute of `Filters` (the new filter attribute is `sources`), i.e. `TypeError: __init__() got an unexpected keyword argument 'source'` before any search runs. The wiring should be `kinds=a.kind, sources=a.source`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/commands/viewers_search.py:40 (`sources=a.kind` / `source=a.source`)

chunk_findings.detail: `test_source_selects_only_that_source` discards the exit code of its first search (line 76 uses `_, body, _ = _search(...)`) and then asserts `body == {} or not body.get("rows")`. The `_search` helper returns `{}` for *any* non-JSON stdout, which is precisely what `run_cli` produces on the error path (non-zero exit, message on stderr). So the assertion is satisfied both by "success, no rows" and by "the command failed outright". Concretely, if `--source records` were rejected as an unknown source (exit 3, `unknown source records`) or the search crashed, `body` is `{}`, the assertion passes, and the test still claims to have verified that the `records` source does not surface the `r-gourd` rule when in reality no source was exercised. Demonstrated by changing line 76's argument to `--source nope`: the test still passes. The check needs `assert code == 0` (line 76 currently throws `code` away) plus `assert not body["rows"]`.

chunk_findings.detail: The search text for a definition is built only from scalar frontmatter values (`isinstance(v, str | int | float)`), so every list-valued field is dropped. For a rule, `tags` and `scope` are exactly such lists, and [D-rules-format] makes them part of the rule frontmatter (`id, title, tags, scope, priority`). Concretely, a rule whose body text does not contain a word but whose `tags` do will not be found: `ddflow search zebra --source rules` misses it. The triage itself records that this reproduces ("roborev reproduced the same"), and the diff under review adds the rules source plumbing but does not change `_def_docs`, so the fix is not present.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/search.py `_def_docs`

chunk_findings.detail: `_rule_docs` deliberately de-duplicates the two sources of truth for a rule (`have = {d.id for d in out}` … `if r.id in have: continue`), but `_skill_docs` and `_agent_docs` read the same kind of overlap (`_def_docs(c.st, "skill", …)` plus `SK.inventory`, and `_def_docs(c.st, "agent", …)` plus the agent files) without any such de-duplication. Given an agent that is both recorded as a definition and present as a file of the same id, the same item is emitted twice, inflating/duplicating results vs. the rule source's behavior. The triage confirmed this with the "recorded agent + file of same id" probe, and the diff hunk shown adds the agent/skill sources' constants and the `def` log-suppression but does not add the `have`/`continue` dedup to these functions.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/search.py `_skill_docs` / `_agent_docs`

chunk_findings.detail: `_schedule_docs` unions two producers of schedule definitions without the id de-duplication every sibling branch performs: it starts from `out = _def_docs(c.st, "schedule", "schedule")` (the state-recorded definitions of kind `schedule`) and then, inside the repo branch, appends one row per entry of `SCH.definitions(c.repo, c.cfg, c.st).jobs` for every `d.source != SOURCE_CADENCE`. `SCH.definitions` is given `c.repo`, `c.cfg` *and* `c.st`, i.e. it is the merged resolver of repo-file, config and state definitions; the `SOURCE_CADENCE` skip in the same loop only removes the config defaults, so state-recorded schedules are still emitted by it. Compare `_rule_docs`, which does exactly this two-source union and guards it with `have = {d.id for d in out}` / `if r.id in have: continue`, and `_skill_docs`/`_agent_docs`, which were fixed to dedup against `have` for the same reason. Concretely: record a schedule definition (state def of kind `schedule`, id `nightly`), then run `ddflow search nightly --source schedules`; `_def_docs` returns a row with id `nightly`, and `SCH.definitions(...)` returns the same id again with `d.source` != `SOURCE_CADENCE`, so the schedule is listed twice (both rows share id `nightly` but differ in `updated_at`/`text`, so a later id-based dedup, if any, cannot collapse them cleanly). The fix is the same one applied to `_rule_docs`: compute `have = {d.id for d in out}` before the loop and `continue` when `jid in have`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/search.py:238 (`_schedule_docs`)

chunk_findings.detail: `_docs` builds the result by unconditionally concatenating `out += src.hits(ctx, kinds)` with no de-duplication, and the skill/agent builders union the recorded definitions (`_def_docs(c.st, "skill", …)`) with the repo inventory without de-duplicating (unlike `_rule_docs`, which guards with `have = {d.id for d in out}` / `if r.id in have: continue`). The diff registers `skills` and `agents` as sources but changes neither builder. Input: a skill that is both recorded in `State.defs` and present in `.claude/skills/*` with the same id (or an agent recorded as a definition and present under `.claude/agents/*.md`), then `ddflow search <term> --source skills` / `--source agents` returns the same hit twice, so hit counts and ranked output are wrong. The fix is not in the reviewed diff, and the new dispatcher does not dedup across or within sources.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/search.py `_docs` / `_skill_docs` / `_agent_docs`

chunk_findings.detail: The search text for a definition is built only from scalar frontmatter values (`isinstance(v, str | int | float)`), so every list-valued field is dropped. For a rule, `tags` and `scope` are exactly such lists, and [D-rules-format] makes them part of the rule frontmatter (`id, title, tags, scope, priority`). Concretely, a rule whose body text does not contain a word but whose `tags` do will not be found: `ddflow search zebra --source rules` misses it. The triage itself records that this reproduces ("roborev reproduced the same"), and the diff under review adds the rules source plumbing but does not change `_def_docs`, so the fix is not present.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/search.py `_def_docs`

chunk_findings.detail: `_rule_docs` deliberately de-duplicates the two sources of truth for a rule (`have = {d.id for d in out}` … `if r.id in have: continue`), but `_skill_docs` and `_agent_docs` read the same kind of overlap (`_def_docs(c.st, "skill", …)` plus `SK.inventory`, and `_def_docs(c.st, "agent", …)` plus the agent files) without any such de-duplication. Given an agent that is both recorded as a definition and present as a file of the same id, the same item is emitted twice, inflating/duplicating results vs. the rule source's behavior. The triage confirmed this with the "recorded agent + file of same id" probe, and the diff hunk shown adds the agent/skill sources' constants and the `def` log-suppression but does not add the `have`/`continue` dedup to these functions.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/search.py `_skill_docs` / `_agent_docs`

chunk_findings.detail: `_schedule_docs` unions two producers of schedule definitions without the id de-duplication every sibling branch performs: it starts from `out = _def_docs(c.st, "schedule", "schedule")` (the state-recorded definitions of kind `schedule`) and then, inside the repo branch, appends one row per entry of `SCH.definitions(c.repo, c.cfg, c.st).jobs` for every `d.source != SOURCE_CADENCE`. `SCH.definitions` is given `c.repo`, `c.cfg` *and* `c.st`, i.e. it is the merged resolver of repo-file, config and state definitions; the `SOURCE_CADENCE` skip in the same loop only removes the config defaults, so state-recorded schedules are still emitted by it. Compare `_rule_docs`, which does exactly this two-source union and guards it with `have = {d.id for d in out}` / `if r.id in have: continue`, and `_skill_docs`/`_agent_docs`, which were fixed to dedup against `have` for the same reason. Concretely: record a schedule definition (state def of kind `schedule`, id `nightly`), then run `ddflow search nightly --source schedules`; `_def_docs` returns a row with id `nightly`, and `SCH.definitions(...)` returns the same id again with `d.source` != `SOURCE_CADENCE`, so the schedule is listed twice (both rows share id `nightly` but differ in `updated_at`/`text`, so a later id-based dedup, if any, cannot collapse them cleanly). The fix is the same one applied to `_rule_docs`: compute `have = {d.id for d in out}` before the loop and `continue` when `jid in have`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/search.py:238 (`_schedule_docs`)

chunk_findings.detail: `_docs` builds the result by unconditionally concatenating `out += src.hits(ctx, kinds)` with no de-duplication, and the skill/agent builders union the recorded definitions (`_def_docs(c.st, "skill", …)`) with the repo inventory without de-duplicating (unlike `_rule_docs`, which guards with `have = {d.id for d in out}` / `if r.id in have: continue`). The diff registers `skills` and `agents` as sources but changes neither builder. Input: a skill that is both recorded in `State.defs` and present in `.claude/skills/*` with the same id (or an agent recorded as a definition and present under `.claude/agents/*.md`), then `ddflow search <term> --source skills` / `--source agents` returns the same hit twice, so hit counts and ranked output are wrong. The fix is not in the reviewed diff, and the new dispatcher does not dedup across or within sources.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/search.py `_docs` / `_skill_docs` / `_agent_docs`

chunk_findings.detail: `_def_docs` still builds the searched text from scalar fields only (`_join(rec.id, *(v for v in rec.fields.values() if isinstance(v, str | int | float)))`), so every list-valued frontmatter field is silently excluded. For rules the format is TOML frontmatter with `tags` and `scope` as lists [D-rules-format], and `_rule_docs` records the definition and then does `if r.id in have: continue`, so the file copy of the rule is skipped once the definition is seen. Input: a rule whose `tags = ["zebra"]` and a query for `zebra`; `ddflow search zebra --source rules` returns no hit even though the rule exists, and the same happens for any term that appears only inside a list-valued field. The reviewed diff wires `rules` as a `--source` value but contains no change to `_def_docs`, so the reachable defect remains.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/search.py `_def_docs` (rule search text)

chunk_findings.detail: `_def_docs` builds the text passed to the ranker as `_join(rec.id, *(v for v in rec.fields.values() if isinstance(v, str | int | float)))`, so every list-valued frontmatter field is filtered out. For a rule the `tags` and `scope` fields are exactly such lists, and [D-rules-format] defines the rule frontmatter as "(id, title, tags, scope, priority)". `_rule_docs` then does `have = {d.id for d in out}` and `if r.id in have: continue`, so once a rule is recorded as a definition its file text is never indexed. The recorded probe `ddflow search zebra --source rules` returns no hit for a rule whose `tags` contains `zebra`, which is wrong. Nothing in this diff changes `_def_docs` or `_rule_docs`, so the defect is unaddressed [D-rules-format].
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/search.py `_def_docs` / `_rule_docs`

chunk_findings.detail: `_rule_docs` deliberately deduplicates its two sources of truth (`have = {d.id for d in out}` … `if r.id in have: continue`), but `_skill_docs` and `_agent_docs` read the same kind of overlap — `_def_docs(c.st, "skill", …)` plus `SK.inventory`, and `_def_docs(c.st, "agent", …)` plus `.claude/agents/*.md` — and never deduplicate. Given a skill/agent that is both recorded in `State.defs` and present in the repo inventory (the confirmed probe: recorded agent + file of the same id), a single query emits two identical hits, corrupting the result list and the BM25 ordering. The diff contains no change to these functions, so this still holds.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/search.py `_skill_docs` / `_agent_docs`

chunk_findings.detail: The `Filters(...)` call behind `ddflow search` still does not populate the attribute the service reads for source selection. With the new `Filters` attribute `sources` (`+ sources: str = ""`) and `_source_names(f)` parsing `f.sources.split(",")`, the viewer instead passes the `--kind` value into `sources=a.kind` and the new `--source` value into `source=a.source`. Given `ddflow search "x" --source rules`, the source token never reaches `_source_names`, so every source is searched (or the kind value is misread as a source name), while `ddflow search "x" --kind rule` silently restricts sources instead. The README added in this diff (`--source` picks the sources; `--kind` narrows by kind) documents the opposite of what the code does, so the defect is now externally asserted as fixed. Nothing in the visible diff rewires the call.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/commands/viewers_search.py:40 (`sources=a.kind` / `source=a.source`)

chunk_findings.detail: The module's accepted-token tuple and its enumeration still disagree. The docstring was rewritten to the group vocabulary (`records`, `sessions`, `prompts`, `log`, `rules`, `skills`, `agents`, `jobs`, `schedules`), yet `SOURCES` was updated with per-row/registry names rather than the group tokens the CLI/MCP now accept. `_source_names(f)` validates user input against `SOURCES`, so `--source records` / `--source rules` would be refused with a choices list that does not match the README's documented choices, and the `--source` values the README promises cannot all be selected.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/search.py `SOURCES`

chunk_findings.detail: The same as the earlier finding: the rules path immediately above dedupes recorded definitions against on-disk files (`have = {d.id for d in out}` … `if r.id in have: continue`), but `_skill_docs` and `_agent_docs` append every `SK.inventory(c.repo)` entry / `.claude/agents/*.md` file without consulting the ids already produced by `_def_docs(c.st, "skill", "skill")` / `_def_docs(c.st, "agent", "agent")`. A skill or agent that is both recorded in `State.defs` and present on disk therefore appears twice in the results and consumes `--limit` slots. This is unchanged in the visible diff.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/search.py `_skill_docs` / `_agent_docs` / `_schedule_docs`

chunk_findings.detail: `test_source_selects_only_that_source` still discards the exit status of its first search (`_, body, _ = _search(...)`) and then asserts only `body == {} or not body.get("rows")`. Since `_search` returns `{}` for any non-JSON stdout — exactly what `run_cli` produces when the command fails with a message on stderr — the assertion passes equally for "no rows" and "the command errored". If `--source records` were rejected as an unknown source (a plausible consequence of the `SOURCES` mismatch above), this test would still go green, so it cannot detect the regression it is meant to guard.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_search_sources.py:77

chunk_findings.detail: The `Filters(...)` construction that backs `ddflow search` still binds the CLI values to the wrong attributes. `Filters` now carries the source-group filter in the field read by `_source_names(f)` (`f.sources.split(",")`), while the kind filter is read from `f.kinds`. The CLI passes the `--kind` value as `sources=a.kind` and the new `--source` value as `source=a.source`, so `ddflow search --kind task <q>` feeds "task" into the source-group filter (no group named "task" → no rows) and `--source records` never lands in the attribute the service parses. The reviewed hunk only repairs the parallel API path: `api/viewers.py` builds `S.Filters(sources, state, phase, owner, since, source)` positionally, so the viewer's first value goes into the kind field and the new value into the appended source-group field. It does not touch `viewers_search.py`, so the defect still holds on the CLI.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/commands/viewers_search.py:40 (`sources=a.kind` / `source=a.source`)

chunk_findings.detail: The rules builder immediately above dedups recorded definitions against on-disk files (`have = {d.id for d in out}` … `if r.id in have: continue`), but the skill/agent/schedule builders append every `SK.inventory(c.repo)` entry and every `.claude/agents/*.md` file without consulting the ids already emitted by `_def_docs(...)`. An entity that exists both as a recorded definition and as a file on disk therefore produces two rows. This hunk (`api/viewers.py`) does not change those builders, so the duplication stands.
