chunk_findings.detail: Still holds; nothing in the change rebinds these. The `Filters(...)` built for `ddflow search` passes the `--kind` value into `sources=` and the new `--source` value into `source=`, while the service reads `f.kinds` in `_sources(f)` and `f.sources` in `_source_names(f)` (the new `Filters.sources` attribute is what `--source` must populate, per the same diff). Concretely, `ddflow search --source rules foo` sets `source="rules"`, `Filters.given()` maps `source` to `self.sources`, but the viewer feeds `sources=a.kind` and `source=a.source`, so `self.sources` ends up as the `--kind` value (empty by default) and the requested source is dropped — the search silently runs across the default set instead of the requested source.

chunk_findings.detail: Still holds. The docstring was rewritten to the group vocabulary pinned by the intent (`records`, `sessions`, `prompts`, `rules`, `skills`, `agents`, `jobs`, `schedules`) but `SOURCES` still enumerates only per-row singular tokens (`task…lesson`, `session`, `prompt`, `log`, `rule`, `skill`, `command`, `agent`, `job`, `schedule`). None of `records`, `sessions`, `prompts`, `rules`, `skills`, `agents`, `jobs`, `schedules` is present. Given input `ddflow search --source rules foo` (exactly the invocation the docstring and intent document), validation against `SOURCES` (or the MCP enum derived from it) rejects `rules` as unknown, so the documented/required `--source` values cannot be used. The rules path above them defends against the same entity appearing both as a recorded definition (`State.defs`) and as a file on disk (`have = {d.id for d in out}` … `if r.id in have: continue`), while the skill/agent/schedule paths append every `SK.inventory(c.repo)` entry / every `.claude/agents/*.md` / schedule file without checking the ids already produced by `_def_docs(c.st, "skill", "skill")` etc. Given a skill that is both recorded as a definition and present on disk, `--source skill` returns two hits for the same id; the hint in this hunk (the new `def`-event skip in the log source is gated on the definition kind being requested) does not address it.

chunk_findings.detail: Still holds. `test_source_selects_only_that_source` discards the exit code of its first search (`_, body, _ = _search(...)`) and then asserts `body == {} or not body.get("rows")`. `_search` returns `{}` for any non-JSON stdout, which is what `run_cli` produces on the error path (non-zero exit, message on stderr), so the assertion passes both for "success, no rows" and for "the command failed outright" — e.g. if `--source records` were rejected as an unknown source, the test still passes.

chunk_findings.detail: `_schedule_docs` still drops the record-vs-file dedup guard that the rule path immediately above it uses (`have = {d.id for d in out}` … `if r.id in have: continue`) and that this same diff adds to `_skill_docs` and `_agent_docs`. It starts with `out = _def_docs(c.st, "schedule", "schedule")` (the schedules recorded as definitions in `State.defs`) and then, when `c.repo is not None`, unconditionally appends `Doc("schedule", jid, …)` for every entry of `SCH.definitions(c.repo, c.cfg, c.st).jobs` that is not `SOURCE_CADENCE`. Because `SCH.definitions` is passed `c.st` (it folds the same state), a schedule that exists in both places — e.g. a schedule defined via the repo/state path and thus also present as a recorded definition — is emitted twice with the same id, so `ddflow search --source schedules` (and the MCP equivalent) returns duplicate rows for one schedule and skews ranking counts. The fix applied to `_skill_docs`/`_agent_docs` is exactly the pattern needed here (`have = {d.id for d in out}`, skip `jid in have`).
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/search.py:_schedule_docs

chunk_findings.detail: The diff only fixes half of the earlier "wrong attribute" problem. The service reads the *kind* filter from `Filters.kinds` (`_sources(f)` in `ddflow/services/search.py` does `f.kinds.split(",")`), and the only mapping this diff adds is for the new `--source` value (`source=a.source`, with `Filters.source` and `_source_names(f)` reading `f.source`). The `--kind` value is still bound to `sources=a.kind`, which is not the attribute `_sources` reads. So `ddflow search --kind bug foo` will either raise `TypeError` at filter construction (if `Filters` has no `sources` field at all — which is the case if the `+ source: str = ""` in this diff replaced the earlier `sources` field) or silently run the search over every kind because `f.kinds` is empty. In both cases the `--kind` narrowing is not applied; the new `source=a.source` line does not address this half of the finding, so it still holds.

An entity that exists both as a recorded definition in `State.defs` and as a file on disk (e.g. a skill in `.claude/skills` also recorded as a `skill` def) is emitted twice by these sources, so a single hit shows up as two rows and inflates scoring; the diff neither dedupes in `_docs` nor in these functions, so the earlier finding is not answered.

This slice corroborates the split rather than removing it: the rewritten `tests/test_search_core.py` asserts `names == S.source_names()` (group names) and separately `sorted(covered) == sorted(S.SOURCES)` (one kind per owner), so the two vocabularies demonstrably coexist and the docstring/constant mismatch the earlier review reported is untouched. Anything that derives the accepted `--source` tokens from `SOURCES` (rather than `source_names()`) will advertise/reject exactly the wrong set.

chunk_findings.detail: The old dispatcher compared the incoming method with `==` against literal strings, so any JSON value was tolerated and fell through to the terminal `return _err(mid, -32601, f"method not found: {method}")`. The new first statement, `handler = self._METHODS.get(method)`, hashes the key, so a message whose `method` is a non-hashable JSON value now raises instead of producing a JSON-RPC error. Concretely, given `{"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 7, "method": []}` (or `{"method": {...}}`), `_dispatch` raises `TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'` out of `_dispatch` rather than returning `{"id": 7, "error": {"code": -32601, ...}}` as it did before; the same holds for any non-string, non-hashable value a malformed/older client might send. If the serve loop does not wrap `_dispatch` in a per-message `except Exception`, one malformed frame now tears down the connection (or converts a spec-compliant `-32601` into an internal error) where the previous code answered and kept going. Guarding with `isinstance(method, str)` (or `str`-coercing before the lookup) restores the old behavior.

chunk_findings.detail: The guard only inspects module-level `Assign`/`AnnAssign` nodes and only accepts `ast.Name` targets. Anything else that reintroduces a retired table in a test file passes silently. Two concrete evasions: (1) a table defined inside a function or class body — `def test_x(): PROSE_TOOLS = {"ddflow_read": "returns prose"}` — is never walked, because the loop iterates only `ast.parse(...).body` (top-level statements) instead of using `ast.walk`; (2) a destructuring assignment such as `NOT_EXPOSED, LEAF_VIA = {}, {}` yields an `ast.Tuple` target, which `isinstance(t, ast.Name)` filters out. Both are exactly the "second place to forget" the test's own docstring says it exists to prevent, so the test can pass green while a retired exemption table has been re-added. Using `ast.walk(...)` and recursing into tuple/list targets (or flattening targets with `ast.iter_child_nodes`) would close it.

chunk_findings.detail: This still holds and the triage's probe does not answer it. The finding is about a *non-hashable* `method`; `.get(method)` hashes the key exactly like `__getitem__` does, so switching from indexing to `.get` only fixes the unknown-*string* case (no `KeyError`), not the crash for non-string JSON. Input `{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":7,"method":[]}`, or `{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":7,"method":{}}`, still reaches `self._METHODS.get([])` and raises `TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'` instead of the JSON-RPC error the old `==`-chain dispatcher returned (`_err(mid, -32601, ...)`). The cited probe, `test_a_method_that_is_not_a_known_string_is_method_not_found`, by its own name feeds a *string* method; a string is hashable and `.get` returns `None` for it, producing the same `-32601` response the pre-change code produced — so that test cannot distinguish the old from the new code and certainly cannot exercise the unhashable case. A guard such as `if not isinstance(method, str): return _err(mid, -32600, ...)` (or wrapping the lookup) is what would answer this, and no part of the shown diff does it. Severity stays LOW (malformed-client conformance), but it is a real behavior regression introduced by this change and remains unprobed.

chunk_findings.detail: The loop collects `n.id` for `ast.Name` nodes under each assignment target, and the inline comment claims "`x.A = ...` count". It does not: for an attribute assignment the target is an `ast.Attribute` whose base is an `ast.Name` and whose attribute is stored as a plain Python string in `Attribute.attr` (not a child AST node), so `ast.walk` over the target yields only the base name. Concrete input: a test file containing `import ddflow.surfaces.mcp as m` followed by `m.PROSE_TOOLS = {"ddflow_list": "still a table"}`. `ast.walk` over `Attribute(value=Name('m'), attr='PROSE_TOOLS')` yields `Name(id='m')` only; `m` is not in `_RETIRED_TABLES`, so `kept` stays empty and the guard passes even though an exemption table has been reintroduced as an attribute assignment — exactly the "second place to forget" the test exists to prevent. The comment should not promise coverage the walk cannot deliver (or the check should also inspect `Attribute.attr`).

chunk_findings.detail: The guard only enforces its stated invariant ("an exemption ... in a test file would be a second place to forget") over files whose basename matches `test_*.py` and only over binding forms that are `Assign`/`AnnAssign` targets. Concretely: create `tests/_parity_exemptions.py` containing `NOT_EXPOSED = {"ddflow_x": "..."}`; `rglob("test_*.py")` never opens it. Same for `tests/conftest.py`, which is a perfectly natural home for a shared exemption mapping. Even when the table is re-introduced directly in a scanned file via `from tests._parity_exemptions import NOT_EXPOSED` (or `import tests._parity_exemptions as e`), the `ast.ImportFrom`/`ast.Import` alias nodes are neither `Assign` nor `AnnAssign`, so the inner loop `continue`s past them and `kept` stays empty. The earlier finding ("anything else that reintroduces a retired table passes silently") is therefore only partially answered by switching to `ast.walk` over assignment targets: the destructuring and function-body cases are fixed, but re-binding the same table by import, and placing it in any non-`test_*.py` file under `tests/`, still passes with no failure. A test that guards a data location should assert on the data's home (the Command registry) or scan the whole tests tree for bindings/imports of those names, not just assignment targets in `test_*.py`.

chunk_findings.detail: This still holds and the triage's probe does not answer it. The finding is about a *non-hashable* `method`; `.get(method)` hashes the key exactly like `__getitem__` does, so switching from indexing to `.get` only fixes the unknown-*string* case (no `KeyError`), not the crash for non-string JSON. Input `{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":7,"method":[]}`, or `{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":7,"method":{}}`, still reaches `self._METHODS.get([])` and raises `TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'` instead of the JSON-RPC error the old `==`-chain dispatcher returned (`_err(mid, -32601, ...)`). The cited probe, `test_a_method_that_is_not_a_known_string_is_method_not_found`, by its own name feeds a *string* method; a string is hashable and `.get` returns `None` for it, producing the same `-32601` response the pre-change code produced — so that test cannot distinguish the old from the new code and certainly cannot exercise the unhashable case. A guard such as `if not isinstance(method, str): return _err(mid, -32600, ...)` (or wrapping the lookup) is what would answer this, and no part of the shown diff does it. Severity stays LOW (malformed-client conformance), but it is a real behavior regression introduced by this change and remains unprobed.

chunk_findings.detail: The loop collects `n.id` for `ast.Name` nodes under each assignment target, and the inline comment claims "`x.A = ...` count". It does not: for an attribute assignment the target is an `ast.Attribute` whose base is an `ast.Name` and whose attribute is stored as a plain Python string in `Attribute.attr` (not a child AST node), so `ast.walk` over the target yields only the base name. Concrete input: a test file containing `import ddflow.surfaces.mcp as m` followed by `m.PROSE_TOOLS = {"ddflow_list": "still a table"}`. `ast.walk` over `Attribute(value=Name('m'), attr='PROSE_TOOLS')` yields `Name(id='m')` only; `m` is not in `_RETIRED_TABLES`, so `kept` stays empty and the guard passes even though an exemption table has been reintroduced as an attribute assignment — exactly the "second place to forget" the test exists to prevent. The comment should not promise coverage the walk cannot deliver (or the check should also inspect `Attribute.attr`).

chunk_findings.detail: The guard only enforces its stated invariant ("an exemption ... in a test file would be a second place to forget") over files whose basename matches `test_*.py` and only over binding forms that are `Assign`/`AnnAssign` targets. Concretely: create `tests/_parity_exemptions.py` containing `NOT_EXPOSED = {"ddflow_x": "..."}`; `rglob("test_*.py")` never opens it. Same for `tests/conftest.py`, which is a perfectly natural home for a shared exemption mapping. Even when the table is re-introduced directly in a scanned file via `from tests._parity_exemptions import NOT_EXPOSED` (or `import tests._parity_exemptions as e`), the `ast.ImportFrom`/`ast.Import` alias nodes are neither `Assign` nor `AnnAssign`, so the inner loop `continue`s past them and `kept` stays empty. The earlier finding ("anything else that reintroduces a retired table passes silently") is therefore only partially answered by switching to `ast.walk` over assignment targets: the destructuring and function-body cases are fixed, but re-binding the same table by import, and placing it in any non-`test_*.py` file under `tests/`, still passes with no failure. A test that guards a data location should assert on the data's home (the Command registry) or scan the whole tests tree for bindings/imports of those names, not just assignment targets in `test_*.py`.

chunk_findings.detail: `_staged_noun(staged, exports, rules)` never reads `rules`: the "rule file" branch is the final `else`, so it is returned not only when a rule file is staged but whenever no generated view and no exported document is staged. `_unrecorded_log_lines` — which takes that same `noun` plus the same `staged`/`exports` dicts — is likewise never given `rules`, so it has nothing to name in its remedy. Input that shows it: a working tree with a staged rule file (e.g. `.ddflow/rules/*.toml`), no staged view and no staged exported document, and an unstaged change under the event-log dir (`_unstaged_under` non-empty). `check_views` then builds the refusal with noun `"rule file"`, whose text is "a rule file is staged, but the event log it is rendered from has N change(s) … Stage both:", yet the help lines are `*remedy`, `*(["    ddflow render…"] if staged else [])`, `*([…ddflow export…] if exports else [])` and finally `"    git add " + " ".join(shlex.quote(p) for p in sorted({**staged, **exports}))` — with both dicts empty that last element is the literal string `    git add ` (empty pathspec, stages nothing), and the rule file the refusal is about is never listed or staged anywhere in the message. The presence of the unused `rules` parameter is itself the evidence that the rule-file case was meant to be handled by these helpers; it must either feed the noun condition or (together with `staged`/`exports`) be threaded into `_unrecorded_log_lines` so the emitted `git add` line selects the rule files instead of degenerating to an empty command.

Per the slice's own inventory the entry covers `_check_lease` (F 48), `check_views` (E 40) and `check_item_trailer` (E 34), while the only enforce work described is splitting `_check_lease` into a `(predicate, reason)` decision table ("F/E functions (enforce._check_lease, importer.plan_import) split"); `check_views` and `check_item_trailer` are not touched by this change and stay E-grade, which is worse than D. So the measured value for the module is 2, not 0. Running the pinned guard (`uv run pytest tests/test_architecture_guards.py -q`) will either fail (measured 2 > the now-absent/0 baseline) or, if a missing per-module file means "module not ratcheted", silently drop the ratchet for the two remaining D-or-worse functions. Either way this violates the slice rule "Lower every guard baseline you reduced in the SAME change" and the file's own "delete the file at zero" instruction: it must stay at the measured value (2) in this change, or the two remaining functions must actually be split here.

Given a tree with a staged ordinary document that is neither a generated view nor an exported document and with no `.ddflow/rules/*.toml` staged, the function still returns "rule file", and `_unrecorded_log_lines` (which was never handed `rules`) builds its remedy around a rule file the user did not stage. chunk_findings.detail: The function has an explicit "only a rule file is staged" case — `_staged_noun` falls through to `"rule file"` when `staged` and `exports` are both empty, and the message then reads "a rule file is staged, but the event log it is rendered from has N change(s)…". But the remedy is built exclusively from the two dicts that are empty in exactly that case: `"    git add " + " ".join(shlex.quote(p) for p in sorted({**staged, **exports}))`. Input: a tree with a staged `.ddflow/rules/*.toml`, an unstaged event-log shard, and no staged view/export (the case the noun exists for). The last line printed by `ddflow enforce` is then the literal `    git add ` with an empty pathspec — `git add` with no pathspec stages nothing and exits non-zero, and the rule file the message just named is never named in the remedy; the `ddflow render` / `ddflow export … --update` hints are skipped too. This is the earlier finding's substance, and its refutation does not answer it: the probe `git diff main -- ddflow/services/enforce.py | grep -n 'rule file'` only shows that the *string* survives the edit — it does not show that the rule-file path is passed into this function or into the `git add` set, and the code above shows it is not (`rules` is no longer a parameter, `{**staged, **exports}` is empty).

chunk_findings.detail: `lines += [*([""] if lines else []), *_wrong_views(log, fresh_cfg, staged)]` emits the blank separator as soon as `staged` is non-empty, i.e. *before* it knows whether `_wrong_views` returns anything; the export branch right below guards correctly (its separator is only reached inside `if bad:`). Input: a wrong staged rule file (`_wrong_rule_files` returns lines) together with a staged generated view that is byte-identical, so `_wrong_views` returns `[]` — the returned list ends with `""`, so `ddflow enforce`'s refusal text gains a trailing blank line, and if an export disagreement follows as well, the rule section and the export section are separated by two blank lines instead of one. The slice pins `ddflow enforce` output before/after on this tree, so a spurious empty line is a changed byte, not cosmetics.

chunk_findings.detail: The triage's probe (`git diff main -- ddflow/services/enforce.py | grep -n 'rule file'`) does not answer the finding: it only shows that the literal message text "rule file" occurs somewhere in the diff, which is exactly what the finding predicts (the branch is the fall-through `else`). It says nothing about whether `_staged_noun` ever consults the `rules` argument it is handed, nor about whether `_unrecorded_log_lines` is given `rules`. The described input therefore still misreports: with a staged file that is neither a rendered view nor an exported document (e.g. an ordinary `.md` picked up by `doc_globs`, or no rule file staged at all), `_staged_noun(staged, exports, rules)` falls through to the "rule file" branch, so the refusal names a rule file that was not staged, and `_unrecorded_log_lines` — which receives that noun plus the same `staged`/`exports` dicts but never `rules` — has nothing to substitute in its remedy. That is a user-visible wrong reason/remedy produced by the split of `_check_lease` into `(predicate, reason)` pairs, and a grep for the phrase cannot refute it; only showing that `rules` participates in the branch selection (or that the catch-all reason is unreachable for non-rule files) would.

chunk_findings.detail:
The `["Item"]` fallback is applied only to the list that is used to build the "missing trailer" message; the matching set `canon` is built from `keys` alone, and `checked` keeps a trailer only when `k.lower() in canon or k.lower() in words`. So when the required-key list is empty — the exact case the `or ["Item"]` fallback was written for — a commit message containing

    Item: P1.T3

yields `checked == []` (because `"item"` is in neither `canon` nor `words`), and `check_item_trailer` returns `_missing_trailer_verdict(["Item"], {})`. The remedy the hook prints tells the author to write an `Item: <id>` trailer, and writing that trailer is refused again with the same message, forever: with `[enforce] require_item_trailer = true` and `item_trailer_keys = []`, no commit can ever pass, including one carrying the very trailer the default names. The default has to be applied to the matching set as well (`keys = list(keys) or ["Item"]` before `canon`/`accepted` are built) or `canon` must be seeded with the fallback key.

chunk_findings.detail: This hunk deletes the "A finished task that an OPEN task depends on…" section (`_pull_in_needed(plan, deferred_done, held)`, `in_plan`, `ticked`, `plan.ticked_left_out = len(ticked)`, `_note_withheld(plan, ticked, [f.ident for f in closed …], held)`) from its former position *before* the cap check, and re-homes the cap check as the first statement of the new module-level `_cap_or_settle`. That block cannot have travelled with the cap check: `_cap_or_settle` is a module-level function (no closure over `plan_import`'s locals) and its signature carries no `closed` and no `held`, while `_pull_in_needed` takes `held` and `_note_withheld` takes both — so the deleted block either was dropped outright or now runs *after* `_cap_or_settle`. chunk_findings.detail:
The `["Item"]` fallback is applied only to the list that is used to build the "missing trailer" message; the matching set `canon` is built from `keys` alone, and `checked` keeps a trailer only when `k.lower() in canon or k.lower() in words`. So when the required-key list is empty — the exact case the `or ["Item"]` fallback was written for — a commit message containing

    Item: P1.T3

yields `checked == []` (because `"item"` is in neither `canon` nor `words`), and `check_item_trailer` returns `_missing_trailer_verdict(["Item"], {})`. The remedy the hook prints tells the author to write an `Item: <id>` trailer, and writing that trailer is refused again with the same message, forever: with `[enforce] require_item_trailer = true` and `item_trailer_keys = []`, no commit can ever pass, including one carrying the very trailer the default names. The default has to be applied to the matching set as well (`keys = list(keys) or ["Item"]` before `canon`/`accepted` are built) or `canon` must be seeded with the fallback key.
